Approach the holy God with reverence, clothed in his righteousness — and take up your appointed burden in his house, for no faithful service is overlooked by the God who counts every servant by name.

5.title: Laws on Uncleanness and Unfaithfulness
5.text: <sup>2</sup>“Command the people of Israel that they put out of the camp everyone who is leprous or has a discharge and everyone who is unclean through contact with the dead. <sup>3</sup>You shall put out both male and female, putting them outside the camp, that they may not defile their camp, in the midst of which I dwell.”
5.overview:
With the camp ordered and the servants assigned, chapter 5 turns to the purity of the camp itself. Because God dwells in the midst, the camp must be holy; the unclean are put outside, wrongs must be confessed and restored, and unfaithfulness in marriage is addressed by a solemn ordeal.

The governing reason is stated plainly: “in the midst of which I dwell.” The presence of God among his people is the reason for every command about purity. Holiness is not arbitrary fussiness but the necessary response to the nearness of a holy God.

The ordeal of bitter water in the latter half of the chapter is one of Scripture’s strangest passages, yet it reveals a God who defends the wronged, exposes hidden sin, and refuses to let secret unfaithfulness corrode his people. The God who sees in secret will bring every hidden thing to light.

For the Christian, the chapter presses two truths: that sin defiles the community where God dwells, and that there is a way of confession, restitution, and cleansing. And it points to Christ, who bore our uncleanness outside the camp (Heb 13:12), drank the bitter cup we deserved, and brings the defiled back into the dwelling of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Putting the Unclean Outside the Camp
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who are ceremonially unclean must be put outside the camp because God dwells in its midst.
verseByVerse.theology: The presence of God demands the purity of his dwelling place; holiness flows from his nearness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the unclean put outside the camp. Now: Christ bore our uncleanness outside the camp to bring us in.

verseByVerse.quote: “The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Command the people of Israel that they put out of the camp everyone who is leprous or has a discharge and everyone who is unclean through contact with the dead... that they may not defile their camp, in the midst of which I dwell.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: The reason is stated with breathtaking directness: “in the midst of which I dwell.” The presence of the holy God among his people is the ground of all these purity laws. Wenham notes that the three named impurities — leprosy, bodily discharge, and contact with the dead — are all associated with death and decay, the very opposite of the living God. Where the Author of life dwells, the marks of death must be put far off. This is not cruelty toward the afflicted but the logic of holiness; the camp is a sanctuary because God lives in it. Sproul stressed that we have largely lost the category of the holy, and passages like this recover it; the God who dwells with men is not tame, and his nearness reorders everything. Calvin observes that these external uncleannesses were appointed to teach an inward truth — that sin and corruption cannot dwell with God. The putting out of the unclean was a daily, visible sermon on the incompatibility of defilement with the divine presence. And the gospel turns the picture inside out: the One who is holiness itself went outside the camp, bearing our uncleanness (Heb 13:12), that we, the leprous and the dead in sin, might be brought in to dwell with God forever.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the people of Israel did so, and put them outside the camp; as the LORD said to Moses, so the people of Israel did.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Once more the refrain of obedience: “as the LORD said to Moses, so the people of Israel did.” Wenham notes that the opening chapters of Numbers repeatedly portray Israel obeying with exactness, a portrait of the ideal that will soon shatter against their rebellions. Here the people comply even with a hard command — to put out from among them the leprous, the discharging, the defiled, perhaps their own family members. Obedience to God’s holiness is costly; it touches the tenderest relationships. Calvin observes that true reverence for God will sometimes require painful separations, and that the people’s compliance shows a right fear of the LORD. Yet the verse also stirs compassion, for to be put outside the camp was a grievous thing — to be cut off from the worshiping community, from the presence, from the warmth of belonging. Ferguson noted that this very pathos prepares us for the gospel, where the One who deserved the innermost place took the outermost, “suffered outside the gate” (Heb 13:12), so that the outcast might come home. The people’s sad obedience in putting out the unclean is answered, generations later, by the Savior who goes out to the leper, touches the untouchable, and brings the excluded back into the dwelling of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When a person wrongs another and so breaks faith with the LORD, they must confess, make full restitution, and add a fifth.
verseByVerse.theology: Sin against a neighbor is sin against God; true repentance includes confession and concrete restitution.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: full restitution with a fifth added. Now: gospel repentance bears the fruit of confession and restored relationships.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Speak to the people of Israel, When a man or woman commits any of the sins that people commit by breaking faith with the LORD, and that person realizes his guilt, he shall confess his sin that he has committed. And he shall make full restitution for his wrong, adding a fifth to it and giving it to him to whom he did the wrong.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: A profound truth is embedded here: a sin against one’s neighbor is described as “breaking faith with the LORD.” Wenham notes that horizontal wrongs are vertical offenses; to defraud a brother is to be unfaithful to God. David grasped this when, having sinned against Bathsheba and Uriah, he cried, “Against you, you only, have I sinned” (Ps 51:4). True repentance, the passage shows, has three marks: realizing one’s guilt, confessing the specific sin, and making full restitution with a fifth added. Keller observed that biblical repentance is never merely a feeling; it issues in concrete amends. The added fifth ensures that repentance costs the offender more than the original gain, killing the calculus of profitable sin. Calvin stresses that confession without restitution is hollow; the truly penitent heart does not merely apologize but repairs. Zacchaeus embodied this when, gripped by grace, he restored fourfold (Luke 19:8). The gospel does not abolish restitution but fulfills its spirit; the forgiven heart longs to make right what it broke. Here, in the wilderness law, is a beautiful anatomy of repentance that the church has too often softened — guilt acknowledged, sin named, neighbor restored, and God himself honored in the mending of the wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: “But if the man has no next of kin to whom restitution may be made for the wrong, the restitution for wrong shall go to the LORD for the priest, in addition to the ram of atonement... And every contribution, all the holy donations of the people of Israel, which they bring to the priest, shall be his.”
verseByVerse.commentary: What if the wronged party has died and left no kinsman to receive restitution? The debt does not simply evaporate; it is paid “to the LORD for the priest.” Wenham notes the principle: a wrong against a neighbor is ultimately a debt to God, and so where no human creditor remains, God himself receives the restitution. There is no such thing as a victimless or forgotten sin; the books of heaven keep every account. Calvin observes that this provision closes every loophole by which a guilty conscience might excuse itself — even the death of the offended cannot cancel the obligation. The ram of atonement accompanies the restitution, for restitution to the neighbor does not by itself make peace with God; sacrifice is still required. Here the two dimensions of sin are held together: the horizontal repaired by restitution, the vertical covered by atonement. Sproul saw in this the wholeness of biblical reconciliation — we must both make things right with men and be made right with God, and the latter requires blood. And the gospel gathers both: Christ is our ram of atonement, and in him we are moved to make restitution to those we have wronged, knowing that even the debts we can no longer repay to men are answered in the One who paid all to God on our behalf.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–31 — The Ordeal of Bitter Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A husband suspecting his wife of unfaithfulness brings her to the priest for a solemn ordeal that exposes guilt or vindicates innocence.
verseByVerse.theology: The God who sees in secret defends the wronged and brings hidden sin to light, refusing to let unfaithfulness corrode his people.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: bitter water to test hidden unfaithfulness. Now: every hidden thing will be brought to light before the One who judges righteously.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Speak to the people of Israel, If any man’s wife goes astray and breaks faith with him... and the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife... then the man shall bring his wife to the priest and bring the offering required of her.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: The law turns to one of the most painful threats to a community where God dwells: the corrosive suspicion of marital unfaithfulness. Where adultery is hidden and unprovable, the marriage festers in jealousy and the camp is poisoned by secret sin. Wenham notes that this ordeal, unique in the Pentateuch, actually functions to protect the woman; in a patriarchal world where a suspicious husband might otherwise take matters into his own hands, the matter is removed from his power and placed before God. The accused is not left to mob justice or domestic violence but brought to the sanctuary, where God himself will judge. Calvin observes that God here addresses the secret sins that human courts cannot reach; what no witness can prove, the all-seeing God can expose. The “spirit of jealousy” is acknowledged as a real and destructive force, capable of tormenting a marriage whether the suspicion is true or false. By providing a divine resolution, the law refuses to let the matter remain a festering wound. The principle endures: God cares about the integrity of marriage and the purity of his people, and he will not allow hidden unfaithfulness to corrode the community in which he dwells. He sees, and he will judge righteously.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the priest shall bring her near and set her before the LORD. And the priest shall take holy water in an earthenware vessel and take some of the dust that is on the floor of the tabernacle... And the priest shall make the woman take the oath of the curse... ‘may this water that brings the curse pass into your bowels and make your womb swell and your thigh fall away.’ And the woman shall say, ‘Amen, Amen.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: The woman is set “before the LORD,” for this is no human verdict but a divine one. The ingredients are humble — holy water, dust from the tabernacle floor, the written curse washed into the cup — yet the outcome rests entirely in God’s hands. Wenham notes that the ordeal contains no natural mechanism of harm; the water itself is harmless. Any effect must come directly from God, making this not a superstitious trial by ordeal but an appeal to the omniscient Judge. The woman’s double “Amen, Amen” is striking; she submits herself to the judgment of God, placing her vindication or condemnation in his hands alone. Sproul observed that this is the posture every soul must finally take — standing before the LORD, owning that he knows the secret truth of our hearts. Calvin notes that the dust from the floor of the tabernacle links the ordeal to the very dwelling of God; she is judged in his presence, by his power. The procedure dramatizes a permanent reality: every hidden thing is open before God, and one day all will stand before him and answer. The trembling “Amen, Amen” of the accused woman foreshadows the day when every knee will bow and every secret be laid bare before the One who judges the living and the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: “Then the priest shall write these curses in a book and wash them off into the water of bitterness... and shall make the woman drink the water... And if she has defiled herself and has broken faith with her husband, the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain... But if the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, then she shall be free and shall conceive children.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The verdict belongs to God alone. If guilty, the woman suffers the curse; if innocent, she is vindicated and blessed — “she shall be free and shall conceive children.” Wenham notes the mercy in the outcome: the innocent woman is not merely cleared but blessed with fruitfulness, her honor publicly restored before the community that suspected her. The ordeal thus has the power to clear the wrongly accused as surely as to expose the guilty. Calvin observes that God here shows himself the defender of the innocent and the exposer of the secret sinner; nothing escapes his all-seeing eye. There is a sobering beauty in the washed-off curses being drunk — the written judgment internalized, swallowed, made real in the body. Sproul reflected that sin always comes home to the sinner; what is hidden will be tasted. Yet for the Christian, the bitter cup of curse points beyond itself. Ferguson saw the shadow of the cross here: Christ, the truly innocent One, drank the bitter cup of the curse we deserved (Matt 26:39; Gal 3:13), taking into himself the judgment our unfaithfulness merited. The water of bitterness that would expose the guilty is answered by the cup of suffering the sinless Savior drained to the dregs, that we, the faithless, might be declared clean and made fruitful in him.

verseByVerse.quote: “This is the law in cases of jealousy, when a wife, though under her husband’s authority, goes astray and defiles herself... The man shall be free from iniquity, but the woman shall bear her iniquity.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The law concludes by summarizing the ordeal and clarifying that the husband who brings a genuine suspicion to God is “free from iniquity” — he has not sinned by submitting the matter to the LORD rather than acting in vengeance. Wenham notes the protective function once more: by channeling jealousy into a sacred process, the law prevents both private retribution and the slow poison of unresolved suspicion. The phrase “the woman shall bear her iniquity” acknowledges that, where guilt is real, judgment is just; God does not wink at unfaithfulness. Yet the whole procedure has removed the verdict from human hands and placed it in God’s, where alone the secret truth is known. Calvin draws the enduring lesson: the integrity of marriage matters to God, and unfaithfulness, even when undetectable by men, is fully seen by him. The covenant of marriage images the covenant between God and his people, and Israel’s frequent “breaking faith” with the LORD is described throughout Scripture as spiritual adultery. This chapter, then, quietly indicts the whole nation; the people who would soon prove unfaithful to their divine Husband are warned here of the God who sees all and judges all. And it magnifies the grace of the gospel, where the unfaithful bride is not destroyed but redeemed, washed, and presented spotless by the love of Christ her Husband (Eph 5:25–27).

5.theology:
Holiness Because God Dwells. The unclean are put outside the camp “in the midst of which I dwell.” Every purity command flows from the presence of the holy God. Where God lives, the marks of sin and death cannot remain.

Repentance That Restores. True repentance confesses the specific sin, makes full restitution with a fifth added, and honors God in mending the wrong. Sin against a neighbor is breaking faith with the LORD; gospel repentance bears concrete fruit.

The God Who Sees in Secret. The ordeal of bitter water reveals a God who exposes hidden sin, defends the innocent, and refuses to let unfaithfulness corrode his people. Every secret thing will be brought to light before the righteous Judge.
5.examples:
Then: The leprous were put outside the camp, wrongs were restored with a fifth added, and the bitter water exposed hidden unfaithfulness — all because the holy God dwelt in Israel’s midst.

Now: Christ went outside the camp bearing your uncleanness, drank the bitter cup of curse you deserved, and brings the defiled home to dwell with God. Walk in the light, confess your sins, make things right with those you have wronged, and rest in the One who knows every secret and yet declares you clean.

6.title: The Nazirite Vow and the Priestly Blessing
6.text: <sup>24</sup>“The LORD bless you and keep you; <sup>25</sup>the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; <sup>26</sup>the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace.”
6.overview:
Chapter 6 gives us two of the most beautiful provisions in all the Law: the Nazirite vow of total consecration, and the priestly benediction by which God puts his name upon his people. Together they answer the question raised by chapter 5 — how can a sinful people dwell with a holy God? By consecration and by blessing.

The Nazirite vow allowed any Israelite, man or woman, to draw near to the intensity of consecration normally reserved for priests. Abstaining from the vine, leaving the hair uncut, avoiding all contact with death, the Nazirite was a living picture of wholehearted devotion to the LORD.

The chapter then rises to its summit in the Aaronic blessing — three lines, each beginning with the covenant name, each ascending in glory: blessing and keeping, shining face and grace, lifted countenance and peace. Wenham notes that this is the priest placing the very name of God upon Israel.

Both consecration and blessing find their fulfillment in Christ. He is the perfectly consecrated One, the true Nazirite of heart, who never touched the death of sin; and he is the great High Priest who, lifting his hands at Bethany (Luke 24:50–51), blessed his people and ascended — the face of God shining upon us forever in him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Nazirite Vow of Consecration
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Any Israelite may take a vow of special consecration, abstaining from the vine, leaving the hair uncut, and avoiding all contact with the dead.
verseByVerse.theology: Total devotion to the LORD is open to all his people, not priests alone; consecration touches every part of life.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Nazirite set apart by visible signs. Now: every believer called to wholehearted consecration to God.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When either a man or a woman makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD, he shall separate himself from wine and strong drink... He shall eat nothing that is produced by the grapevine, not even the seeds or the skins.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: The word “Nazirite” means “separated one,” and the vow is open to “either a man or a woman” — a striking democratization of holiness. Wenham notes that the intense consecration normally reserved for priests is here made available to any Israelite who desires to draw near. Holiness is not the preserve of a clerical caste; the longing to be wholly the LORD’s may seize the heart of any believer. The first sign is abstinence from the vine in every form, even seeds and skins. Calvin observes that the renunciation of wine, the symbol of earthly joy and feasting, signifies a heart fixed on a higher joy — the LORD himself. The Nazirite forgoes a legitimate good as a sign of total devotion, a visible parable that God is his exceeding joy. There is no suggestion that wine is evil; rather, the Nazirite surrenders it as an offering of love. Keller noted that consecration often means laying down good things, not merely bad ones, to declare that God is better. The vow teaches that devotion to God may call us to a glad relinquishment, holding loosely even lawful pleasures for the sake of nearness to him. And it anticipates the Son who said, “I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until... I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom” (Matt 26:29).

verseByVerse.quote: “All the days of his vow of separation, no razor shall touch his head. Until the time is completed for which he separates himself to the LORD, he shall be holy. He shall let the locks of hair of his head grow long.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The second sign is the uncut hair, the most visible mark of the Nazirite. Wenham notes that the long, untouched hair was a public banner of consecration, declaring to all who saw it that this person belonged wholly to the LORD. The growing locks were a living, visible token of a vow taken and kept. Calvin observes that the outward sign was meant to nourish inward devotion; the Nazirite could not forget his consecration, for he wore it on his head. There is something profound in this visible separation — holiness made tangible, devotion worn openly. Samson, Samuel, and John the Baptist all bore the marks of lifelong Nazirite consecration, set apart from the womb. The hair declared, “I am not my own.” Ferguson noted that the Christian, too, is called to a visible consecration, not by uncut hair but by a transformed life that openly testifies, “I belong to the Lord.” The phrase “he shall be holy” summarizes the whole; the Nazirite is, for the days of his vow, a walking emblem of what all Israel was called to be — a people set apart, marked out, belonging to God. And the truest Nazirite of heart was Jesus, separated to the Father in every fiber, holy in a way no razor or vow could signify, wholly the LORD’s from eternity to eternity.

verseByVerse.quote: “All the days that he separates himself to the LORD he shall not go near a dead body. Not even for his father or for his mother, for brother or sister, if they die, shall he make himself unclean, because his separation to God is on his head. All the days of his separation he is holy to the LORD.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The third sign is the most demanding: the Nazirite must avoid all contact with death, even the death of his nearest kin. Wenham notes that this requirement equals or exceeds that of the high priest himself (Lev 21:11); the Nazirite stands in the closest possible relation to the living God, and death — the great enemy and the mark of sin’s curse — must not touch him. To forgo the funeral of one’s own father or mother for the sake of consecration is a wrenching cost, yet the principle is clear: devotion to the living God takes precedence even over the deepest natural bonds. Sproul observed that Christ pressed a similar radical priority when he said, “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt 8:22). The Nazirite’s separation from death is a vivid picture of holiness as the embrace of life and the rejection of all that belongs to the realm of death. Calvin draws the gospel line: the Nazirite who could not touch death points to Christ, the truly consecrated One, who never contracted the defilement of sin’s death in his soul, yet who in love willingly went into death itself to conquer it. He touched our death and was not defiled but rather destroyed its power, that we who were dead might be made alive and consecrated to God forever.

verseByVerse.quote: “And if any man dies very suddenly beside him and he defiles his consecrated head, then he shall shave his head on the day of his cleansing... and the priest shall make atonement for him... and he shall separate himself to the LORD for the days of his separation and bring a male lamb a year old for a guilt offering. But the previous period shall be void, because his separation was defiled.”
verseByVerse.commentary: What if death intrudes accidentally, beyond the Nazirite’s control? Even then the consecration is broken, the previous days are void, and atonement must be made. Wenham notes the severity: even unintended defilement nullifies the vow and requires sacrifice. This teaches the exacting nature of holiness — it is not measured merely by intention but by reality; defilement defiles, whether sought or suffered. Yet mercy is woven in: there is a way back. Atonement is provided, the head is reshaved, and the vow may begin afresh. Calvin observes that God here teaches both the seriousness of impurity and the availability of restoration. The guilt offering acknowledges that even involuntary defilement is no light thing in the presence of the holy God. Sproul reflected that this guards against the modern presumption that only deliberate sins matter; before God, all defilement is real and must be cleansed. But the gospel comfort shines: where the Nazirite’s broken consecration could be restored only by sacrifice and a fresh start, Christ has secured a consecration that cannot be voided. He is the Nazirite whose devotion was never broken, whose perfect consecration is credited to us, so that our standing before God rests not on our unbroken vows but on his. When death intruded upon him, it did not defile him; it was swallowed up in his victory, securing for us an unbreakable holiness in him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Completion of the Vow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the days of separation are fulfilled, the Nazirite brings offerings, shaves his head, and burns the hair on the altar.
verseByVerse.theology: Consecration culminates in joyful sacrifice and offering; the dedicated life is given back to God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the completed vow sealed with sacrifice. Now: the consecrated life offered to God as a living sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: “And this is the law for the Nazirite, when the time of his separation has been completed: he shall be brought to the entrance of the tent of meeting, and he shall bring his gift to the LORD, one male lamb a year old without blemish for a burnt offering, and one ewe lamb a year old without blemish as a sin offering, and one ram without blemish as a peace offering...”
verseByVerse.commentary: The completion of the vow is no quiet affair but a rich procession of offerings — burnt, sin, and peace offerings together. Wenham notes that the burnt offering signifies total devotion, the sin offering acknowledges remaining sinfulness, and the peace offering celebrates fellowship with God. Even the most consecrated Israelite, at the height of his devotion, must bring a sin offering; no human consecration is so pure as to need no atonement. Calvin observes this humbling truth: the Nazirite’s vow, however earnest, does not render him sinless, and he ends his consecration confessing his need for the blood. There is gospel wisdom here — our best devotion is still imperfect and must be covered by sacrifice. Yet the peace offering crowns the sequence, for the consecrated life issues in joyful communion with God and a shared meal of fellowship. Sproul observed that the Christian life follows the same shape: total dedication, ongoing repentance, and abiding fellowship, all resting on sacrifice. The Nazirite, having drawn near in special devotion, does not boast in his achievement but lays it all at the altar, acknowledging that even his holiness is accepted only through blood. And every offering points to Christ, our burnt offering of perfect devotion, our sin offering, and our peace, in whom alone our consecration is received by God.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the Nazirite shall shave his consecrated head at the entrance of the tent of meeting and shall take the hair from his consecrated head and put it on the fire that is under the sacrifice of the peace offering... This is the law of the Nazirite. But if he vows an offering to the LORD above his Nazirite vow... he shall do according to the vow that he vows.”
verseByVerse.commentary: At the vow’s completion, the Nazirite shaves the consecrated hair — the very emblem of his separation — and burns it on the altar fire. Wenham notes the striking symbolism: the sign of his devotion is offered up to God in the flames, the consecration given wholly back to the One to whom it was dedicated. Nothing of the vow is kept as a trophy; it all ascends in smoke to God. Calvin observes that this teaches the end of all true consecration — not self-display but the offering of the self entirely to the LORD. The hair, grown for months or years as a public mark of holiness, is not preserved as a relic of personal achievement but consumed on the altar, that God alone might receive the glory. There is deep wisdom against spiritual pride here; the most visible badge of devotion is reduced to ash before the LORD. The closing provision, that one may vow “above” the required offerings, shows that devotion may freely give beyond the minimum; love is not content with the bare command. The Christian parallel is plain: we present ourselves as “a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God” (Rom 12:1), offering up not merely the symbols but the substance of our lives, keeping nothing back, that God alone may be glorified in our consecration.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives Aaron and his sons the words by which they are to bless Israel, putting the divine name upon the people.
verseByVerse.theology: God himself is the source of all blessing; the priest is only the channel of the name and favor of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the priest pronouncing God’s name over Israel. Now: the face of God shines upon us forever in Christ, our great High Priest.

verseByVerse.quote: “The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, Thus you shall bless the people of Israel: you shall say to them...’”
verseByVerse.commentary: Before the words of blessing, note who commands them. The blessing is not Aaron’s invention but God’s gift; the priest does not bestow his own favor but conveys God’s. Wenham notes that this is the climactic provision of the opening chapters — having ordered, counted, consecrated, and purified his people, God now puts his blessing upon them. The priest is merely the appointed channel; the source is God himself. Calvin observes the great comfort in this: the words spoken over Israel are not pious wishes but the very pledge of God, who stands behind the blessing to fulfill it. When the priest spoke, God blessed. Sproul stressed that the benediction is no empty formality but an actual conveyance of divine favor through God’s appointed means. There is profound pastoral weight here for the church; when the minister pronounces the blessing of God over the gathered people, it is God’s own word of favor, not the minister’s. The whole movement of these chapters has been toward this moment — the holy God, dwelling in the midst of his ordered people, now lifting his hand to bless. And it anticipates the One who, having accomplished all, “lifted up his hands and blessed them” at Bethany (Luke 24:50), the great High Priest pronouncing the final, unbreakable benediction over his church.

verseByVerse.quote: “The LORD bless you and keep you;”
verseByVerse.commentary: The blessing rises in three ascending lines, and each begins with the covenant name, YHWH — “the LORD.” Wenham notes the deliberate structure: three lines of increasing length, the divine name three times, a crescendo of grace. The first line pairs blessing with keeping: God grants good and guards it. To be blessed is to receive God’s favor and gifts; to be kept is to have that favor preserved, defended, secured. Calvin observes that the two belong together — what use is blessing if it slips away? God not only gives but guards; he is the keeper of his people. The Psalter takes up this very note: “The LORD is your keeper... he will keep your life” (Ps 121:5–7). Sproul reflected on the security of the saints embedded here; the God who blesses is the God who keeps, and none can pluck his own from his hand (John 10:28–29). There is tender shepherd-love in this opening line. The God who has just ordered his people for war and march now assures them that he will both enrich and protect them. For the Christian, the words are fulfilled in Christ, in whom every spiritual blessing is ours (Eph 1:3) and by whom we are “kept by the power of God through faith” (1 Pet 1:5). To be blessed and kept by the LORD is the foundation of all assurance and the first note of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: “the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you;”
verseByVerse.commentary: The second line ascends to the radiance of God’s face. Wenham notes the imagery of a shining countenance — the warm, beaming favor of a face turned toward the beloved. To have God’s face shine upon you is to know his smile, his pleasure, his delighted regard. The opposite, a hidden face, is the terror of judgment (Ps 13:1; 27:9). Here God promises to turn his face toward his people in grace. Keller observed that the deepest human need is to know we are seen with delight by the One whose opinion ultimately matters; here is that need answered by God himself. The line pairs the shining face with grace — unmerited favor — for God shines upon his people not because they have earned his smile but because he is gracious. Calvin stresses that all of God’s goodness flows from his free grace; the shining face is the face of mercy, not merit. Sproul reflected that the whole gospel is the shining of God’s face upon undeserving sinners through Jesus Christ. Indeed, Paul tells us that “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God” shines “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Cor 4:6). The face of God, once hidden by our sin, now beams upon us in the face of his Son. To live under the shining, gracious face of God is heaven begun on earth.

verseByVerse.quote: “the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The blessing reaches its summit in peace — shalom, the comprehensive flourishing of life under God’s favor. Wenham notes that this third and longest line crowns the benediction; everything has been moving toward peace. To “lift up his countenance” is to look upon his people with attentive favor, the very opposite of turning away in displeasure. And the result is shalom — not mere absence of conflict but wholeness, completeness, the deep well-being of being right with God and at rest in his love. Calvin observes that this peace is the sum of all blessings, the goal toward which the whole blessing aspires; where God lifts up his face, there is nothing lacking. Sproul stressed that true peace is found only in reconciliation with God, and that this final word of the benediction is fulfilled in the gospel of “peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom 5:1). Keller noted that the world chases a thousand counterfeit peaces, but the only lasting shalom is the smile of God resting upon a forgiven soul. The benediction thus moves from blessing and keeping, through the shining and gracious face, to the lifted countenance and peace — an ascending ladder of grace, each rung higher than the last. And it finds its perfect fulfillment in Christ, our peace (Eph 2:14), who made peace by the blood of his cross and gives a peace the world cannot give (John 14:27).

verseByVerse.quote: “So shall they put my name upon the people of Israel, and I will bless them.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter closes with God’s own commentary on the blessing: through these words the priests “put my name upon the people of Israel.” Wenham notes the staggering significance — the threefold repetition of YHWH in the blessing is not incidental; the benediction is the placing of God’s own name upon his people, marking them as belonging to him. To bear the name of God is to be claimed by him, owned, identified as his treasured possession. And God adds his pledge: “I will bless them.” The priest speaks the words, but God himself performs the blessing; the human voice is the channel, the divine will is the power. Calvin observes that this guarantees the blessing is no empty ceremony; God binds himself to make good what his priest pronounces. Sproul reflected that to have the name of God placed upon us is the highest dignity a creature can know. The New Testament gathers this up: in baptism we are marked with the name of the triune God (Matt 28:19), and the redeemed will at last have his name written on their foreheads (Rev 22:4). The whole opening movement of Numbers — counting, ordering, consecrating, purifying, blessing — culminates here, in a people who bear the name of God and live under his pledged blessing. And it all flows to us through Christ, the great High Priest who has put the Father’s name upon us forever, and whose lifted hands at his ascension sealed the benediction over his church for all eternity.

6.theology:
Consecration for All. The Nazirite vow opened priestly intensity of devotion to any Israelite, man or woman. Holiness is not the preserve of a clerical caste; every believer is called to wholehearted, visible, costly consecration to the LORD, even relinquishing good things to declare that God is better.

God Is the Source of Blessing. The priest only pronounces; God himself blesses. The threefold benediction puts the divine name upon his people, an ascending ladder of grace — blessing and keeping, shining face and grace, lifted countenance and peace — all guaranteed by God’s pledge, “I will bless them.”

Christ the Consecrated High Priest. Jesus is the true Nazirite, wholly the Father’s, who touched our death and conquered it; and he is the great High Priest who, lifting his hands at Bethany, blessed his people. In his face the light of God shines upon us forever, and he is our peace.
6.examples:
Then: Israelites took the Nazirite vow to be wholly the LORD’s, and Aaron lifted his hands to put God’s name upon the people, pronouncing blessing, grace, and peace.

Now: You are called to consecration — to hold even good things loosely for the joy of nearness to God. And you live under a greater benediction: the face of God shines upon you in Christ, your great High Priest, who has put the Father’s name upon you and given you a peace the world cannot take away.

7.title: The Offerings of the Chiefs: God Receives Each One
7.text: <sup>1</sup>On the day when Moses had finished setting up the tabernacle and had anointed and consecrated it with all its furnishings... <sup>2</sup>the chiefs of Israel, heads of their fathers’ houses, who were the chiefs of the tribes... came and brought their offerings before the LORD.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is the longest chapter in Numbers, and at first glance the most tedious: twelve tribal chiefs bring offerings for the dedication of the altar, and their identical gifts are recorded twelve separate times, day by day. Yet the very repetition is the sermon.

God could have summarized: “each chief brought the same offering.” Instead, the Spirit lingers over every silver plate, every basin, every spoon, every animal, naming each chief and his gift on his own day. Why? Because God receives each worshiper individually. Your offering is not lost in the crowd.

Wenham notes the deliberate equality: every tribe brings exactly the same gift, so that none is greater or lesser before God. And yet each is recorded separately, so that none is overlooked. Here is the gospel paradox — we are equal before God, yet known and loved individually.

The chapter closes with God speaking to Moses from above the mercy seat, between the cherubim. The dedication of the altar leads to communion; the gifts of the people open the way to the voice of God. And it all points to Christ, in whom every offering finds its meaning, and through whom God speaks to us still.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Wagons and Oxen for the Levites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the tabernacle’s dedication, the chiefs bring wagons and oxen, distributed to the Gershonites and Merarites for transport.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides means for the service he commands; the gifts of the people equip the work of his house.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: wagons given for carrying the tabernacle. Now: God supplies what his church needs to bear his glory forward.

verseByVerse.quote: “On the day when Moses had finished setting up the tabernacle... the chiefs of Israel... brought their offerings before the LORD, six wagons and twelve oxen, a wagon for every two of the chiefs, and for each one an ox.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The dedication of the tabernacle overflows into the glad generosity of the people’s leaders. Wenham notes that this chapter flashes back to the day the tabernacle was first set up (Exod 40), gathering the chiefs’ offerings into one account. The leaders set the pace of giving; the chiefs come first, modeling sacrificial devotion for the whole nation. The six wagons and twelve oxen are eminently practical gifts — the means of transporting the heavy tabernacle through the wilderness. Calvin observes that true devotion is not only spiritual but concrete; love for God’s house expresses itself in tangible provision for its needs. The gifts are not flashy religious trinkets but working equipment, freely offered for the Lord’s service. Sproul reflected that godly leadership leads in generosity; those who would direct God’s people must first give themselves and their goods. There is beauty in the voluntary nature of these offerings — they are brought, not extracted. The chiefs perceive a need and meet it gladly. The Christian parallel is rich: God’s work requires provision, and he stirs the hearts of his people, especially their leaders, to supply it freely. What the chiefs offered for the tabernacle’s transport, believers offer still for the advance of Christ’s kingdom, knowing that the God who commands the work also provides the means.

verseByVerse.quote: “Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Accept these from them, that they may be used in the service of the tent of meeting, and give them to the Levites, to each man according to his service.’ ... two wagons and four oxen he gave to the sons of Gershon... and four wagons and eight oxen he gave to the sons of Merari... But to the sons of Kohath he gave none, because they were charged with the service of the holy things that had to be carried on the shoulder.”
verseByVerse.commentary: God accepts the gifts and directs their distribution with perfect wisdom, “to each man according to his service.” Wenham notes the careful proportion: the Merarites, who carry the heavy frames and bases, receive twice the wagons of the Gershonites, who carry the lighter curtains. God matches provision to burden. But the most striking detail is that the Kohathites receive no wagons at all, “because they were charged with the service of the holy things that had to be carried on the shoulder.” The ark and the sacred vessels were never to be carted; they were to be borne on the shoulders of consecrated men, on poles, with reverent care. Sproul drew the sober lesson, fulfilled tragically when David later put the ark on a new cart and Uzzah died (2 Sam 6): the holiest things demand the most careful handling, not the most convenient. Calvin observes that God’s provision is never one-size-fits-all; he gives wagons where wagons are fitting and withholds them where reverence requires the shoulder. There is gospel dignity here — to bear the holiest burden on one’s own shoulder is a higher honor than to be relieved by a wagon. The Kohathites carried the throne of God on their backs, a living parable of taking up one’s cross to bear the presence of God into the world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–88 — The Twelve Days of Offerings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For twelve days, one chief each day brings an identical offering for the dedication of the altar; each is recorded separately.
verseByVerse.theology: God receives each worshiper individually; the repetition declares that no offering is lost in the crowd, and all are equal before him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: twelve identical gifts, each named and recorded. Now: every act of worship seen, valued, and received by God.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the chiefs offered offerings for the dedication of the altar on the day it was anointed; and the chiefs offered their offering before the altar. And the LORD said to Moses, ‘They shall offer their offerings, one chief each day, for the dedication of the altar.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: God ordains the pattern: “one chief each day.” He could have received all twelve offerings at once, in a single grand ceremony. Instead he spreads them over twelve days, giving each chief his own day, his own moment before the altar. Wenham notes that this deliberate individualizing is the theological heart of the chapter. The dedication of the altar — the place of atonement, where heaven and earth meet — is honored by the unhurried, personal devotion of each leader in turn. Keller observed that God is never in a hurry to process his worshipers in bulk; he delights to receive each one personally, as if there were no other. There is profound pastoral comfort here for any believer who feels lost in the vast crowd of the church. God gives you your own day, your own audience, your own welcome at the altar. Calvin reflects that the protracted ceremony magnified the importance of the altar and the seriousness of approaching God; the dedication was no trifling matter to be rushed. Twelve days of focused devotion declared that the meeting place between God and his people is worthy of patient, individual honor. And it points to the cross, the true altar, where the one offering of Christ secured for each of his people a personal welcome into the presence of God.

verseByVerse.quote: “He who offered his offering the first day was Nahshon the son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah. And his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels... both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb... for a burnt offering...”
verseByVerse.commentary: Judah goes first, as in the camp and the march, and Nahshon — ancestor of David and of Christ (Matt 1:4) — leads the offering. Wenham notes the rich completeness of each chief’s gift: silver vessels for grain offerings, a golden dish of incense, and animals for burnt, sin, and peace offerings. Every dimension of worship is represented: dedication, atonement, and fellowship. The silver plate “full of fine flour mixed with oil” speaks of consecrated provision; the golden dish of incense pictures prayer ascending to God; the burnt offering signifies total devotion, the sin offering atonement, the peace offering communion. Calvin observes that the comprehensiveness of the offering teaches that we are to give ourselves to God wholly — body, prayer, and substance. That the messianic line of Judah leads the procession is no accident; the tribe of the coming King heads the dedication of the altar, as if to say that all true worship will one day center on the Lion of Judah. Sproul reflected that every element of these offerings finds its meaning in Christ — he is the incense of perfect prayer, the bread of consecrated life, the burnt offering of total devotion, the sin offering, and our peace. Nahshon’s gift, first of the twelve, opens a procession that quietly proclaims the gospel in silver, gold, and blood.

verseByVerse.quote: “On the second day Nethanel the son of Zuar, the chief of Issachar, made an offering... [and so each chief in turn, day by day, through all twelve tribes — Zebulun, Reuben, Simeon, Gad, Ephraim, Manasseh, Benjamin, Dan, Asher, Naphtali — each bringing the identical offering of silver plate and basin, golden dish, and animals].”
verseByVerse.commentary: For seventy verses the Spirit records what could have been said in one: each chief brought the same offering. The modern reader is tempted to skim, but Wenham insists the repetition is the message. God lingers over each gift, each name, each day, refusing to summarize. Why? Because to summarize would be to lose the individual, and God loses no one. Keller captured it: in the kingdom of God you are never a statistic, never a face in the crowd; you are known, named, received one by one. The identical nature of the offerings teaches equality — Judah’s gift is no greater than Naphtali’s, the firstborn’s no more accepted than the handmaid’s son’s; all are equal at the altar. Yet the separate recording teaches individuality — none is merged into a faceless mass; each stands alone before God. Calvin marvels that God condescends to record the same words twelve times rather than overlook a single worshiper. Here is the gospel paradox: we are leveled to perfect equality before God, for all come on the same terms, by the same blood; yet we are known with perfect particularity, each loved as if the only one. The tedium of these verses, rightly read, becomes a hymn — that the God of all the earth bends low to receive each child by name, day after day, gift after gift, forgetting none.

verseByVerse.quote: “This was the dedication offering for the altar, on the day when it was anointed, from the chiefs of Israel: twelve silver plates, twelve silver basins, twelve golden dishes... all the gold of the dishes 120 shekels... all the oxen for the burnt offering twelve bulls... and the male goats for a sin offering twelve. This was the dedication offering for the altar after it was anointed.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Now, after the patient enumeration of each gift, the totals are tallied — twelve of everything, the sum of the tribes’ devotion. Wenham notes the satisfying completeness: nothing is missing, every tribe has brought its full and equal share, and the grand total testifies to a united, generous people. The number twelve, the number of the tribes, the number of fullness in Israel, recurs in every category, a seal of the whole nation’s participation. Calvin observes that the careful summing demonstrates God’s exact accounting; not one plate or basin or goat is forgotten in the reckoning. The dedication of the altar is complete, sealed by the offerings of all Israel. There is a beautiful corporate dimension here that balances the individual: each chief gave personally, yet together they form one complete and harmonious whole. Sproul reflected that this is the picture of the church — many members, each known individually, yet together forming one body, one offering, one people of God. The altar, now dedicated by the gifts of the whole nation, stands ready as the meeting place between God and Israel. And the twelvefold offering anticipates the day when a great multitude from every tribe and tongue will bring their worship to the throne, each known by name, all united in one song to the Lamb who was slain.

verseByVerse.ref: v. 89 — God Speaks from the Mercy Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Moses entered the tent to speak with God, he heard the voice from above the mercy seat, between the cherubim.
verseByVerse.theology: The dedication of the altar opens the way to communion; the gifts of the people lead to the voice of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God’s voice from between the cherubim. Now: God speaks to us in his Son, from the throne of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: “And when Moses went into the tent of meeting to speak with the LORD, he heard the voice speaking to him from above the mercy seat that was on the ark of the testimony, from between the two cherubim; and it spoke to him.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The long chapter of giving culminates in receiving: God speaks. After twelve days of offerings, Moses enters the tent and hears the very voice of God “from above the mercy seat... from between the two cherubim.” Wenham notes the profound climax — the dedication of the altar and the people’s worship open the way to communion with God; giving leads to hearing. The mercy seat (Hebrew kapporet, the place of atonement) is where the blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement, and from precisely that blood-covered throne the voice of God issues. This is the deepest gospel logic: God speaks from the place of propitiation. Sproul stressed that we hear God’s gracious voice only over the mercy seat, only where atonement has been made; apart from the blood, the holy God is a consuming fire, but over the mercy seat he communes. Calvin observes that the cherubim, who guarded Eden’s entrance with flaming sword (Gen 3:24), now overshadow the place where God meets man in peace — the way back to God’s presence reopened through atonement. The New Testament declares that God “has spoken to us by his Son” (Heb 1:2), who is himself the true mercy seat (Rom 3:25), the propitiation from whom the voice of grace forever issues. To hear God now, we come not to a tent but to Christ, the meeting place where atoning blood and the living voice of God are one.

7.theology:
God Receives Each One Individually. Twelve identical offerings are recorded twelve separate times, day by day. The repetition declares that no worshiper is lost in the crowd; God knows and welcomes each by name, giving each his own day at the altar.

Equal Yet Known. The offerings are identical, teaching that all come to God on the same terms, by the same blood; none is greater or lesser. Yet each is recorded separately, teaching that each is known and loved with perfect particularity. Here is the gospel paradox.

The Voice from the Mercy Seat. God speaks from above the place of atonement, between the cherubim. Communion with God comes only over the blood-covered mercy seat — fulfilled in Christ, the true propitiation, through whom God now speaks to us by his Son.
7.examples:
Then: Twelve chiefs each brought identical gifts on his own day, all recorded separately, and the dedication of the altar opened the way to the voice of God from between the cherubim.

Now: You are never a statistic to God. He receives your worship individually, gives you your own welcome at the altar, and speaks to you in his Son from the throne of grace. Give freely as the chiefs did, and draw near to hear the voice that issues from the mercy seat — Christ himself.

8.title: The Levites Consecrated: Cleansed and Given to God
8.text: <sup>14</sup>“Thus you shall separate the Levites from among the people of Israel, and the Levites shall be mine. <sup>15</sup>And after that the Levites shall go in to serve at the tent of meeting, when you have cleansed them and offered them as a wave offering.”
8.overview:
Chapter 8 opens with the lighting of the lampstand and then turns to the consecration of the Levites — their cleansing, dedication, and presentation to God as a “wave offering.” Having been chosen as substitutes for the firstborn (ch 3), the Levites are now formally set apart for service.

The imagery is rich with grace. The Levites are sprinkled, shaved, and washed; the people lay hands on them; and Aaron presents them before the LORD as a living offering. They are given twice — given by the people to God, and given by God back to Aaron for the service of the tent.

Wenham notes the striking phrase: the Levites are “wholly given” to God, a living wave offering. They do not merely perform duties; they are themselves the gift. Their whole existence is dedicated.

The lampstand that opens the chapter, casting its light before the LORD, frames the whole: the consecrated servants are to be light-bearers in the house of God. And it all anticipates the Romans 12 call to present ourselves as living sacrifices, and Christ, the truly consecrated Servant, given by the Father and giving himself wholly for us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Lampstand Lit Before the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Aaron is to set up the seven lamps so they give light in front of the lampstand, made of hammered gold as God showed Moses.
verseByVerse.theology: The light of the sanctuary shines before God; his servants are called to be light-bearers in his house.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: seven lamps burning before the LORD. Now: the church shines as light in a dark world, in Christ the true Light.

verseByVerse.quote: “Now the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Speak to Aaron and say to him, When you set up the lamps, the seven lamps shall give light in front of the lampstand.’ And Aaron did so... The lampstand was made of hammered gold... according to the pattern that the LORD had shown Moses, so he made the lampstand.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter opens in golden light. Aaron sets up the seven lamps so they shine “in front of the lampstand,” casting their glow across the holy place. Wenham notes that the lampstand (the menorah) was the only source of light in the windowless sanctuary, a tree of light burning perpetually before the LORD. The hammered gold, fashioned exactly “according to the pattern that the LORD had shown Moses,” underscores again that worship is on God’s terms, conformed to his revealed design, not human invention. Calvin observes that the perpetual light signified the abiding presence and truth of God among his people; the lamps must never go out. Sproul reflected that the menorah pointed beyond itself to the God who is light and in whom is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5). The seven lamps, the number of fullness, picture the complete and perfect illumination God provides for his worship. And the New Testament gathers the imagery: Christ is the true Light of the world (John 8:12), and his church is the lampstand (Rev 1:20), called to shine his light before God and the world. That this radiant scene introduces the consecration of the Levites is fitting — the servants set apart in this chapter are to be light-bearers in the house of God, reflecting the glory of the One who is light, made to shine according to the pattern he has shown.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–22 — The Cleansing and Dedication of the Levites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levites are sprinkled, shaved, and washed; the people lay hands on them; Aaron presents them as a wave offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: The servants of God must be cleansed and wholly given; the Levites are themselves the offering, dedicated entirely to God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Levites washed and offered to God. Now: believers present themselves as living sacrifices, cleansed by Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Take the Levites from among the people of Israel and cleanse them. Thus you shall do to them to cleanse them: sprinkle the water of purification upon them, and let them go with a razor over all their body, and wash their clothes and cleanse themselves.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: Before the Levites may serve, they must be cleansed — sprinkled with water, shaved over all the body, their clothes washed. Wenham notes the threefold purification, a thorough cleansing that touches the whole person inside and out. The servant of God must be clean; one cannot handle holy things with defiled hands. The sprinkling of the “water of purification” recalls the cleansing from contact with death (ch 19), for the Levites are being separated unto the living God. Calvin observes that this outward washing signified the inward purity God requires of those who draw near to serve him; the ceremony preached the necessity of holiness. The shaving of the whole body marks a radical new beginning, the old life laid aside, a fresh consecration. Sproul reflected that no one serves God acceptably while clinging to defilement; the gospel’s first word to the servant is cleansing. There is profound grace here — the Levites are not required to cleanse themselves by their own merit; the means of purification are provided by God. The Christian parallel is clear and glorious: we who would serve God are first washed, “the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:5), sprinkled with a better blood than that of bulls and goats (Heb 10:22). The Levites’ outward cleansing points to the inward purification Christ secures, fitting us for the service of the holy God.

verseByVerse.quote: “Then let them take a bull from the herd and its grain offering... and you shall take another bull from the herd for a sin offering. And you shall bring the Levites before the tent of meeting and assemble the whole congregation of the people of Israel. When you bring the Levites before the LORD, the people of Israel shall lay their hands on the Levites, and Aaron shall offer the Levites before the LORD as a wave offering from the people of Israel, that they may do the service of the LORD.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The dedication ceremony is striking: the whole congregation lays hands on the Levites, and Aaron presents them “as a wave offering” to the LORD. Wenham notes the remarkable imagery — the Levites are themselves the offering, living men presented to God as the people’s gift. The laying on of hands signifies identification and transfer; just as a worshiper laid hands on a sacrificial animal to designate it as his substitute, so the people lay hands on the Levites, designating them as their representatives, given in place of the firstborn. The “wave offering,” normally a portion lifted and presented before the LORD, here describes living men dedicated wholly to God. Calvin observes the dignity and the cost of this consecration; the Levites are not merely employed but offered, their whole lives surrendered to the service of God on behalf of the people. Sproul reflected that this is the very pattern Paul invokes in Romans 12:1 — “present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God.” The Christian, too, is a living wave offering, dedicated entirely to the LORD. The sin offering and burnt offering that accompany the ceremony remind us that even this consecration rests on atonement; the Levites are given to God only because sacrifice has been made. And it all points to Christ, the true Servant, given by the Father and giving himself wholly, the one perfect living offering for us all.

verseByVerse.quote: “Then the Levites shall lay their hands on the heads of the bulls, and you shall offer the one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering to the LORD to make atonement for the Levites. And you shall set the Levites before Aaron and his sons, and shall offer them as a wave offering to the LORD. Thus you shall separate the Levites from among the people of Israel, and the Levites shall be mine.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the Levites in turn lay their hands on the sacrificial bulls — sin offering and burnt offering — “to make atonement for the Levites.” Wenham notes the layered substitution: the people laid hands on the Levites, and the Levites lay hands on the bulls. Atonement flows down the chain so that the servants of God may be acceptable in his sight. Even those set apart for sacred service need atoning blood; their consecration does not exempt them from sin but requires its covering. Calvin observes the humbling truth that the ministers of God are sinners saved by sacrifice, no less than the people they serve. The climactic word rings out again: “the Levites shall be mine.” As in chapter 3, God’s claim of ownership is the heart of the matter. The Levites are separated from the people and given wholly to God; they belong to him utterly. Sproul stressed that to be the LORD’s is the highest privilege and the deepest security; those whom God claims, he keeps. There is unspeakable grace in being able to say with the Levites, “I am his.” And the believer in Christ shares this very status — separated from the world, atoned for by a better sacrifice, and claimed forever by God: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Cor 6:19–20). The Levites’ consecration is the Christian’s portrait: cleansed, atoned for, given to God, and gloriously owned by him.

verseByVerse.quote: “And after that the Levites shall go in to serve at the tent of meeting, when you have cleansed them and offered them as a wave offering. For they are wholly given to me from among the people of Israel. Instead of all who open the womb, the firstborn of all the people of Israel, I have taken them for myself... And I have given the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons from among the people of Israel, to do the service for the people of Israel at the tent of meeting and to make atonement for the people of Israel, that there may be no plague among the people of Israel when the people of Israel come near the sanctuary.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Two phrases shine. First, the Levites are “wholly given to me” — the Hebrew doubles the word, “given, given,” an emphatic total dedication. They are not partly God’s but entirely his. Wenham notes the intensity; nothing is held back. Second, God then “gives” these given ones as “a gift to Aaron and his sons.” The Levites are given twice — surrendered to God by the people, then granted by God to the priesthood for service. Calvin observes the beautiful economy of grace: what is offered to God is returned for the blessing of his people. The purpose is protective: the Levites serve “that there may be no plague... when the people come near the sanctuary.” Their mediating service shields the people from the danger of the holy. Sproul reflected that this is the heart of all ministry — to stand between a holy God and a sinful people, that they may safely draw near. The repeated phrase “the people of Israel” drums through the verse, six times, anchoring everything in God’s concern for his whole nation. And the gospel fulfillment is glorious: Christ is the One wholly given by the Father, given as a gift to his people, whose mediating work removes the plague of wrath so that we may come near to God and live. The Levites’ double giving is a faint shadow of the Father’s gift of the Son and the Son’s gift of himself.

verseByVerse.quote: “Thus did Moses and Aaron and all the congregation of the people of Israel to the Levites. According to all that the LORD commanded Moses concerning the Levites, the people of Israel did to them. And the Levites purified themselves from sin and washed their clothes, and Aaron offered them as a wave offering before the LORD, and Aaron made atonement for them to cleanse them. And after that the Levites went in to do their service in the tent of meeting before Aaron and his sons.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The consecration is carried out in full obedience — “according to all that the LORD commanded Moses.” Wenham notes the now-familiar refrain that seals the opening chapters; everything is done exactly as God directed. The Levites are purified, offered, atoned for, and then — “after that” — they go in to serve. The order is essential and unchangeable: cleansing and atonement first, then service. One cannot reverse it. Calvin observes that this sequence enshrines a permanent gospel principle: we serve God acceptably only after we have been cleansed and reconciled by sacrifice; works of service flow from grace received, never the reverse. Sproul stressed that the great error of religion is to put service before cleansing, to try to earn God’s favor by labor rather than receive it by atonement. The Levites teach the opposite: first washed, first atoned for, then sent to serve. There is deep rest in this for the weary servant of God; our acceptance does not hang on the quality of our service but on the atonement already made. We labor as those already cleansed, already received, already owned by God. And the “after that” of verse 22 echoes through every Christian life — first justified, then sanctified; first reconciled, then commissioned. The consecrated Levite entering the tent to serve is the picture of every believer, washed by Christ and sent to serve from the security of grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — The Term of Levitical Service
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levites serve from age twenty-five to fifty, after which they retire from heavy duty but may still assist.
verseByVerse.theology: God appoints seasons of service and of rest; even his servants are given a tender provision for their later years.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a fixed term of Levitical service. Now: faithful service in its season, resting in the God who appoints our times.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘This applies to the Levites: from twenty-five years old and upward they shall come to do duty in the service of the tent of meeting. And from the age of fifty years they shall withdraw from the duty of the service and serve no more. They minister to their brothers in the tent of meeting by keeping guard, but they shall do no service. Thus shall you do to the Levites in assigning their duties.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: God fixes the term of Levitical service: heavy duty from twenty-five to fifty, then withdrawal from the hardest labor. Wenham notes the tender wisdom — the physically demanding work of carrying and assembling the tabernacle belongs to the years of strength, and God graciously releases his older servants from burdens their bodies can no longer bear. Yet the retirement is not idleness; the older Levites still “minister to their brothers... by keeping guard,” their wisdom and presence still valued though their heavy lifting ceases. Calvin observes the kindness of God toward his aging servants; he does not drive them until they collapse but appoints a season of lighter service and honored rest. There is gospel humanity here. God knows our frame, remembers that we are dust (Ps 103:14), and tempers his appointments to our strength. Sproul reflected that there is a season for active labor and a season to step back, and the godly servant accepts both from God’s hand without bitterness or pride. The principle blesses the church still: the energetic years are for the heaviest work, but the seasoned years bring the irreplaceable gifts of guarding, counseling, and presence. And underneath it all is the comfort that our times are in God’s hands (Ps 31:15); he who appoints the season of service also appoints the season of rest, and both are sanctified by his love. The retired Levite, still keeping guard, reminds us that there is no true retirement from belonging to God.

8.theology:
Wholly Given to God. The Levites are offered as a living wave offering, “given, given” to the LORD — themselves the gift, not merely the performers of duties. This anticipates Romans 12:1: present your bodies as a living sacrifice. The servant of God is the offering.

Cleansing Before Service. The Levites are sprinkled, washed, and atoned for, and only “after that” do they serve. The order is unbreakable: grace and cleansing first, then service. We labor from acceptance, not for it — a permanent gospel principle.

Given Twice, for the People. The Levites are given by the people to God, then given by God to the priesthood, that there be “no plague” when Israel draws near. So Christ is given by the Father and gives himself, the Mediator whose work lets us approach God and live.
8.examples:
Then: The Levites were cleansed, atoned for, and presented to God as a living offering, then sent to serve and to shield the people from the danger of the holy.

Now: Present yourself to God as a living sacrifice, cleansed by the blood of Christ. Serve not to earn his favor but from the security of grace already received — washed first, then sent. And rest in the God who appoints your seasons of labor and of rest, for you are wholly his.

9.title: The Passover Kept; the Cloud of Guidance
9.text: <sup>15</sup>On the day that the tabernacle was set up, the cloud covered the tabernacle, the tent of the testimony. And at evening it was over the tabernacle like the appearance of fire until morning. <sup>16</sup>So it was always: the cloud covered it by day and the appearance of fire by night.
9.overview:
Chapter 9 holds together two great gospel themes: redemption remembered and presence experienced. First Israel keeps the Passover in the wilderness, the second since leaving Egypt; then the cloud and fire of God’s presence settle upon the tabernacle to guide every step of the journey.

The Passover anchors the whole journey in redemption. Before Israel moves an inch toward the land, they remember the blood of the lamb. The wilderness pilgrimage flows out of redemption accomplished; we travel as a redeemed people.

A tender provision follows: those unclean or away on a journey at Passover may keep it a month later. God makes a way for the excluded to draw near; no one truly desiring to keep the feast is shut out. Yet the high-handed despiser who neglects it is cut off — grace is not license.

Then comes the cloud — God’s visible presence, leading by day and fire by night. Israel moves only when the cloud moves and rests when it rests. Here is the life of faith: total dependence on the guidance of God, going and staying at his word. And it all points to Christ, our Passover (1 Cor 5:7) and our guide, who leads his people home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Passover in the Wilderness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel keeps the Passover at Sinai; provision is made for the unclean and the traveler to keep it a month later.
verseByVerse.theology: Redemption is remembered before the journey begins; God makes a way for the excluded, yet the despiser is cut off.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Passover lamb remembered in the wilderness. Now: Christ our Passover, the redemption from which all pilgrimage flows.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the LORD spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the first month of the second year after they had come out of the land of Egypt, saying, ‘Let the people of Israel keep the Passover at its appointed time...’ And they kept the Passover in the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, at twilight, in the wilderness of Sinai.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Before Israel takes a single step toward Canaan, they keep the Passover — the memorial of the blood of the lamb by which they were redeemed from Egypt. Wenham notes the chronological significance: this Passover, in the first month of the second year, actually precedes the census of chapter 1 (the second month), placed here thematically to anchor the whole journey in redemption. The pilgrimage to the promised land begins with remembering the price of deliverance. Calvin observes that God would have his people perpetually mindful of their redemption; the Passover was the fountain from which all their identity and obligation flowed. They were a redeemed people, and the feast kept that truth ever before them. Sproul stressed that the Christian life, too, flows out of redemption accomplished; we do not journey in order to be saved but because we have been saved. The blood of the lamb comes first; everything else follows. There is deep pastoral wisdom in beginning the wilderness narrative here. Before the grumbling, the rebellion, and the long years of wandering that fill the rest of Numbers, God establishes the people in remembered grace. And it points unmistakably to Christ, “our Passover lamb,” who “has been sacrificed” (1 Cor 5:7). Every Christian pilgrimage begins and is sustained at the same place — the blood of the true Lamb, the redemption from which all our journeying flows.

verseByVerse.quote: “And there were certain men who were unclean through touching a dead body, so that they could not keep the Passover on that day, and they came before Moses and Aaron on that day. And those men said to him, ‘We are unclean through touching a dead body. Why are we kept from bringing the LORD’s offering at its appointed time among the people of Israel?’ And Moses said to them, ‘Wait, that I may hear what the LORD will command concerning you.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: A poignant problem arises: some men are ceremonially unclean and cannot keep the Passover, yet they long to. Their plea is beautiful — “Why are we kept from bringing the LORD’s offering?” Wenham notes the tender heart of these men; they do not resent the feast or shrug off their exclusion but ache to participate, grieved at being kept from the LORD’s table. Here is a spiritual hunger God will not despise. Moses, instead of improvising, responds with humble dependence: “Wait, that I may hear what the LORD will command.” Calvin admires Moses’ restraint; faced with a case not covered by existing law, he does not presume but seeks fresh instruction from God. Sproul reflected that this is a model of godly leadership — to wait on God rather than rush to one’s own judgment. But the deeper note is the longing of the unclean to draw near. Keller observed that the gospel is for those who feel their exclusion and yearn to come in; the men who grieve at being kept from the LORD are precisely those God will make a way for. Their hunger anticipates the gospel’s glad answer to every excluded sinner who cries, “Why am I kept from God?” The God of the Passover delights to make a way for such longing hearts, as the next verses will show.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If any one of you or of your descendants is unclean through touching a dead body, or is on a long journey, he shall still keep the Passover to the LORD. In the second month on the fourteenth day at twilight they shall keep it. They shall... leave none of it until the morning, nor break any of its bones; according to all the statute for the Passover they shall keep it.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: God’s answer is pure grace: the unclean and the traveler may keep the Passover one month later. Wenham notes the remarkable accommodation — rather than simply excluding those providentially hindered, God opens a second door so that no truly desiring heart is permanently shut out. The principle is profound: God makes a way for the excluded to draw near. Yet grace does not lower the standard; the second Passover must be kept “according to all the statute,” with none left till morning and no bone broken. Calvin observes the balance — mercy provides the opportunity, but the feast must still be honored rightly. The detail “nor break any of its bones” is a quiet prophecy; it was fulfilled at the cross when the soldiers, finding Jesus already dead, broke not his legs, “that the Scripture might be fulfilled” (John 19:36; cf. Exod 12:46). The true Passover Lamb’s bones remained unbroken. Sproul reflected on the gospel pattern here: God is the God of the second chance for the hindered and the longing, but never the God who waters down the cost of redemption. The provision teaches that no obstacle — uncleanness, distance, providence — can finally bar the soul that hungers to keep the feast. In Christ, the door stands open even to those who feel themselves too defiled or too far; he makes a way.

verseByVerse.quote: “But if anyone who is clean and is not on a journey fails to keep the Passover, that person shall be cut off from his people because he did not bring the LORD’s offering at its appointed time; that man shall bear his sin. And if a stranger sojourns among you and would keep the Passover to the LORD, according to the statute of the Passover and according to its rule, so shall he do. You shall have one statute, both for the sojourner and for the native.’”
