The tragedy of the ten is the tragedy of every faithless heart: forgetting the LORD, we shrink before our troubles and surrender the inheritance he has already given.

13.theology:
The Anatomy of Unbelief. Ten spies measured the giants against themselves and became grasshoppers; faith measures the giants against God. Unbelief is rarely a denial of facts but a misreading of them — leaving God out of the equation, so that the obstacle eclipses the promise.

The Same Evidence, Two Responses. All twelve saw the same land, fruit, and giants. The difference was not in the eyes but in the heart. God surrounds the call to obedience with tokens of his goodness, yet abundant evidence does not produce faith in an unbelieving heart; faith is a response to the trustworthiness of God.

Joshua, the LORD Saves. Moses renames Hoshea “Joshua” — “the LORD is salvation.” The faithful spy who will lead Israel into the land bears the very name of Jesus, pointing to the One who, unlike that faithless generation, brings his people into the true and eternal rest.
13.examples:
Then: Twelve spies saw the same good land and the same giants; ten shrank in fear like grasshoppers, but Caleb and Joshua, factoring in God, cried, “Let us go up at once, for we are well able.”

Now: At the edge of every hard obedience, the question is never the size of the obstacle but the size of your God. Beware the “however” of unbelief that admits God’s goodness then lets fear overrule it. Measure your giants against the LORD who saves, and go up at once.

14.title: Israel’s Rebellion: The Wilderness Decreed
14.text: <sup>2</sup>And all the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron... <sup>3</sup>“Why is the LORD bringing us into this land, to fall by the sword?”... <sup>9</sup>“Only do not rebel against the LORD. And do not fear the people of the land, for they are bread for us...”
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is the catastrophe toward which the whole book has been building. The people, swayed by the ten, rebel outright — weeping all night, longing to return to Egypt, even proposing to stone Caleb and Joshua and choose a leader to take them back to slavery. It is the great refusal of grace.

Caleb and Joshua tear their clothes and plead: the land is exceedingly good, the LORD is with us, do not rebel, do not fear. But the congregation reaches for stones. Only the appearing of the glory of the LORD halts the murder.

Then comes Moses’ great intercession — one of the high points of the Old Testament. God threatens to disinherit Israel and make Moses a great nation, and Moses, refusing the offer, pleads not his own glory but God’s name and God’s revealed character: “The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity.” He prays God’s own self-revelation back to him.

God pardons — and yet justice falls. The faithless generation will not enter; they will wander forty years, a year for each day, until they die in the wilderness. Only Caleb and Joshua will enter. Hebrews 3–4 makes this the great warning: “they were unable to enter because of unbelief.” And it drives us to the better Mediator, whose intercession secures not a forty-year reprieve but everlasting pardon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Rebellion and the Plea of Caleb and Joshua
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people weep, long for Egypt, and plot to return; Caleb and Joshua plead for faith, but the congregation moves to stone them.
verseByVerse.theology: Unbelief hardens into open rebellion and the rejection of God’s gift; faith pleads, but the rebellious heart reaches for stones.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel longs to return to Egypt. Now: a warning against the heart that despises grace and shrinks back to bondage.

verseByVerse.quote: “Then all the congregation raised a loud cry, and the people wept that night. And all the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron. The whole congregation said to them, ‘Would that we had died in the land of Egypt! Or would that we had died in this wilderness!... Would it not be better for us to go back to Egypt?’ And they said to one another, ‘Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: The unbelief of the ten erupts into the full rebellion of the nation. The people weep all night, grumble against their leaders, and reach the unthinkable conclusion: “Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt.” Wenham notes the staggering depth of the apostasy; they would depose Moses, reject God’s deliverance, and return voluntarily to the house of slavery from which God redeemed them. Calvin observes that this is the very nadir of ingratitude and unbelief — to prefer bondage to promise, Egypt to Canaan, death to the inheritance. Their wish, “would that we had died in Egypt,” is a blasphemous rejection of redemption itself. Sproul reflected that there is a fearful logic to apostasy; once God is removed from the equation, his greatest gifts appear as threats, and the chains of the past seem safer than the freedom of faith. To “choose a leader” other than the one God appointed is to reject God’s rule outright. Keller noted how unbelief always idealizes the bondage it was rescued from; the soul that draws back from grace romanticizes its former slavery. This is the great refusal — the redeemed people, standing at the very door of the promised land, weeping to return to Egypt. It is a sobering portrait of the human heart’s capacity to despise grace, and a warning that Hebrews will press upon the church: take care lest there be in any of you “an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God” (Heb 3:12).

verseByVerse.quote: “Then Moses and Aaron fell on their faces before all the assembly... And Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh... tore their clothes and said to all the congregation, ‘The land, which we passed through to spy it out, is an exceedingly good land. If the LORD delights in us, he will bring us into this land and give it to us... Only do not rebel against the LORD. And do not fear the people of the land, for they are bread for us. Their protection is removed from them, and the LORD is with us; do not fear them.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: In the face of the rebellion, Caleb and Joshua make their impassioned plea, tearing their clothes in anguish. Their argument is pure faith: the land is “exceedingly good,” the LORD will bring them in if he delights in them, and the giants who terrified the ten are “bread for us.” Wenham notes the stunning reversal of perspective; what the ten called devouring giants, the two call dinner. The same facts, seen through faith, are entirely transformed. The key is in their words: “Their protection is removed from them, and the LORD is with us.” Calvin observes that faith’s confidence rests not in Israel’s strength but in God’s presence; because the LORD is with them, the giants are already defenseless. Sproul reflected that the heart of the plea is “do not rebel against the LORD... do not fear” — the twin commands that faith obeys and unbelief refuses. To fear the people of the land is, at root, to rebel against the LORD, for it disbelieves his promise and his presence. Keller noted the courage of standing alone for faith against a hostile majority; Caleb and Joshua risked their lives to call the people back to trust. Their cry, “the LORD is with us; do not fear,” is the perpetual word of faith to every fearful heart. It anticipates the gospel’s “Immanuel, God with us,” and the Savior’s repeated “fear not,” for if God is with us, who can be against us (Rom 8:31)?

verseByVerse.quote: “Then all the congregation said to stone them with stones. But the glory of the LORD appeared at the tent of meeting to all the people of Israel.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The congregation answers the plea of faith with stones. Wenham notes the terrible climax; they would murder the two faithful men for daring to call them to trust God. Unbelief, fully ripened, becomes violent toward faith. Calvin observes the dreadful spectacle — the people, redeemed and led and fed by God, now seeking to kill those who urge them to believe him. The reaching for stones reveals how far the heart had fallen; faith had become intolerable to them. But at the very moment of intended murder, “the glory of the LORD appeared.” Sproul reflected on the timing of this intervention; God himself steps in to halt the violence and to take up the matter directly. The appearing of the glory is both rescue and reckoning — it saves Caleb and Joshua and summons the nation to judgment. There is a pattern here that runs through redemptive history: the world reaches for stones against the messengers of faith, but God vindicates his own. Stephen would later be stoned for a faithful witness, yet he saw the glory of God and the Son of Man standing to receive him (Acts 7:55–56). And the ultimate Faithful Witness, Jesus, was killed by those he came to save, yet God raised him in glory. The glory that appeared at the tent stood between the rebels and the faithful; in Christ, that glory stands forever as the vindication of faith and the judgment of unbelief.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God threatens to disinherit Israel; Moses pleads God’s name and revealed character, and God pardons, though judgment remains.
verseByVerse.theology: The mediator intercedes on the ground of God’s own glory and self-revelation; God pardons for his name’s sake.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses pleads God’s character back to him. Now: Christ intercedes on the ground of his own glory, securing our pardon.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the LORD said to Moses, ‘How long will this people despise me? And how long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs that I have done among them? I will strike them with the pestilence and disinherit them, and I will make of you a nation greater and mightier than they.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: God’s diagnosis cuts to the root: the people “despise me” and “will not believe in me, in spite of all the signs.” Wenham notes that the two charges are intertwined — their unbelief is contempt, and their contempt is unbelief. To refuse to trust God after all his mighty works is to despise him. Then comes the staggering offer: God proposes to destroy Israel and make Moses into a great nation. Calvin observes that this is a real test of Moses’ heart, not a mere formality; God sets before his servant the chance for unparalleled personal greatness. Would Moses seize it? Sproul reflected that the offer exposes what kind of man Moses truly is; many a leader would have leapt at the chance to be the father of a new and mightier nation. But Moses, the meek man who would not defend his own honor in chapter 12, will now refuse his own exaltation for the sake of God’s glory and the people who sought to stone him. The repeated “how long” conveys the divine patience stretched to its limit; God has borne with this people through sign after sign, and still they will not believe. There is a sobering reality here about the persistence of unbelief even amid overwhelming evidence. Yet the very fact that God consults Moses, that he opens the door to intercession, reveals a heart inclined to mercy. The God who threatens judgment invites a mediator to plead — and a greater Mediator would one day plead for a people who despised him still more.

verseByVerse.quote: “But Moses said to the LORD, ‘Then the Egyptians will hear of it... and they will tell the inhabitants of this land... Now if you kill this people as one man, then the nations who have heard your fame will say, “It is because the LORD was not able to bring this people into the land...” And now, please let the power of the Lord be great as you have promised, saying, “The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity and transgression...” Please pardon the iniquity of this people, according to the greatness of your steadfast love...’”
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses’ intercession is a masterclass in prayer. He pleads not Israel’s worthiness — they have none — nor his own glory, which he refuses. He pleads God’s name, God’s reputation among the nations, and above all God’s own revealed character. Wenham notes the brilliance of the argument: if God destroys Israel, the nations will conclude he was unable to fulfill his promise, and his name will be dishonored. But the heart of the prayer is verse 18, where Moses quotes God’s self-revelation from Exodus 34: “The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity.” Calvin marvels that Moses prays God’s own words back to him, holding God to his self-disclosed character. Sproul reflected that this is the very secret of bold prayer — to plead not our merit but God’s nature, to ask him to be who he has revealed himself to be. Keller noted that Moses appeals to grace, not to Israel’s improvement; he asks for pardon “according to the greatness of your steadfast love,” not according to any change in the people. This is gospel praying. Moses stands as the mediator between a holy God and a rebellious people, pleading the divine mercy on the ground of God’s own glory and grace. It is a luminous foreshadowing of Christ, our great High Priest, who intercedes for us not on the ground of our worthiness but on the ground of his own glory and the Father’s steadfast love.

verseByVerse.quote: “Then the LORD said, ‘I have pardoned, according to your word. But truly, as I live, and as all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the LORD, none of the men who have seen my glory and my signs that I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and yet have put me to the test these ten times and have not obeyed my voice, shall see the land that I swore to give to their fathers... But my servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me fully, I will bring into the land...’”
verseByVerse.commentary: God’s answer holds mercy and judgment in perfect balance: “I have pardoned, according to your word” — yet “none of these men... shall see the land.” Wenham notes the crucial distinction; the nation is spared destruction, but the faithless generation forfeits the inheritance. Pardon does not always remove all consequences; God forgives the people yet decrees that those who refused to enter will die in the wilderness. Calvin observes the harmony of grace and justice here; God is true to his steadfast love in sparing the nation and true to his holiness in barring the unbelieving from the rest. The charge is solemn: they “have put me to the test these ten times” — a persistent pattern of unbelief, not a single lapse. Sproul reflected on the sobering truth that forgiveness and discipline can coexist; God may pardon the sin and still appoint its temporal fruit. But shining against the dark is Caleb, commended in glorious terms: “he has a different spirit and has followed me fully.” Here is the man of faith singled out for honor, promised entry into the land. Keller noted the beauty of “followed me fully” — wholehearted faith that does not draw back. The contrast is stark and instructive: a whole generation barred for unbelief, one man (and Joshua) brought in for faith. And the great gospel hope shines through the judgment: “all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the LORD” — the unbelief of one generation cannot thwart God’s purpose to fill the earth with his glory through the seed of promise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–38 — The Sentence of Forty Years
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God decrees forty years of wandering, a year for each day; the ten faithless spies die by plague, but Caleb and Joshua live.
verseByVerse.theology: The faithless generation forfeits the rest because of unbelief; faith alone enters the inheritance.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: forty years in the wilderness for unbelief. Now: Hebrews warns the church not to fail to enter God’s rest through unbelief.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying... ‘Say to them, “As I live, declares the LORD, what you have said in my hearing I will do to you: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness... not one shall come into the land where I swore that I would make you dwell, except Caleb... and Joshua. But your little ones... I will bring in... According to the number of the days in which you spied out the land, forty days, a year for each day, you shall bear your iniquity forty years...”’”
verseByVerse.commentary: The sentence is pronounced with terrible precision. God takes the people’s own words — “would that we had died in this wilderness” (v. 2) — and grants exactly that: “your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness.” Wenham notes the dreadful justice; they get the death they foolishly wished for. The duration matches the test: “a year for each day,” forty years for forty days of spying. Calvin observes the fitting symmetry of divine discipline; the punishment is measured to the sin. Yet mercy threads through the judgment: “your little ones... I will bring in.” The children the faithless said would become prey will inherit the land their parents forfeited. God’s promise will not fail; it simply passes to the next generation. Sproul reflected on the sobering pattern — unbelief disqualifies from the inheritance, but God’s purpose advances through those who will trust him. The forty years are not random but redemptive in their way; the unbelieving generation must pass away before the faithful can enter. There is profound warning here for the church. Hebrews 3:17–19 presses the lesson: “With whom was he provoked forty years?... And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient? So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief.” The bodies in the wilderness preach to us still: do not, through unbelief, forfeit the rest that God in Christ holds out.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land, who returned and made all the congregation grumble against him by bringing up a bad report about the land—the men who brought up a bad report of the land—died by plague before the LORD. Of those men who went to spy out the land, only Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh remained alive.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The ten who brought the bad report die first, “by plague before the LORD” — a swift and pointed judgment on those who led the nation into unbelief. Wenham notes the appropriateness; the men who spread the faithless report and ignited the rebellion are struck down immediately, while the consequences for the people unfold over forty years. Calvin observes the heightened accountability of leaders; those who lead others into sin bear a heavier judgment. Sproul reflected on the sober warning to all who would teach or influence God’s people — to lead others into unbelief is a grievous thing in God’s sight. But against the death of the ten stands the survival of the two: “only Joshua... and Caleb... remained alive.” Wenham notes the deliberate contrast; the same mission that doomed the ten preserved the two, because the difference was faith. The two men of faith outlive the ten men of fear and the entire generation they swayed. Here is the great theme crystallized: faith enters, unbelief perishes. Caleb and Joshua, standing alive amid the dying, are living proof that the LORD honors those who trust him fully. And the survival of Joshua — “the LORD saves” — points beyond himself to the One whose name he bears, the Savior who alone brings his people safely through the wilderness and into the rest that the faithless can never reach.

verseByVerse.quote: “When Moses told these words to all the people of Israel, the people mourned greatly. And they rose early in the morning and went up to the heights of the hill country, saying, ‘Here we are. We will go up to the place that the LORD has promised, for we have sinned.’ But Moses said, ‘Why now are you transgressing the command of the LORD, when that will not succeed?... the LORD will not be with you.’ But they presumed to go up... Then the Amalekites and the Canaanites... came down and defeated them...”
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends with a final, tragic irony: having refused to go up when God commanded, the people now presume to go up when God forbids. Their late “repentance” is really only remorse at the consequences, not faith. Wenham notes the fatal reversal; yesterday they would not enter though God said go, and today they will enter though God says stay. Both are unbelief — the refusal to take God at his word. Calvin observes that this is not true repentance but a stubborn self-will that, having been told no, insists on its own way to undo the sentence. The people say, “we have sinned,” yet their very action proves they have not learned obedience, for they transgress a fresh command. Moses warns them plainly: “the LORD will not be with you,” for the ark and Moses himself do not go with them. To go up without God is to go up to defeat, and so it proves — the Amalekites and Canaanites rout them at Hormah. Sproul reflected on the deadly presumption of trying to claim God's promises on our own terms and timing, apart from his word and his presence. The lesson is sobering: obedience delayed and then attempted in self-will is not obedience at all. Without the presence of God, even an assault on the promised land is doomed. The generation that would not believe could not, by mere effort, force its way into the rest it had despised. Only faith enters; presumption perishes at Hormah.

14.theology:
Unbelief Forfeits the Inheritance. The faithless generation, refusing to enter the good land, is barred from the rest and dies in the wilderness. Hebrews makes this the great warning to the church: “they were unable to enter because of unbelief.” The promised rest is received by faith alone.

Intercession on the Ground of God’s Glory. Moses refuses his own exaltation and pleads God’s name and revealed character, praying God’s own self-disclosure back to him: “slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love.” This is gospel praying, fulfilled in Christ, who intercedes not on our merit but on the ground of his glory and the Father’s love.

Pardon and Discipline Together. “I have pardoned... but truly... none of these men shall see the land.” God spares the nation yet bars the unbelieving from the rest. Forgiveness does not always remove consequences; mercy and holiness meet in the wise discipline of a faithful God.
14.examples:
Then: Israel wept to return to Egypt and reached for stones against Caleb and Joshua; Moses interceded on the ground of God’s name, and God pardoned the nation yet decreed forty years in the wilderness for the unbelieving generation.

Now: Take heed lest an evil, unbelieving heart lead you to draw back from grace and forfeit God’s rest. Pray boldly as Moses did, pleading not your worthiness but God’s revealed character. And follow Christ, your Joshua, the one who brings his people into the rest that unbelief can never enter.

15.title: Offerings and the Sabbath-Breaker: Grace After Judgment
15.text: <sup>2</sup>“When you come into the land you are to inhabit, which I am giving you...” <sup>30</sup>“But the person who does anything with a high hand... reviles the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from among his people.” <sup>39</sup>“...you shall remember all the commandments of the LORD, to do them.”
15.overview:
After the devastating judgment of chapter 14, chapter 15 opens with the most surprising word: “When you come into the land...” The very generation barred from the land is given laws for life in the land. Grace persists after judgment; the promise stands, though this generation forfeits it.

The chapter gives laws for offerings, for the stranger (one law for native and sojourner alike), and for unintentional sin, which can be atoned for. Then it draws a sharp line between unintentional sin, covered by sacrifice, and the “high-handed” sin of defiant rebellion, which is cut off.

A startling narrative follows: a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath is stoned — a vivid case study of high-handed sin, defiance of God’s revealed will. The severity shocks us, but it dramatizes the seriousness of deliberate rebellion against the holy God.

The chapter closes with the command to wear tassels with a cord of blue — visible reminders to obey, lest the heart wander after its own eyes. From offerings to tassels, the message is grace that calls forth holiness. And it all points to Christ, who bore both our unintentional failings and our high-handed rebellion, and who clothes us with reminders of grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Offerings in the Land; One Law for All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives laws for grain and drink offerings when Israel enters the land, with one statute for native and sojourner alike.
verseByVerse.theology: Grace persists after judgment; the promise of the land stands, and God’s welcome extends equally to the foreigner.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: laws for offerings in the promised land. Now: the gospel’s welcome to all peoples on equal terms in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: “The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land you are to inhabit, which I am giving you, and you offer to the LORD from the herd or from the flock a food offering... then he who brings his offering shall offer to the LORD a grain offering of a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with a quarter of a hin of oil...’”
verseByVerse.commentary: The timing of this chapter is itself a sermon. Immediately after God decrees that the present generation will die in the wilderness, he says, “When you come into the land... which I am giving you.” Wenham notes the deliberate juxtaposition; the very promise that this generation forfeited is reaffirmed for the next. Grace persists after judgment. The land remains a certainty; the gift stands, though the unbelieving will not see it. Calvin observes the tender comfort here — God does not abandon his purpose because of human sin; the promise to Abraham will be kept. Sproul reflected that this is the steadfastness of God’s covenant love; even in the shadow of judgment, he speaks of the inheritance as sure. The detailed laws for grain and drink offerings teach that worship in the land will be ordered and full; the offerings of the herd and flock are to be accompanied by grain and wine, the fruit of the very land God will give. There is a forward-looking hope woven through these regulations; they assume entry, settlement, harvest, and worship in the promised inheritance. For the discouraged reader, reeling from chapter 14, the message is clear: God’s discipline does not cancel his grace, and his promise is more durable than his people’s unbelief. The land is coming; the offerings will be made; the covenant holds — because God is faithful even when his people are not.

verseByVerse.quote: “Thus it shall be done for each bull or ram, or for each lamb or young goat... For the assembly, there shall be one statute for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you, a statute forever throughout your generations. You and the sojourner shall be alike before the LORD. One law and one rule shall be for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Twice the principle rings out: “one statute... one law and one rule... for you and for the stranger.” Wenham notes the remarkable inclusivity; the foreigner who sojourns among Israel and worships the LORD is placed on equal footing with the native-born “before the LORD.” There is no second-class worship, no inferior access for the outsider who comes to Israel’s God. Calvin observes that this anticipates the breadth of God’s mercy, which was never meant to be confined to one nation but to reach the nations through Israel. Sproul reflected on the gospel trajectory embedded here; the equal standing of the sojourner foreshadows the day when in Christ there would be “neither Jew nor Greek” (Gal 3:28), when the dividing wall would be broken down (Eph 2:14), and when people from every tribe and tongue would worship on equal terms before the throne. Keller often noted how the Old Testament law, far from being narrowly nationalistic, repeatedly makes room for the stranger, planting the seeds of the gospel’s universal reach. The phrase “alike before the LORD” is precious; before God, the redeemed are leveled to perfect equality, all coming by the same sacrifice, all welcomed on the same terms. The native Israelite has no advantage over the believing foreigner. This is the heart of the gospel — one law, one way, one Savior, one welcome — for all who come to God through the appointed sacrifice.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Provision is made for atoning unintentional sin, but the one who sins defiantly, with a high hand, is cut off.
verseByVerse.theology: There is atonement for the sin of weakness and ignorance, but defiant rebellion against God despises his word and finds no sacrifice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the line between weakness and defiance. Now: grace covers our failings, but presumptuous rebellion despises the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: “The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land to which I bring you and when you eat of the bread of the land, you shall present a contribution to the LORD. Of the first of your dough you shall present a loaf as a contribution...’”
verseByVerse.commentary: Again the gracious refrain: “When you come into the land to which I bring you.” Wenham notes the repetition reinforces the certainty of the promise. The law of the firstfruits of the dough teaches that the first and best of the land’s produce belongs to God. Before Israel eats the bread of the land, they are to acknowledge the LORD as the giver by presenting a loaf as a contribution. Calvin observes the principle of consecrating the firstfruits; by giving God the first portion, the whole harvest is acknowledged as his gift and is sanctified. Sproul reflected that this guards the heart against the great temptation of the settled life — to forget the Giver once the gifts are abundant. The wilderness people depended on daily manna; the settled people would eat the bread of their own harvests, and the danger was that they would credit themselves rather than God. The firstfruits offering kept gratitude alive. There is enduring wisdom here for every believer; we are to give God the first and best, acknowledging that all we have is from his hand. The New Testament gathers up the principle — Christ himself is “the firstfruits” (1 Cor 15:20), and we present our lives and substance to God in grateful acknowledgment that everything we have is grace. The loaf of firstfruits preached, in every Israelite home, that the bread on the table was a gift from the God who keeps his promises.

verseByVerse.quote: “But if you sin unintentionally, and do not observe all these commandments... then if it was done unintentionally without the knowledge of the congregation, all the congregation shall offer one bull from the herd for a burnt offering... and they shall be forgiven, because it was a mistake... And if one person sins unintentionally... the priest shall make atonement before the LORD for the person who makes a mistake, when he sins unintentionally, to make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven.”
verseByVerse.commentary: God graciously provides for the sins of weakness and ignorance — the failures committed “unintentionally,” “by mistake.” Wenham notes the tender provision; not all sin is defiant, and for the sins of frailty and oversight there is full atonement. Whether the whole congregation or a single person sins in ignorance, sacrifice is appointed, and “they shall be forgiven.” Calvin observes the comfort this brings to the tender conscience; the believer who stumbles through weakness rather than defiance has a remedy. Sproul reflected that this distinction is profoundly pastoral. God knows our frame; he distinguishes between the sin of the heart that loves him yet fails, and the sin of the heart that defies him. For the former, there is abundant atonement. There is great relief here for every Christian who is grieved by their many unintended failings; the gospel provides full forgiveness for the sins of weakness. The repeated assurance, “he shall be forgiven,” is balm to the wounded conscience. And it all points to the one sacrifice that covers every unintentional sin — the blood of Christ, which cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). The believer who loves God yet stumbles need not despair; for the sins of frailty there is a Savior whose atonement is more than sufficient, and the gracious word stands: “he shall be forgiven.”

verseByVerse.quote: “But the person who does anything with a high hand, whether he is native or a sojourner, reviles the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from among his people. Because he has despised the word of the LORD and has broken his commandment, that person shall be utterly cut off; his iniquity shall be on him.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the sharp line is drawn. Against the atonable sins of weakness stands the “high-handed” sin — the defiant, deliberate, fist-shaking rebellion that “reviles the LORD.” For this there is no sacrifice mentioned; “that person shall be utterly cut off.” Wenham notes the crucial distinction that governs the whole chapter: the difference is not in the act but in the posture of the heart. To sin with a high hand is to sin in proud defiance, despising God’s word, refusing his authority. Calvin observes that such presumptuous sin is essentially apostasy — a rejection of God himself, not a mere stumbling. Sproul reflected on the sobering theology here; there is a sin of defiance that spurns the very provision of grace, and for the heart that despises God’s word, the sacrifices avail nothing. The phrase “reviles the LORD” (literally, blasphemes) reveals the nature of high-handed sin; it is not weakness but contempt. The New Testament echoes this gravity in its warnings against those who “go on sinning deliberately” and so trample the Son of God underfoot (Heb 10:26–29). The difference between the two sins is the difference between the believer who stumbles and grieves, and the rebel who defies and despises. Yet even here, the gospel goes further than the law dared; the blood of Christ can cleanse even the blasphemer who repents — as Paul, once a blasphemer (1 Tim 1:13), discovered. The line is real, but grace in Christ reaches even to the high-handed who turn and trust.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–41 — The Sabbath-Breaker and the Tassels
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man gathering sticks on the Sabbath is stoned as a case of high-handed sin; Israel is given tassels with a cord of blue as reminders to obey.
verseByVerse.theology: Defiant sin is deadly serious, but God graciously provides visible reminders to keep his commandments and resist wandering hearts.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: tassels of blue to prompt obedience. Now: the believer needs constant reminders of grace to walk in holiness.

verseByVerse.quote: “While the people of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath day. And those who found him gathering sticks brought him to Moses and Aaron... They put him in custody, because it had not been made clear what should be done to him. And the LORD said to Moses, ‘The man shall be put to death; all the congregation shall stone him...’ And all the congregation brought him outside the camp and stoned him to death...”
verseByVerse.commentary: A startling narrative interrupts the laws — a man caught gathering sticks on the Sabbath, and stoned for it. The severity shocks the modern reader, but Wenham notes that this is a deliberate case study of the high-handed sin just described. The man was not gathering sticks in ignorance; the Sabbath law was clear and central, sealed with the death penalty (Exod 31:14–15). His act was open, deliberate defiance of God’s known command — the very “high-handed” sin of verse 30 enacted before the camp. Calvin observes that the gravity of the punishment matches the gravity of despising God’s revealed will; the Sabbath was the sign of the covenant, and its deliberate violation was a public renunciation of allegiance to God. Sproul reflected that we recoil at the severity precisely because we have lost the sense of God’s holiness and the seriousness of defying him. The stoning dramatizes that high-handed rebellion against the holy God is no light matter. Yet there is gospel here, hidden in the horror. The man was taken “outside the camp” to bear the penalty of his sin against God’s law. And Hebrews tells us that Jesus too “suffered outside the gate” (Heb 13:12), bearing the curse of the law-breaker in our place. The one who deserved no death died the death of the high-handed sinner, so that we, who have all defied God’s word, might be spared and brought into the rest the Sabbath foreshadowed.

verseByVerse.quote: “The LORD said to Moses, ‘Speak to the people of Israel, and tell them to make tassels on the corners of their garments throughout their generations, and to put a cord of blue on the tassel of each corner. And it shall be a tassel for you to look at and remember all the commandments of the LORD, to do them, not to follow after your own heart and your own eyes, which you are inclined to whore after. So you shall remember and do all my commandments...’”
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter closes with grace clothed in blue. God commands tassels on the corners of every garment, with a cord of blue, so that Israel will “look at and remember all the commandments of the LORD, to do them.” Wenham notes the tender pedagogy; God knows the human heart is forgetful and prone to wander, and so he provides a visible, daily reminder woven into their very clothing. The cord of blue, the color of heaven and of the priestly garments, marked Israel as a holy people belonging to God. Calvin observes the gracious condescension; God accommodates our weakness, giving tangible aids to memory and obedience. The purpose is explicit and searching: “not to follow after your own heart and your own eyes, which you are inclined to whore after.” The eyes lead the heart astray; the tassels were to catch the eye and turn it back to God. Sproul reflected that we all need such reminders, for the heart drifts and the eyes wander. The tassel was a mercy against our spiritual amnesia. There is deep wisdom here for the believer; we are forgetful creatures who need constant prompts to remember the commands and the grace of God. The Word, the sacraments, the gathering of the saints — these are our tassels, the appointed reminders that turn our wandering eyes back to the Lord. And the closing words, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt,” ground all obedience in redemption: we remember and obey because we have been redeemed.

15.theology:
Grace After Judgment. Immediately after decreeing the wilderness wandering, God says, “When you come into the land which I am giving you.” The promise outlasts the failure; God’s covenant is more durable than his people’s unbelief. His discipline never cancels his grace.

Weakness and Defiance. God distinguishes the unintentional sin of weakness, fully atonable, from the high-handed sin of defiant rebellion that despises his word. Grace abounds for the stumbling believer; but presumptuous contempt for God spurns the very provision of mercy — a warning Hebrews presses upon the church.

Reminders of Grace and Holiness. The tassels of blue are God’s tender provision for forgetful hearts, turning wandering eyes back to his commandments, grounded in redemption: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt.” We obey because we have been redeemed.
15.examples:
Then: The generation barred from the land was given laws for life in the land; a defiant Sabbath-breaker was stoned outside the camp; and Israel was clothed with tassels of blue to remember and obey.

Now: Rest in the grace that covers your stumbling, but beware the high-handed heart that despises God’s word. Christ suffered outside the gate, bearing the law-breaker’s curse for you. Surround yourself with reminders of grace — the Word, the table, the saints — that your wandering eyes may turn back to the Lord who redeemed you.

16.title: Korah’s Rebellion: The One Mediator
16.text: <sup>3</sup>...“You have gone too far! For all in the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?” <sup>48</sup>And he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped.
16.overview:
Chapter 16 records the most serious challenge yet to God’s appointed order — Korah, a Levite, with Dathan and Abiram, leading 250 chiefs in revolt against Moses and Aaron. Their slogan sounds almost pious: “all the congregation are holy... why do you exalt yourselves?” But it is rebellion against God’s own appointment of the priesthood.

The issue is the mediator. Korah wants access to God without the appointed priest; he despises the principle that sinful men may approach the holy God only through the one God appoints. It is, at root, the rejection of mediation itself.

God’s judgment is swift and terrible. The earth opens and swallows Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and their households; fire consumes the 250. Yet even after this, the people grumble against Moses, and a plague breaks out.

Then comes one of the most breathtaking images in all Scripture: Aaron, with his censer of incense, “stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped.” The priest interposes himself, and the wrath is halted. Here is the gospel in a single picture — the mediator standing between the dead and the living, holding back the judgment. It points unmistakably to Christ, our great High Priest, who stands between us and the wrath of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and 250 chiefs challenge Moses and Aaron, claiming all are holy; Moses calls for a test before the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: Rebellion against God’s appointed mediation, however pious its rhetoric, is rebellion against God himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Korah despises the appointed priesthood. Now: a warning against rejecting the one Mediator God has appointed.

verseByVerse.quote: “Now Korah the son of Izhar... and Dathan and Abiram... took men. And they rose up before Moses, with a number of the people of Israel, 250 chiefs of the congregation... And they assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron and said to them, ‘You have gone too far! For all in the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?’”
verseByVerse.commentary: The rebellion is led by Korah, a Levite, joined by Reubenites Dathan and Abiram and 250 prominent chiefs — a formidable coalition of the influential. Wenham notes the dangerous plausibility of their slogan: “all in the congregation are holy... the LORD is among them.” It sounds like a celebration of the priesthood of all believers, even quoting God’s own purpose (Exod 19:6). But the charge — “Why then do you exalt yourselves?” — reveals the poison; they accuse Moses and Aaron of self-promotion, when in fact God appointed them. Calvin observes the subtlety of the rebellion; it cloaks ambition in the language of equality and piety. The truth that all Israel is holy is twisted to overthrow the mediation God himself established. Sproul reflected that this is the perennial pattern of religious rebellion — using a half-truth to reject God’s order. Korah wanted the priesthood without God’s appointment; he resented that access to God came through a mediator he did not choose. Keller noted how often spiritual pride masquerades as a stand for the people; the rhetoric of “we’re all equal” can mask a refusal to submit to God-given authority. At its root, Korah’s rebellion was a rejection of mediation itself — the insistence on coming to God on one’s own terms. And that is the deepest sin of the human heart, answered only by the one Mediator God appointed, whom to reject is to perish.

verseByVerse.quote: “When Moses heard it, he fell on his face, and he said to Korah and all his company, ‘In the morning the LORD will show who is his... Hear now, you sons of Levi: is it too small a thing for you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation... to do service in the tabernacle... and that he has brought you near him...? And would you seek the priesthood also? Therefore it is against the LORD that you and all your company have gathered together.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses, ever the meek mediator, “fell on his face” — not in self-defense but in dependence on God, who alone can vindicate his appointment. Then he exposes the heart of Korah’s sin. As a Levite, Korah already had the immense privilege of being “separated” and “brought near” for tabernacle service — yet he despised it: “is it too small a thing for you?” Wenham notes the diagnosis of discontent; Korah was not content with the high honor God gave him but grasped for the priesthood God withheld. Calvin observes that this is the essence of ambition — to despise one’s own God-given calling and covet another’s. Sproul reflected that contentment with one’s assigned place is a great safeguard against rebellion; discontent is the seedbed of revolt. Moses’ piercing conclusion strips away the pretense: “it is against the LORD that you... have gathered together.” To rebel against God’s appointed mediator is to rebel against God himself. The quarrel was never really with Moses and Aaron; it was with the God who appointed them. There is a sober lesson here for every heart tempted to resent God’s ordering of his church and our place within it. To despise the calling God has given and covet what he has withheld is, at bottom, to quarrel with God. And the one who refuses the mediator God appoints — supremely, the one who refuses Christ — gathers, however unwittingly, against the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: “And Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, and they said, ‘We will not come up. Is it a small thing that you have brought us up out of a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, that you must also make yourself a prince over us? Moreover, you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey... Will you put out the eyes of these men? We will not come up.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: Dathan and Abiram refuse even to come to Moses, hurling a contemptuous reply that turns reality upside down. In a stunning inversion, they call Egypt “a land flowing with milk and honey” — the phrase God reserved for Canaan — while accusing Moses of leading them to die in the wilderness. Wenham notes the breathtaking distortion; the house of slavery is now the land of promise, and the deliverer is now the killer. Calvin observes how rebellion rewrites history to justify itself; the rebels recast their redemption as oppression and their redeemer as a tyrant. Sproul reflected on the blinding power of a rebellious heart, which can call Egypt paradise and freedom bondage. Their charge that Moses would “make himself a prince over us” reveals their real grievance — resentment of authority, the refusal to be ruled. And their accusation that he had not brought them into the land conveniently forgets that their own generation’s unbelief forfeited it (ch 14). The blame is projected entirely onto Moses. Keller noted how the rebellious heart always casts itself as victim and its God-given leaders as oppressors. The flat refusal — “We will not come up,” repeated twice — is the language of hardened defiance. Here is the high-handed sin of chapter 15 embodied: open, deliberate contempt for God’s appointed order. The tragedy is that they were so close to the very land they now slandered, and their refusal to submit would cost them everything.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s glory appears; the earth opens and swallows the rebels and their households, and fire consumes the 250 offering incense.
verseByVerse.theology: God vindicates his appointed mediation with terrible judgment; to usurp the priesthood is to perish before the holy God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the earth swallows the rebels. Now: the fearful seriousness of rejecting God’s appointed way of approach.

verseByVerse.quote: “And Moses was very angry and said to the LORD, ‘Do not respect their offering...’ And Moses said to Korah, ‘Be present, you and all your company, before the LORD... each of you with his censer...’ ... Then the glory of the LORD appeared to all the congregation. And the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying, ‘Separate yourselves from among this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses sets the test: let Korah and the 250 come with censers of incense, and let the LORD show whom he has chosen. Incense was the prerogative of the priests; for the rebels to offer it was to seize the very function in dispute. Wenham notes that the test puts the matter squarely in God’s hands — God himself will decide who may approach him. When “the glory of the LORD appeared,” the verdict was at hand. God’s declaration is terrifying: “that I may consume them in a moment.” Calvin observes the holiness of God that cannot abide the usurpation of his appointed order; to intrude upon the priesthood uninvited is to court destruction. Sproul reflected on the gravity of the scene; the glory that could bless is the glory that can consume, and the unauthorized approach to the holy God is lethal. Yet even here, mercy stirs in the very midst of judgment, as the next verses reveal — Moses and Aaron will intercede for the people God threatens to consume. The appearing of the glory is the pivot of the chapter; God steps forward to settle the dispute himself. The censers of the rebels, meant to vindicate their claim, become the instruments of their doom. The lesson stands stark and clear: God alone determines how he may be approached, and to defy his appointed mediation is to stand before the consuming fire of his holiness unprotected.

verseByVerse.quote: “And Moses said, ‘Hereby you shall know that the LORD has sent me to do all these works... If these men die as all men die... then the LORD has not sent me. But if the LORD creates something new, and the ground opens its mouth and swallows them up... then you shall know that these men have despised the LORD.’ And as soon as he had finished speaking, the ground under them split apart. And the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up... And fire came out from the LORD and consumed the 250 men offering the incense.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The judgment falls exactly as Moses foretold, vindicating his divine appointment beyond all doubt. The earth splits and swallows Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and their households alive into Sheol, while fire from the LORD consumes the 250 who dared offer incense. Wenham notes the “something new” that God creates — an unprecedented act of judgment that leaves no question of natural coincidence. The very ground refuses to bear the rebels. Calvin observes the dreadful demonstration that to despise God’s appointed mediator is to despise the LORD, and that such contempt brings swift destruction. Sproul reflected on the sobering display of divine holiness; the same fire that had consecrated the altar now consumes the presumptuous. The two judgments — the earth below and the fire above — testify that there is no escape for those who defy God’s order, neither in the depths nor in the heights. Yet the gospel reader cannot miss the deeper note. These men perished because they rejected the appointed mediation and tried to approach God on their own terms. It is the very sin of all who would come to God apart from the one Mediator he has appointed. The fearful judgment of Korah is a warning against the deadliest of errors — the refusal of God’s appointed way of approach. And it magnifies the wonder that we who deserve the same judgment are spared, because a better Mediator stood in our place and bore the fire we had earned.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–50 — Aaron Between the Dead and the Living
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rebels’ censers are made into altar plating as a warning; the people grumble again, a plague breaks out, and Aaron’s incense halts it.
verseByVerse.theology: The priest interposes himself between the wrath of God and the people — the gospel in a single image, fulfilled in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Aaron stands between the dead and the living. Now: Christ stands between us and the wrath of God, halting our destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: “Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Tell Eleazar... to take up the censers... and scatter the fire far and wide, for they have become holy. As for the censers of these men who have sinned at the cost of their lives, let them be made into hammered plates as a covering for the altar... to be a reminder...’ But on the next day all the congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron, saying, ‘You have killed the people of the LORD.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: The censers of the dead rebels are hammered into plating for the altar — a permanent “reminder” that no unauthorized person may approach to offer incense. Wenham notes the somber memorial; the very instruments of rebellion become a lasting warning embedded in the place of worship. But astonishingly, the lesson is lost on the people. “On the next day” — incredibly, the very day after the earth swallowed the rebels and fire consumed the 250 — the whole congregation grumbles, accusing Moses and Aaron of having “killed the people of the LORD.” Calvin observes the appalling hardness of the human heart; even the most terrifying judgment cannot soften a people determined to rebel. They call the rebels “the people of the LORD” and blame the mediators for a judgment that came directly from God. Sproul reflected on the staggering persistence of unbelief; here is proof that judgment alone cannot change the heart — only grace can. The people who should have trembled instead doubled down in defiance. There is a sobering realism here about the depth of human depravity; the same hearts that watched the earth open in judgment turned the next morning to accuse God’s servants. It sets the stage for the most beautiful act of the chapter — for in response to this fresh rebellion, the wrath of God breaks out, and the mediator will rush in to stand between the dead and the living.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Get away from the midst of this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment.’ And they fell on their faces. And Moses said to Aaron, ‘Take your censer, and put fire on it from off the altar and lay incense on it and carry it quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from the LORD; the plague has begun.’ ... And he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the gospel painted in fire and incense. The plague breaks out; the people are dying. Moses cries to Aaron, “Carry it quickly... and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from the LORD.” And Aaron, the high priest, runs — runs into the midst of the dying with his censer of incense — and “he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped.” Wenham notes the unforgettable image; the priest interposes his own person and his atoning incense between the wrath of God and the perishing people, and the destruction is halted at the line where he stands. Calvin observes that this is the very office of the mediator — to stand in the breach, to come between divine wrath and sinful man. Sproul preached on this with awe; the priest with the incense is a living picture of intercession, the one who steps into the path of judgment to save the condemned. The same people who, the day before, accused Aaron of killing them are now saved by Aaron’s atoning intercession. The mediator they despised becomes their deliverer. And it points unmistakably to Christ, our great High Priest, who, when the wrath of God had gone out against us, ran into the midst of our death, took his stand between the living and the dead, and by his own atoning sacrifice stopped the plague of judgment forever. Aaron stood at the line and the dying stopped; Christ stood at the cross and death itself was conquered. He stands still, between us and the wrath we deserve, and because he stands, we live.

16.theology:
Rebellion Against the Mediator Is Rebellion Against God. Korah’s pious-sounding slogan masked a refusal of God’s appointed mediation and a grasping for the priesthood God withheld. “It is against the LORD that you have gathered.” To reject the one Mediator God appoints — supremely Christ — is to perish before the holy God.

The Holiness That Consumes. The earth swallowed the rebels and fire consumed the 250. God alone determines how he may be approached, and to defy his appointed way is lethal. The same glory that blesses can consume; we are spared only because a better Mediator bore the fire in our place.

The Priest Between the Dead and the Living. Aaron ran with his censer and “stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped.” Here is the gospel in a single image — the mediator interposing himself to halt the wrath, fulfilled in Christ our High Priest, who stands forever between us and the judgment of God.
16.examples:
Then: Korah grasped for the priesthood and was swallowed by the earth; the people grumbled and a plague broke out; and Aaron ran into the midst of death and stood between the dead and the living until the plague was stopped.

Now: Do not despise the place God has given you or grasp for what he has withheld; rebellion against his order is rebellion against him. And rest in the wonder that Christ, your great High Priest, has run into the midst of your death and stands between you and the wrath of God. Because he stands, the plague is stopped, and you live.

17.title: Aaron’s Staff Buds: Resurrection and the Confirmed Priesthood
17.text: <sup>8</sup>And behold, the staff of Aaron for the house of Levi had sprouted and put forth buds and produced blossoms, and it bore ripe almonds.
17.overview:
After the trauma of Korah’s rebellion, God gives a quiet, beautiful sign to settle the question of the priesthood forever. Twelve staffs — one for each tribe — are laid up before the LORD overnight. In the morning, only Aaron’s staff has come alive: it has “sprouted and put forth buds and produced blossoms, and it bore ripe almonds.”

A dead stick blossoming and bearing fruit — here is resurrection logic. God confirms his chosen priest not by power or argument but by bringing life out of death. The other staffs remained dead wood; Aaron’s alone was raised to vibrant, fruitful life.

The almond is significant. In Hebrew, the almond tree (shaqed) is the “waker,” the first tree to bloom, the herald of new life. Aaron’s staff bearing almonds proclaims that the true priest is the one God awakens to life.

The staff is then kept before the testimony as a perpetual sign against rebellion. And it points unerringly to Christ, whose priesthood is confirmed not by a budding stick but by the empty tomb. As Aaron’s dead staff was raised to bear fruit, so Christ was “declared to be the Son of God in power... by his resurrection” (Rom 1:4), the true and living High Priest forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Twelve Staffs Laid Up
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commands a staff from each tribe, with Aaron’s name on Levi’s, to be placed before the testimony to settle the question of the priesthood.
verseByVerse.theology: God will end the grumbling not by argument but by a sign, choosing his priest through a demonstration of life.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: twelve dead staffs laid before the LORD. Now: God settles disputes by his own vindicating act, not human contention.

verseByVerse.quote: “The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Speak to the people of Israel, and get from them staffs, one for each fathers’ house... twelve staffs. Write each man’s name on his staff, and write Aaron’s name on the staff of Levi... Then you shall deposit them in the tent of meeting before the testimony, where I meet with you. And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: After the violence of Korah’s rebellion, God moves to settle the question of the priesthood once and for all — and he does it gently, with a sign rather than a slaughter. Twelve staffs, one per tribe, each bearing its leader’s name, are laid before the testimony, and “the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout.” Wenham notes the wisdom of the method; rather than continued judgment, God gives a quiet, unmistakable confirmation that will silence the grumbling. The staff — a dead piece of wood, a symbol of authority but also of lifelessness — becomes the instrument of God’s choice. Calvin observes that God condescends to the weakness of his people, giving a tangible proof to end their endless disputes. Sproul reflected that God’s purpose, “I will make to cease... the grumblings,” reveals his patient mercy; even after repeated rebellion, he seeks to bring his people to rest rather than to ruin. There is grace in this approach. God could have answered the grumbling with more fire; instead he answers with a living sign. The staffs are deposited “where I meet with you,” in the very presence of God, so that the choice will be his alone, beyond all human manipulation. The stage is set for a miracle that will speak more powerfully than any argument — for God will choose his priest not by debate but by bringing life out of death.

verseByVerse.quote: “Moses spoke to the people of Israel. And all their chiefs gave him staffs, one for each chief, according to their fathers’ houses, twelve staffs. And the staff of Aaron was among their staffs. And Moses deposited the staffs before the LORD in the tent of the testimony.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The staffs are gathered and laid up before the LORD — twelve dead sticks, indistinguishable, each the symbol of a tribe’s authority. Wenham notes the deliberate equality of the setup; “the staff of Aaron was among their staffs,” no different in appearance, given no special placement. The test is utterly fair; whatever happens will be God’s doing, not human contrivance. Calvin observes that by depositing them “before the LORD,” Moses removes the matter entirely from human hands; the verdict will rest with God alone, overnight, in the secret place of his presence. There is a quiet drama in this scene — twelve lifeless staffs lying in the darkness of the tent, while the people wait to see what the morning will reveal. Sproul reflected that this is faith’s posture: to lay the matter before God and wait for his vindication. The staffs are dead wood; nothing in them can produce life. Whatever sprouts will sprout by the power of God alone. The very ordinariness of the staffs heightens the wonder to come; there is no trick, no advantage, no human explanation possible. When one of these dead sticks comes alive, all will know that God has spoken. The scene anticipates the greater darkness of a sealed tomb, where the dead body of the true Priest lay through the night, until the morning when God would bring forth life and vindicate his Chosen One forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Budding Staff and the Fear of the People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Aaron’s staff alone sprouts, buds, blossoms, and bears almonds; it is kept as a sign, and the people cry out in fear of the holy God.
verseByVerse.theology: God confirms his priest by bringing life from dead wood — resurrection logic that points to Christ’s vindication.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a dead staff bears living fruit. Now: Christ’s priesthood confirmed by resurrection, the living High Priest forever.

verseByVerse.quote: “On the next day Moses went into the tent of the testimony, and behold, the staff of Aaron for the house of Levi had sprouted and put forth buds and produced blossoms, and it bore ripe almonds.”
verseByVerse.commentary: In the morning, the miracle is revealed: Aaron’s staff alone has come alive. Not merely sprouted, but “put forth buds and produced blossoms, and it bore ripe almonds” — the entire life cycle of a fruit tree compressed into a single night, in a dead stick severed from any root. Wenham notes the overwhelming abundance of the sign; God did not give a single bud but the full flourishing of buds, blossoms, and ripe fruit all at once, a superabundant testimony to his choice. Here is resurrection logic in its purest form: life out of death, fruit from dead wood. The other staffs remained lifeless; Aaron’s alone was raised. Calvin observes that God thus confirmed the priesthood not by human strength or argument but by a creative act of life-giving power that no one could counterfeit or deny. Sproul reflected on the beauty of the sign; God vindicates his chosen one by resurrection, the bringing of life where there was only death. The almond is rich with meaning — in Hebrew the almond tree (shaqed) is the “waker,” the first tree to bloom in spring, the herald of new life after winter. Aaron’s staff bearing almonds proclaims that the true priest is the one God awakens to life. And it points unerringly to Christ, whose priesthood is confirmed not by a budding staff but by the empty tomb; as the dead staff was raised to bear fruit, so Christ was “declared to be the Son of God in power... by his resurrection from the dead” (Rom 1:4), the living High Priest forever.

verseByVerse.quote: “Then Moses brought out all the staffs from before the LORD to all the people of Israel. And they looked, and each man took his staff. And the LORD said to Moses, ‘Put back the staff of Aaron before the testimony, to be kept as a sign for the rebels, that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die.’ Thus did Moses; as the LORD commanded him, so he did.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The verdict is shown to all Israel — each man takes back his own dead staff, while Aaron’s living, fruit-bearing staff is set apart. The contrast is undeniable; eleven sticks of dead wood and one alive with almonds. Wenham notes that the budding staff is then preserved “before the testimony, to be kept as a sign for the rebels,” a permanent memorial to silence all future challenges to the priesthood. The phrase “lest they die” reveals the mercy beneath the sign; God gives this enduring proof precisely to spare his people from the deadly consequences of continued rebellion. Calvin observes that God’s purpose is preservation, not destruction; the sign is a kindness, meant to “make an end of their grumblings” and thus to keep them from perishing. Sproul reflected that God’s warnings are themselves acts of grace, designed to turn his people from the path of death. The living staff, kept beside the tablets of the testimony, would stand as a witness across the generations that God himself had chosen Aaron’s line. The writer of Hebrews tells us this very staff was kept in the ark (Heb 9:4), a perpetual testimony to God’s sovereign appointment of his priest. And the closing words sound the familiar refrain of obedience: “as the LORD commanded him, so he did.” Moses, as ever, obeys to the letter. The living staff preserved in the holiest place is a quiet, abiding sermon — God chooses his priest, and confirms him by life from the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the people of Israel said to Moses, ‘Behold, we perish, we are undone, we are all undone. Everyone who comes near, who comes near to the tabernacle of the LORD, shall die. Are we all to perish?’”
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends not with triumph but with terror. The people, having witnessed the swallowing of Korah, the fire on the 250, the plague, and now the budding staff, cry out in dread: “Behold, we perish... Everyone who comes near... shall die. Are we all to perish?” Wenham notes the genuine spiritual crisis here; the people have finally grasped the lethal holiness of God and the deadly danger of approaching him. Their cry is the cry of sinful man confronted with the unapproachable holiness of the Almighty. Calvin observes that this fear, though painful, was salutary; it taught them the necessity of mediation, that no one may come near the holy God except through the appointed priest. Sproul reflected that this is the right and proper response of the sinner who truly sees God’s holiness — “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isa 6:5). The people are not wrong; apart from a mediator, to draw near to the holy God is indeed to die. Their terror sets up the answer of chapter 18, which assures them that the priests and Levites will bear the danger of the sanctuary on their behalf. But more deeply, their cry expresses the universal human predicament — how can sinful people draw near to a holy God and not perish? The whole sacrificial system, the whole priesthood, the whole of Numbers, presses toward the gospel answer: through a mediator who bears the death we deserve. The people’s desperate question, “Are we all to perish?” finds its final answer in Christ, the living High Priest, through whom we draw near not in terror but in confidence, and live.

17.theology:
Resurrection Vindicates the Priest. God confirms his chosen priest not by argument but by bringing life from dead wood — Aaron’s staff buds, blossoms, and bears almonds overnight. This resurrection logic points to Christ, whose priesthood is confirmed by the empty tomb; he was “declared to be the Son of God in power... by his resurrection.”

The Almond, Herald of Life. The almond, Hebrew shaqed, the “waker,” is the first tree to bloom. Aaron’s staff bearing almonds proclaims that the true priest is the one God awakens to life — the living High Priest who, having died, lives forever to make intercession.

The Terror of Holiness and the Need for a Mediator. The people cry, “we perish... are we all to perish?” Apart from a mediator, to approach the holy God is death. Their dread presses toward the gospel: through the appointed priest — supremely Christ — we draw near and live.
17.examples:
Then: Twelve dead staffs were laid before the LORD; in the morning Aaron’s alone had blossomed and borne almonds, confirming God’s chosen priest by life from the dead, while the people trembled before the holy God.

Now: Your High Priest is confirmed by a greater sign than a budding staff — the empty tomb. The dead wood that bore living fruit foreshadows the risen Christ, who lives forever to intercede for you. Draw near to the holy God not in terror but in confidence, through the living Priest whom God raised and vindicated.

18.title: Duties of Priests and Levites: ‘I Am Your Portion’
18.text: <sup>20</sup>And the LORD said to Aaron, “You shall have no inheritance in their land, neither shall you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel.”
18.overview:
Chapter 18 answers the people’s terrified cry of chapter 17 — “Are we all to perish?” — with a gracious provision: the priests and Levites will bear the danger of the sanctuary on the people’s behalf. The mediators will guard the holy things and shield the congregation from the wrath that holiness provokes.

The priests are charged with the most sacred duties and warned of their grave responsibility; they “bear iniquity” connected with the sanctuary. The Levites assist them, given as a gift to the priesthood. And both are supported not by land but by the offerings of the people.

The crown of the chapter is verse 20: “I am your portion and your inheritance.” The priests receive no allotment of land, for they have something infinitely better — God himself. The tribe that owns no fields possesses the LORD.

This is one of the great treasures of Scripture. To have God as one’s portion is to be richer than all the landed tribes combined. Asaph would later sing it (Ps 73:26), and the New Testament makes it the inheritance of every believer in Christ. The priesthood that owned no land but possessed God points to the saints, who in Christ inherit not earth merely but the God of heaven.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Charge of the Priests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests and Levites bear the responsibility for the sanctuary, guarding it so that wrath may not fall on the people.
verseByVerse.theology: The mediators bear the danger of holiness on the people’s behalf, answering the people’s fear of perishing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: priests guard the sanctuary lest wrath fall. Now: Christ our High Priest bears the danger of holiness for us.

verseByVerse.quote: “So the LORD said to Aaron, ‘You and your sons and your fathers’ house with you shall bear iniquity connected with the sanctuary, and you and your sons with you shall bear iniquity connected with your priesthood... They shall keep guard over you and over the whole tent, but shall not come near to the vessels of the sanctuary or to the altar lest they, and you, die.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: God answers the people’s terror directly to Aaron: “You and your sons... shall bear iniquity connected with the sanctuary.” Wenham notes the profound provision; the priests will bear the responsibility and danger of the holy things on behalf of the whole nation. The people had cried, “Are we all to perish?” and God’s answer is that the priesthood will stand in the gap, absorbing the danger that holiness poses. Calvin observes that this is the very heart of the priestly office — to bear the iniquity, to carry the weight of approach to God so that the people need not be consumed. The repeated boundaries (“shall not come near... lest they, and you, die”) preserve the graded holiness that protects everyone. Sproul reflected on the weight of mediation laid upon the priests; theirs is a perilous privilege, bearing the burden of the sanctuary that the people might live. There is gospel depth here. To “bear iniquity” is the language of substitution; the priest carries what would otherwise fall on the people. And it points unmistakably to Christ, our great High Priest, who did not merely guard the sanctuary but “bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Pet 2:24), bearing the full weight of iniquity so that we, who deserved to perish, might draw near and live. The priests’ bearing of sanctuary-iniquity is a shadow; Christ’s bearing of our sin is the substance. He took the danger of holiness fully upon himself.

verseByVerse.quote: “‘And you shall keep guard over the sanctuary and over the altar, that there may never again be wrath on the people of Israel. And behold, I have taken your brothers the Levites from among the people of Israel. They are a gift to you, given to the LORD, to do the service of the tent of meeting. And you and your sons with you shall guard your priesthood for all that concerns the altar... I give your priesthood as a gift, and any outsider who comes near shall be put to death.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: The purpose is stated plainly: “that there may never again be wrath on the people of Israel.” Wenham notes that the priestly guarding of the sanctuary is fundamentally protective; it shields the people from the wrath that careless approach to the holy God provokes. The memory of Korah and the plague is fresh; the priesthood stands as the appointed safeguard against such judgment. The Levites are described again as “a gift” to the priests, and remarkably, the priesthood itself is called “a gift” God gives: “I give your priesthood as a gift.” Calvin observes the grace embedded in this language; the priesthood is not a human achievement or right but a divine gift, freely bestowed. Sproul reflected that all true ministry is a gift of God, never a possession to be seized — the very lesson Korah failed to learn. The repeated warning, “any outsider who comes near shall be put to death,” preserves the seriousness of the appointed mediation. But the dominant note is grace: God gives the Levites, gives the priesthood, gives the means by which his people may safely draw near. The whole arrangement is a gift designed to make a way for sinful people to live in the presence of a holy God. And it all anticipates the supreme gift — the Father who “gave his only Son” (John 3:16), the great High Priest given to guard us forever from wrath, so that for those in Christ “there is therefore now no condemnation” (Rom 8:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–19 — The Provision for the Priests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests are supported by the offerings, firstfruits, and devoted things of the people — their portion from the LORD’s table.
verseByVerse.theology: Those who serve at the altar live from the altar; God provides for his ministers through the gifts of his people.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: priests fed from the offerings. Now: those who preach the gospel live from the gospel, as God provides for his servants.

verseByVerse.quote: “Then the LORD spoke to Aaron, ‘Behold, I have given you charge of the contributions made to me, all the consecrated things of the people of Israel. I have given them to you as a portion and to your sons as a perpetual due... Every offering of theirs, every grain offering... that they render to me, shall be most holy to you and to your sons. ... Everyone who is clean in your house may eat it.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: Having no land of their own, the priests are provided for from the offerings of the people — “I have given you charge of the contributions made to me... as a portion.” Wenham notes the principle; the priests live from the very gifts the people bring to God. What is offered to the LORD becomes the sustenance of those who minister at his altar. Calvin observes the fittingness of this arrangement; those who devote themselves wholly to the service of the sanctuary, owning no fields, are sustained by the worship they facilitate. The portions are called “most holy,” to be eaten in reverence by the clean of the priestly household. Sproul reflected on the enduring principle that Paul draws from this very arrangement; “those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel” (1 Cor 9:14), and “the laborer deserves his wages” (1 Tim 5:18). God ordains that his ministers be supported by his people, freed from the need to provide for themselves so they may give themselves to the work. There is dignity in this; the priests do not beg but receive what God himself has assigned them from his own table. The provision is generous and abundant, drawn from the firstfruits, the offerings, and the consecrated things. And it teaches a gospel principle still binding on the church — that God’s people are to support those who minister the word and sacraments among them, sharing their material good with those who serve them spiritually.

verseByVerse.quote: “‘Everything that opens the womb of all flesh... shall be yours. Nevertheless, the firstborn of man you shall redeem... All the best of the oil and all the best of the wine and of the grain, the firstfruits of what they give to the LORD, I give to you. ... It is a covenant of salt forever before the LORD for you and for your offspring with you.’”
