The seven altars go up again on the field of Zophim, on the top of Pisgah, and the animals are killed again, and the whole ruinously expensive ritual is repeated on the assumption that the failure was technical.

People do this in church. When God has plainly said no, the temptation is not usually to defy him outright but to seek a different vantage point — another counsellor, another passage, another translation, another congregation — until the view is narrow enough that the answer we wanted looks defensible. Balak was not a stupid man. He simply could not accept that the obstacle was not the arrangement but the Almighty.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD met Balaam and put a word in his mouth and said, "Return to Balak, and thus shall you speak." And he came to him, and behold, he was standing beside his burnt offering, and the princes of Moab with him. And Balak said to him, "What has the LORD spoken?" And Balaam took up his discourse and said, "Rise, Balak, and hear; give ear to me, O son of Zippor: God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not fulfill it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second oracle begins with a summons rather than a report — Rise, Balak, and hear; give ear to me, O son of Zippor — and the king of Moab is made to stand up beside his own burnt offering and be lectured. What follows is one of the towering statements about God in the Old Testament, and it is delivered by a man who has been trying to get round it for three days.

God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not fulfill it? Two things are denied here, and they are the two things men do constantly. We say what is not so, and we say what we mean and then go back on it. God does neither. He is not capable of either — God, who never lies (Titus 1:2), and who confirmed his promise with an oath so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement (Heb. 6:18).

A fair question arises, and it should be answered rather than dodged: does Scripture not also say that God relented — over Nineveh, or after Moses interceded at Sinai (Exod. 32:14; Jonah 3:10)? It does, and those passages are describing something different. They speak of God’s settled and unchanging character meeting a changed human situation: he had always been the God who spares the repentant, and Nineveh repented. What this verse denies is that God is fickle, that his word can be renegotiated, or that his promise might quietly lapse. And the living proof is standing on the mountain saying it. Balaam has now asked three times for a different answer, from three directions, at enormous cost. God has not moved an inch, and the man in his pay is being made to announce it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I received a command to bless: he has blessed, and I cannot revoke it. He has not beheld misfortune in Jacob, nor has he seen trouble in Israel. The LORD their God is with them, and the shout of a king is among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I received a command to bless: he has blessed, and I cannot revoke it. There is the position stated with total clarity by the one person in the story who most wishes it were otherwise. The blessing is not Balaam’s to give and therefore not his to withdraw. Nobody can revoke it, because nobody issued it but God.

Then verse 21, and it is the hardest sentence in the chapter: He has not beheld misfortune in Jacob, nor has he seen trouble in Israel. The two Hebrew words carry a range: they can mean disaster and hardship, as the ESV takes them, or they can mean iniquity and wickedness, which is how many older versions read them. Read the first way, the line says that no calamity can overtake this people because the LORD their God is with them. Read the second, it says something even more startling — that God does not look upon iniquity in his covenant people. Godly readers have taken it both ways, and the sentence is genuinely open.

But on either reading the direction of the verse is the same, and it points forward. God had spent twenty-two chapters recording exactly what was wrong with this nation. He knew. And to an outsider hired to find a fault he could exploit, the answer given is that there is nothing there to be used. Whatever the precise force of the Hebrew, what stands behind such a statement is the truth Paul will make explicit: Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin (Rom. 4:7–8). God saw everything Israel was, and set his blessing on them anyway, and would not permit one syllable against them to be spoken on a foreign mountain. That is not because sin does not matter. It is because he had already determined what he would do about it, on a hill of his own choosing, fourteen centuries later.

verseByVerse.quote: God brings them out of Egypt and is for them like the horns of the wild ox. For there is no enchantment against Jacob, no divination against Israel; now it shall be said of Jacob and Israel, 'What has God wrought!' Behold, a people! As a lioness it rises up and as a lion it lifts itself; it does not lie down until it has devoured the prey and drunk the blood of the slain."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The oracle now piles up images of a strength Moab cannot touch. God brings them out of Egypt and is for them like the horns of the wild ox. The wild ox — the aurochs, the great untamed bull of the ancient world, an animal nobody yoked — is not a picture of Israel here but of God for Israel. Their power is on loan, and the loan is the point.

Then the flat demolition of Balak’s entire business plan: For there is no enchantment against Jacob, no divination against Israel. The professional diviner announces, from the top of his own seven altars, that divination does not work on these people. It is not that Balaam is bad at his job. It is that the job cannot be done. And so the nations end up saying, not what has Israel achieved, but What has God wrought! — a line so charged that when Samuel Morse sent the first telegraph message in 1844 he could think of nothing better to put on the wire.

The last image is the fiercest: Behold, a people! As a lioness it rises up and as a lion it lifts itself. Balak had described Israel as an ox with its head down, grazing (22:4). God describes them as a lion getting up. And there is a line running out of this verse that ends in the last book of the Bible, where the one who rises and is not roused by anybody is named at last: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered (Rev. 5:5). The strength the nations feared in the camp was never really the camp’s. It was the strength of the One who would one day be born inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balak said to Balaam, "Do not curse them at all, and do not bless them at all." But Balaam answered Balak, "Did I not tell you, 'All that the LORD says, that I must do'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balak has had enough. Do not curse them at all, and do not bless them at all. Having failed to purchase a curse, he tries to purchase silence — and cannot get that either. He has now lost twice: he cannot make Balaam say what he wants, and he cannot make him stop saying what he does not want.

There is genuine comedy here, and Scripture means us to see it. A king with an army, a treasury and a hired seer stands on a mountain trying to switch off the word of God like a man slapping a radio, and the blessings keep coming. He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision (Ps. 2:4).

Balaam’s answer — Did I not tell you, “All that the LORD says, that I must do”? — is once again perfectly correct and once again spoken by a man still standing beside the altars, still on the payroll, still willing to walk up one more hill. He is now three for three on telling Balak the truth and three for three on staying for the fee.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–30 — Preparing for a Third Attempt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Still Balak will not give up. He takes Balaam to yet another height, Peor, and builds seven more altars, hoping against hope that this time the curse will come. His stubbornness against God is almost pitiable — and utterly futile.
verseByVerse.theology: Balak’s third attempt (vv.27-30) shows the futility and folly of persisting against God’s revealed will. He keeps changing locations and rebuilding altars, as if the problem were the setting rather than the sovereign God. It is a portrait of stubborn opposition to God that will not learn — and cannot win (Prov 21:30).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twice refused, Balak tried a third hilltop and seven more altars — endlessly rearranging the ritual, never reckoning with the God behind it.

Now: fighting against God’s settled purpose only wastes the fighter. “Whoever knows the right thing to do” must submit to it, not keep looking for a hill from which it might turn out differently.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balak said to Balaam, "Come now, I will take you to another place. Perhaps it will please God that you may curse them for me from there." So Balak took Balaam to the top of Peor, which overlooks the desert. And Balaam said to Balak, "Build for me here seven altars and prepare for me here seven bulls and seven rams." And Balak did as Balaam had said, and offered a bull and a ram on each altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Astonishingly, they go again. Come now, I will take you to another place. Perhaps it will please God that you may curse them for me from there. Perhaps — the same word Balaam used on the first mountain. Two men who have now watched God override them twice are still trying the same door, and their entire theology is contained in that adverb.

And the place they choose should make the reader go cold. So Balak took Balaam to the top of Peor, which overlooks the desert. Peor. Hold that name. In two chapters’ time, Israel will be camped in the valley below this very hill, and the men of Israel will be drawn into the sacrifices of Baal of Peor, and twenty-four thousand of them will die of a plague (25:3, 9). Everything Balak wanted will happen — at this location, involving this people, with this man’s fingerprints on it, because Balaam will go home by way of one last piece of advice about how to get at a nation you cannot curse (31:16; Rev. 2:14).

So the chapter ends with the altars going up a third time, in the one place where the enemy will eventually succeed. It is a warning laid quietly in the geography. No enchantment could touch Israel; no army could reach her; three days of the most expensive sorcery in the ancient world produced nothing but blessing. And the ruin, when it came, walked into the camp on its own feet and was welcomed. The people of God have never been in serious danger from the mountain. The danger has always been in the valley.

24.title: Balaam's Final Oracles: A Star Shall Come Out of Jacob
24.text: <sup>1</sup>When Balaam saw that it pleased the LORD to bless Israel, he did not go, as at other times, to look for omens, but set his face toward the wilderness.<sup>2</sup>And Balaam lifted up his eyes and saw Israel camping tribe by tribe. And the Spirit of God came upon him,<sup>3</sup>and he took up his discourse and said, "The oracle of Balaam the son of Beor, the oracle of the man whose eye is opened,<sup>4</sup>the oracle of him who hears the words of God, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down with his eyes uncovered:<sup>5</sup>How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, your encampments, O Israel!<sup>6</sup>Like palm groves that stretch afar, like gardens beside a river, like aloes that the LORD has planted, like cedar trees beside the waters.<sup>7</sup>Water shall flow from his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters; his king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted.<sup>8</sup>God brings him out of Egypt and is for him like the horns of the wild ox; he shall eat up the nations, his adversaries, and shall break their bones in pieces and pierce them through with his arrows.<sup>9</sup>He crouched, he lay down like a lion and like a lioness; who will rouse him up? Blessed are those who bless you, and cursed are those who curse you."<sup>10</sup>And Balak's anger was kindled against Balaam, and he struck his hands together. And Balak said to Balaam, "I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed them these three times.<sup>11</sup>Therefore now flee to your own place. I said, 'I will certainly honor you,' but the LORD has held you back from honor."<sup>12</sup>And Balaam said to Balak, "Did I not tell your messengers whom you sent to me,<sup>13</sup>'If Balak should give me his house full of silver and gold, I would not be able to go beyond the word of the LORD, to do either good or bad of my own will. What the LORD speaks, that will I speak'?<sup>14</sup>And now, behold, I am going to my people. Come, I will let you know what this people will do to your people in the latter days."<sup>15</sup>And he took up his discourse and said, "The oracle of Balaam the son of Beor, the oracle of the man whose eye is opened,<sup>16</sup>the oracle of him who hears the words of God, and knows the knowledge of the Most High, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down with his eyes uncovered:<sup>17</sup>I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel; it shall crush the forehead of Moab and break down all the sons of Sheth.<sup>18</sup>Edom shall be dispossessed; Seir also, his enemies, shall be dispossessed. Israel is doing valiantly.<sup>19</sup>And one from Jacob shall exercise dominion and destroy the survivors of cities!"<sup>20</sup>Then he looked on Amalek and took up his discourse and said, "Amalek was the first among the nations, but its end is utter destruction."<sup>21</sup>And he looked on the Kenite, and took up his discourse and said, "Enduring is your dwelling place, and your nest is set in the rock.<sup>22</sup>Nevertheless, Kain shall be burned when Asshur takes you away captive."<sup>23</sup>And he took up his discourse and said, "Alas, who shall live when God does this?<sup>24</sup>But ships shall come from Kittim and shall afflict Asshur and Eber; and he too shall come to utter destruction."<sup>25</sup>Then Balaam rose and went back to his place. And Balak also went his way.
24.overview:
The Balaam saga reaches its glorious climax. By now Balaam no longer even resorts to omens; the Spirit of God comes upon him, and his eyes are opened. The third oracle pours out a vision of Israel's beauty and flourishing — “How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, your encampments, O Israel!” (v. 5) — words still sung at the door of synagogues to this day. The hireling who came to curse stands transfixed by the loveliness of the people of God.

But the fourth oracle soars highest of all, into outright Messianic prophecy. “I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel” (v. 17). Balaam sees, across the centuries, the coming of a King — a royal Star, a ruling Scepter — who will arise from Israel and triumph over all her enemies. Sproul and others have long understood this as one of the great Old Testament Messianic prophecies, looking forward to the King who would come from Jacob's line. When the magi from the East followed a star to Bethlehem to worship the newborn King of the Jews (Matt 2), many have heard the echo of Balaam's ancient oracle: the Star out of Jacob had risen at last.

The wonder is who speaks this prophecy: not a faithful Israelite but a pagan, mercenary seer, overruled by the Spirit of God to proclaim the coming of the Messiah. Ferguson notes the sovereign freedom of God, who can put the gospel of the coming King even in the mouth of his enemy. The God who would not let Balaam curse his people compelled him instead to prophesy the King who would save them. And so the deepest comfort of the whole Balaam narrative arrives: the security of God's people rests on the coming of God's King. The Star has risen; the Scepter has been raised; and the Lord Jesus reigns over all who would oppose his people, “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev 19:16).
24.theology:
The Star out of Jacob. Balaam prophesies a coming royal King from Israel, a great Messianic oracle fulfilled in Christ, the Star and Scepter, whose star rose over Bethlehem.

God's sovereign freedom. God overrules even a pagan, mercenary prophet to proclaim the coming Messiah. He can put the gospel in the mouth of his enemy.

The King secures his people. The security of God's people rests on the coming of God's King, who reigns over every hostile nation as King of kings and Lord of lords.
24.examples:
Then: The Spirit overcame Balaam, who beheld the loveliness of Israel and prophesied a Star out of Jacob, a coming King who would crush every enemy.

Now: The Star has risen. The King foretold by a pagan seer has come, and he reigns. Your security rests not in yourself but in Christ the Scepter of Israel, before whom every enemy will bow and every curse be turned to blessing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This time Balaam does not even resort to omens; the Spirit of God comes upon him, and he blesses Israel with a vision of beauty and abundance — “How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, your encampments, O Israel!” He sees a people planted like gardens beside a river, a kingdom exalted, and he ends with the ancient words of the Abrahamic promise: “Blessed are those who bless you, and cursed are those who curse you.”
verseByVerse.theology: The third oracle echoes the Abrahamic covenant almost verbatim (v.9; cf. Gen 12:3; 27:29) — God confirming through a pagan’s mouth the very promise he swore to the patriarchs. That “the Spirit of God came upon him” (v.2) shows God commandeering even an unwilling instrument to bless his people. The blessing reaches its climax in the fourth oracle’s messianic hope, but already here Israel’s flourishing is portrayed as God’s own planting (“like gardens beside a river,” v.6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a diviner hired to curse Israel instead pronounced over them the very blessing of Abraham, moved by the Spirit of God.

Now: the promise still stands over God’s people in Christ, the true offspring of Abraham (Gal 3:16, 29): blessed, planted, flourishing — and no curse can undo it.

verseByVerse.quote: When Balaam saw that it pleased the LORD to bless Israel, he did not go, as at other times, to look for omens, but set his face toward the wilderness. And Balaam lifted up his eyes and saw Israel camping tribe by tribe. And the Spirit of God came upon him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Balaam saw that it pleased the LORD to bless Israel, he did not go, as at other times, to look for omens, but set his face toward the wilderness. Something has finally broken through. Three times he has built the altars and gone off to a bare height to see whether the signs would come out differently, and three times the answer has been the same. He gives up the apparatus. No more omens. He simply turns and looks at the camp.

And what happens next is one of the strangest sentences in the Old Testament. And Balaam lifted up his eyes and saw Israel camping tribe by tribe. And the Spirit of God came upon him. The Spirit of God, on a man for hire.

Do not let that pass without explanation, because it can confuse a reader badly. In the Old Testament the Spirit characteristically comes upon a man to equip him for a task — Samson for strength, Bezalel for craftsmanship, Saul for prophecy after God had rejected him (1 Sam. 19:23–24) — and that coming is not the same thing as a new heart. It is an equipping, and it can be given to a man who is not saved and taken away from a man who is. What Christians are promised is something else and something better: not the Spirit descending on them for a job, but the Spirit taking up residence in them for ever — the Spirit of God dwells in you (Rom. 8:9), he will be in you (John 14:17). Balaam was used. He was never indwelt. There is all the difference in the world between the two, and this chapter is the proof.

verseByVerse.quote: and he took up his discourse and said, "The oracle of Balaam the son of Beor, the oracle of the man whose eye is opened, the oracle of him who hears the words of God, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down with his eyes uncovered:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The oracle opens with a formal self-description, repeated almost word for word at verse 15: The oracle of Balaam the son of Beor, the oracle of the man whose eye is opened, the oracle of him who hears the words of God, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down with his eyes uncovered.

It is a professional’s letterhead, and it is dripping with irony that the reader is meant to catch. The man whose eye is opened — this is the man who two chapters ago sat on a donkey and could not see an armed angel four feet in front of him while the animal underneath him could. Whatever sight he now has is not native to him; God opened his eyes then and God is opening them now, and the seer is the last person in the account to see anything.

Falling down with his eyes uncovered pictures a man flat on the ground and wide awake. He is not asleep, not in a trance, not working himself into anything. He is prostrate, conscious, and being spoken through. And the whole apparatus of pagan religion — the omens, the altars, the fee, the technique — has been stripped away one item at a time until there is nothing left but a man on his face and a word coming out of him that he did not choose and cannot stop.

verseByVerse.quote: How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, your encampments, O Israel! Like palm groves that stretch afar, like gardens beside a river, like aloes that the LORD has planted, like cedar trees beside the waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, your encampments, O Israel! Of all the sentences in Numbers, this is the one the Jewish people have loved most; it opens the morning liturgy, and for centuries a Jew entering the synagogue to pray has begun with these words. They were composed by a pagan diviner standing on a mountain in the pay of a man who wanted the whole camp dead.

Then look at the pictures, and notice what they all have in common. Like palm groves that stretch afar, like gardens beside a river, like aloes that the LORD has planted, like cedar trees beside the waters. Every single one is wet. Palm groves, a river, planted aloes, cedars standing in water — and Balaam is looking down at a tent city pitched in a desert, where the whole nation has spent forty years arguing about where the next drink is coming from. He is not describing what is in front of his eyes. He is describing what God sees when he looks at them, and what God intends to make of them.

And the middle image gives the reason: like aloes that the LORD has planted. Not aloes that grew there. Not a people who turned out well. Planted — by hand, deliberately, in ground the gardener chose. Israel’s loveliness is entirely derivative, and so is the church’s: You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit (John 15:16). What the enemy saw from the mountain that morning was not a nation’s achievement. It was God’s gardening, seen from a distance, and it was beautiful.

verseByVerse.quote: Water shall flow from his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters; his king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted. God brings him out of Egypt and is for him like the horns of the wild ox; he shall eat up the nations, his adversaries, and shall break their bones in pieces and pierce them through with his arrows. He crouched, he lay down like a lion and like a lioness; who will rouse him up? Blessed are those who bless you, and cursed are those who curse you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The oracle now runs forward past anything Balaam could have known. Water shall flow from his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters; his king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted. A king. Israel has no king, will not have one for nearly four centuries, and is at this moment a refugee column with a tent for a capital. Agag is the royal title of the Amalekites, the great power of the southern desert, and the oracle says the coming king of this landless people will overtop him — which is exactly what happened when Saul and then David broke Amalek (1 Sam. 15).

Then the images of strength repeat from the last oracle and intensify. God is for him like the horns of the wild ox; the nation crouched, he lay down like a lion and like a lioness; who will rouse him up? The picture is not of a beast on the hunt but of one lying down — a lion at rest, which is more frightening than a lion on its feet, because it means the lion is not worried. Israel is asleep in the valley. Nobody is going to wake her.

And then the last line, and it is the most delicious sentence in the whole Balaam narrative: Blessed are those who bless you, and cursed are those who curse you. That is the promise God made to Abraham — I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse (Gen. 12:3) — and Balak has paid a fortune, sent two embassies, killed forty-two animals and climbed three mountains to have it reversed. Instead he stands beside his own smoking altar and hears it recited over him, by his own employee, at his own expense. The curse he purchased has turned round in the air and come down on the man who bought it. Nobody outbids God for the last word about his people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Balak explodes. He struck his hands together in rage: “I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed them these three times.” He drives Balaam away without his reward. But Balaam, before he goes, warns the king that he has one more thing to say — what Israel will do to Moab “in the latter days.”
verseByVerse.theology: Balak’s rage (v.10) is the impotent fury of one who has fought God and lost; he can withhold Balaam’s fee but cannot alter God’s decree. Balaam’s insistence that he can speak only God’s word (vv.12-13), though self-serving, is nonetheless true — and sets up the greatest oracle, a word about “the latter days” (v.14) that reaches far beyond Balak’s little kingdom to the coming King.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Balak sent the prophet home in a fury, cheated of his curse — raging against a verdict he could not change.

Now: those who set themselves against God’s purposes for his people may rage, but they cannot prevail. “The One enthroned in heaven laughs” (Ps 2:4) at the fury of kings.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balak's anger was kindled against Balaam, and he struck his hands together. And Balak said to Balaam, "I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed them these three times. Therefore now flee to your own place. I said, 'I will certainly honor you,' but the LORD has held you back from honor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Balak’s anger was kindled against Balaam, and he struck his hands together. It is a gesture of furious contempt, the ancient equivalent of a slow, savage clap, and it is all he has left. I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed them these three times. Therefore now flee to your own place. The contract is torn up. Balaam is dismissed on the spot, unpaid, and told to run.

Then Balak says one true thing, and he says it as an accusation: I said, “I will certainly honor you,” but the LORD has held you back from honor. He is right. God did. The honour, the silver, the standing at a royal court — all of it was within reach, and God stood in the road again, as he had stood on the road from Pethor, and Balaam went home empty.

Here, then, is a man who has just delivered two of the most magnificent oracles in the Old Testament and lost everything he came for. Peter tells us how he felt about it: he was one who loved gain from wrongdoing (2 Pet. 2:15). And that is what makes what happens next so terrible. He could not take Balak’s money for a curse — so before he leaves the district he will find another way to earn it, one that does not require God’s permission, and it will kill twenty-four thousand Israelites and eventually him (31:8, 16). A man who wants the wages badly enough will always find a route to them that his conscience can sign. The route is what the New Testament calls the way of Balaam.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balaam said to Balak, "Did I not tell your messengers whom you sent to me, 'If Balak should give me his house full of silver and gold, I would not be able to go beyond the word of the LORD, to do either good or bad of my own will. What the LORD speaks, that will I speak'? And now, behold, I am going to my people. Come, I will let you know what this people will do to your people in the latter days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam defends himself by quoting himself, and once again every word is impeccable: If Balak should give me his house full of silver and gold, I would not be able to go beyond the word of the LORD, to do either good or bad of my own will. What the LORD speaks, that will I speak. He has now said this three times in three chapters, and it is true three times, and it has never once described his heart. There is such a thing as a man whose doctrine is his alibi.

And now, behold, I am going to my people. He does not go. Seven chapters later the sword finds him still in Midian, fighting on the wrong side (31:8). Men announce their departure from a compromising situation far more often than they actually leave it.

And then the offer that produces the greatest thing he ever says: Come, I will let you know what this people will do to your people in the latter days. He owes Balak nothing now; he has been sacked. He gives the oracle anyway, unpaid, because it is not his to withhold. Which means the crowning prophecy of the Pentateuch outside Genesis is delivered by a dismissed hireling, to a furious pagan king, on a mountain in Moab, for no fee at all. God had said he would put a word in this man’s mouth, and the word came out whether anyone was paying for it or not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–25 — The Fourth Oracle: A Star out of Jacob
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The greatest oracle comes last. Balaam sees, from far off, a coming ruler: “I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel.” A King is coming who will crush his enemies and reign. The prophecy points beyond David to the Messiah — and many have heard its echo in the star that led the Magi to the newborn King.
verseByVerse.theology: The “star... out of Jacob” and “scepter... out of Israel” (v.17) is a messianic prophecy: it is fulfilled in part in David but points ultimately to Christ, the King of Israel. Ancient Jewish interpretation read it messianically, and many see its echo in the star of Bethlehem that brought the Magi to “he who has been born king of the Jews” (Matt 2:2). Astonishingly, this clearest of messianic hopes in the Pentateuch comes through a pagan diviner — God will proclaim his King even by the mouth of a hostile prophet.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: from a distant hilltop a pagan seer glimpsed a rising King, a star and a scepter out of Jacob, centuries before he came.

Now: the Star has risen. “I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star” (Rev 22:16). The King Balaam saw from afar we know by name — Jesus, born under the star, reigning forever.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took up his discourse and said, "The oracle of Balaam the son of Beor, the oracle of the man whose eye is opened, the oracle of him who hears the words of God, and knows the knowledge of the Most High, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down with his eyes uncovered: I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel; it shall crush the forehead of Moab and break down all the sons of Sheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel; it shall crush the forehead of Moab and break down all the sons of Sheth.

Take the near horizon first, because the oracle has one. Four centuries later David subdued Moab and made it tributary, and garrisoned Edom (2 Sam. 8:2, 14) — precisely the two nations named in the next verse. Any honest reading has David in view. But the oracle plainly will not sit down inside David. Not now… not near is a strange way to describe a king four hundred years off in a book that has just been dating events to the month, and verse 19 widens the horizon to a dominion with no stated end. Something larger is coming through a smaller frame.

So look at the two images. A scepter is the ruler’s staff, and Jacob had already said on his deathbed that the scepter shall not depart from Judah… and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples (Gen. 49:10). A star is a king in the language of the ancient East — and it is what Jesus called himself, at the very end of the Bible, in the last words he speaks to the church: I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star (Rev. 22:16). Note too the verb: the Star shall crush the forehead. The first promise ever made to fallen man was that the seed of the woman would crush the serpent’s head (Gen. 3:15). The line runs from a garden, through a pagan mountain, to an empty tomb.

Israel never forgot this verse. The community at Qumran read it of the Messiah; when a rebel leader rose against Rome in AD 132 his followers named him Bar Kokhba, son of a star, from these very words; and readers from the earliest centuries have wondered about the wise men who came from the east following a star to a King of the Jews (Matt. 2:1–2) — out of the same eastern country Balaam himself came from. Matthew does not cite this oracle, and we should not pretend he does. But the shape of it is remarkable: a seer from the east saw a Star rise out of Jacob and could not say when, and fourteen hundred years later men from the east saw a star and went to find out. Balaam looked down a corridor of centuries and glimpsed a King he would never meet, standing on a hill he had climbed for money, and could do nothing about it but say what he saw.

verseByVerse.quote: Edom shall be dispossessed; Seir also, his enemies, shall be dispossessed. Israel is doing valiantly. And one from Jacob shall exercise dominion and destroy the survivors of cities!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom shall be dispossessed; Seir also, his enemies, shall be dispossessed. Israel is doing valiantly. And one from Jacob shall exercise dominion.

Edom is the brother who slammed the door four chapters ago. Israel had asked for nothing but a road and had been met with an army, and had turned away without a fight because God told them to. They did not answer Edom themselves. Now, in an oracle they never heard, delivered on a foreign mountain to their enemy, God answers Edom for them. That is a pattern worth holding on to when you have taken an injustice quietly and had to walk the long way round because of it. Israel’s silence at the border was not the end of the matter. It was simply the transfer of the matter to somebody better placed to settle it: Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Rom. 12:19).

And the last line lifts off the local map altogether: one from Jacob shall exercise dominion. Not Israel collectively — one from Jacob. A single figure, out of this family, ruling. The whole Bible is bending toward a Person here, and a hired diviner in the pay of Moab is the one announcing it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he looked on Amalek and took up his discourse and said, "Amalek was the first among the nations, but its end is utter destruction." And he looked on the Kenite, and took up his discourse and said, "Enduring is your dwelling place, and your nest is set in the rock. Nevertheless, Kain shall be burned when Asshur takes you away captive." And he took up his discourse and said, "Alas, who shall live when God does this? But ships shall come from Kittim and shall afflict Asshur and Eber; and he too shall come to utter destruction." Then Balaam rose and went back to his place. And Balak also went his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four short oracles close the account, and they widen out until the whole world is in view. Amalek was the first among the nations, but its end is utter destruction — first because Amalek was the first nation to attack Israel after the exodus, striking at the stragglers (Exod. 17:8; Deut. 25:17–18), and God had sworn then that he would blot out their memory. Being first to raise a hand against the people of God is a distinction nobody should want.

Then the Kenites, Jethro’s people, friends of Israel, whose nest is set in the rock — high, defensible, and not defensible enough, for Asshur will carry them off. Then Asshur itself falls to ships… from Kittim, the western coastlands, a sea power out of the Mediterranean that would not exist for centuries. Balaam is now naming the rise and fall of empires he has no earthly means of knowing about, and in the middle of it he stops and says the one thing a man ought to say when he sees history from that height: Alas, who shall live when God does this?

And then verse 25, which is the flattest, saddest verse in the Balaam story. Then Balaam rose and went back to his place. And Balak also went his way. No repentance. No worship. The man who saw the Star out of Jacob dusts himself off and goes home — and on his way out he will hand Balak the piece of advice that does what four days of sorcery could not (31:16). It is possible to see more of God than almost anyone in your generation and be lost, because the eye can be opened while the heart is not. Balaam had the Spirit come upon him, the vision of the Almighty, and the Messiah in his mouth, and he went back to his place. There is only one thing worth asking at the end of a chapter like this, and it is not what Balaam saw. It is whether the Star he saw at a distance is the one you have come to.

25.title: Baal of Peor: The Seduction Balaam's Curse Could Not Achieve
25.text: <sup>1</sup>While Israel lived in Shittim, the people began to whore with the daughters of Moab.<sup>2</sup>These invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and bowed down to their gods.<sup>3</sup>So Israel yoked himself to Baal of Peor. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel.<sup>4</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Take all the chiefs of the people and hang them in the sun before the LORD, that the fierce anger of the LORD may turn away from Israel."<sup>5</sup>And Moses said to the judges of Israel, "Each of you kill those of his men who have yoked themselves to Baal of Peor."<sup>6</sup>And behold, one of the people of Israel came and brought a Midianite woman to his family, in the sight of Moses and in the sight of the whole congregation of the people of Israel, while they were weeping in the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>7</sup>When Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose and left the congregation and took a spear in his hand<sup>8</sup>and went after the man of Israel into the chamber and pierced both of them, the man of Israel and the woman through her belly. Thus the plague on the people of Israel was stopped.<sup>9</sup>Nevertheless, those who died by the plague were twenty-four thousand.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD said to Moses,<sup>11</sup>"Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has turned back my wrath from the people of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I did not consume the people of Israel in my jealousy.<sup>12</sup>Therefore say, 'Behold, I give to him my covenant of peace,<sup>13</sup>and it shall be to him and to his descendants after him the covenant of a perpetual priesthood, because he was jealous for his God and made atonement for the people of Israel.'"<sup>14</sup>The name of the slain man of Israel, who was killed with the Midianite woman, was Zimri the son of Salu, chief of a father's house belonging to the Simeonites.<sup>15</sup>And the name of the Midianite woman who was killed was Cozbi the daughter of Zur, who was the tribal head of a father's house in Midian.<sup>16</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>17</sup>"Harass the Midianites and strike them down,<sup>18</sup>for they have harassed you with their wiles, with which they beguiled you in the matter of Peor, and in the matter of Cozbi, the daughter of the chief of Midian, their sister, who was killed on the day of the plague on account of Peor."
25.overview:
What Balaam could not accomplish by cursing, he accomplished by seduction. Numbers 31:16 reveals that Balaam, unable to curse Israel, counseled Balak to corrupt them — to lure them into sexual immorality and idolatry with the women of Moab. And it works where the curse failed. The enemy who cannot defeat the people of God from outside seeks to destroy them from within, through compromise and lust. Israel survives the sorcerer's curse only to fall to the temptress's smile.

The people join themselves to Baal of Peor, eating at idol feasts and committing immorality, until the wrath of God breaks out in a plague. Paul holds this very episode before the Corinthian church: “We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day” (1 Cor 10:8). The point is unmistakable: a people who survived Egypt, the wilderness, and Balaam's curse can still be destroyed by their own appetites. Keller often warned that the church is rarely defeated by external persecution; far more often she is hollowed out by accommodation to the world's sensuality and idolatry. The danger is not the curse outside but the compromise within.

The chapter turns on the zeal of Phinehas, who, when an Israelite brazenly brings a Midianite woman into the camp, takes a spear and drives it through them both, and the plague is stopped. God commends his action and grants him “a covenant of peace” and “a covenant of perpetual priesthood,” because “he was jealous with my jealousy.” Ferguson notes that Phinehas's zeal is not bloodthirsty cruelty but holy jealousy that reflects God's own — a jealousy for the purity of God's people. His act of turning away wrath foreshadows the priestly work of Christ, the truly zealous One, who said “zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:17), and who turns away the wrath of God from his people forever, not by another's death but by his own.
25.theology:
Seduction from within. What Balaam's curse could not do, immorality and idolatry accomplished. The church is rarely defeated from without but often hollowed out by compromise within (1 Cor 10:8).

Holy jealousy. Phinehas was jealous with God's jealousy for the purity of his people. True zeal reflects God's own passion for holiness, not human cruelty.

Turning away wrath. Phinehas stood in the breach and stopped the plague, foreshadowing Christ the zealous Priest who turns away God's wrath by his own atoning death.
25.examples:
Then: Israel, unable to be cursed, was seduced into immorality and idolatry at Peor; the plague raged until Phinehas's holy zeal turned away God's wrath.

Now: Beware the seduction Balaam's curse could not achieve. The world will try to corrupt by pleasure what it cannot defeat by force. Flee sexual immorality and idolatry, and rest in Christ, the zealous Priest who turns God's wrath away forever.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What Balaam could not do by cursing, the enemy accomplishes by seduction. Israel, camped at Shittim, falls into sexual sin with the women of Moab and is drawn into worshiping their god, Baal of Peor. The people who could not be cursed from outside are corrupted from within. God’s anger burns, and a plague breaks out. The greatest danger to God’s people was never the enemy’s sword or curse — it was their own hearts.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the dark sequel to Balaam’s blessing. Unable to curse Israel, Balaam advised Balak to seduce them into idolatry (Num 31:16; Rev 2:14, “the teaching of Balaam... to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality”). What no external curse could achieve, internal compromise did. The lesson is sobering: God’s people are far more endangered by seduction than by opposition (1 Cor 10:8, 12).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the nation no curse could touch was nearly undone by a few tents and a false god — corrupted from within where it could not be conquered from without.

Now: “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor 10:12). The enemy’s most effective weapon against us is not persecution but seduction — the slow drift into compromise.

verseByVerse.quote: While Israel lived in Shittim, the people began to whore with the daughters of Moab. These invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and bowed down to their gods. So Israel yoked himself to Baal of Peor. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the last verse of chapter 24 and the first verse of chapter 25 together, because the join is the point. Balaam rose and went back to his place — and immediately Israel lived in Shittim, the people began to whore with the daughters of Moab. Scripture later tells us plainly that these two sentences are connected. Moses says of the Midianite women, Behold, these, on Balaam’s advice, caused the people of Israel to act treacherously against the LORD in the matter of Peor (31:16); and the risen Christ, writing to a church fifteen centuries later, calls it by name — Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality (Rev. 2:14).

So this is the same campaign, by the same consultant, with the weapon changed. Four days of sorcery on three mountains produced nothing but blessing, because a people God has blessed cannot be cursed. And so Balaam, sacked and unpaid, told Balak the only thing that would work: you cannot get at them from outside; invite them to dinner. What no enchantment could do to Israel, a shared meal and a willing woman did in a fortnight.

Watch the order of the collapse, because it is the ordinary order. First the women, then the sacrifices of their gods, then the people ate, and only then bowed down to their gods. Nobody in that camp got up in the morning intending to worship Baal. The idolatry came in last, through the appetite, when the man was already at the table and already committed and it would have been awkward to leave. That is how it comes in still. Sin rarely opens by asking for your allegiance. It asks for your evening. And the summary verse is chilling in its finality: So Israel yoked himself to Baal of Peor. Yoked — harnessed, joined at the neck, no longer able to turn without the other. It is the word Paul is reaching for when he tells the Corinthians, standing in a city full of exactly this, Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers (2 Cor. 6:14).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Take all the chiefs of the people and hang them in the sun before the LORD, that the fierce anger of the LORD may turn away from Israel." And Moses said to the judges of Israel, "Each of you kill those of his men who have yoked themselves to Baal of Peor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The response is immediate and terrible. Take all the chiefs of the people and hang them in the sun before the LORD. The Hebrew is difficult and the exact form of the execution is uncertain — impaling and public exposure are both likely — but the sense is not in doubt: the ringleaders are to be put to death in the open, in daylight, in full view. There is to be nothing discreet about it. The sin was public; the judgment is public.

And notice who is named. The chiefs. Not the young men, not the weak, not the new generation who had grown up in the wilderness with poor examples. The heads of families. The men who had spent forty years watching what happened to those who despised the Lord and who had every reason to know better. When a nation falls apart at the top, God does not begin his reckoning at the bottom.

Then Moses passes the order down: Each of you kill those of his men who have yoked themselves to Baal of Peor. That command matters enormously for what happens six verses later, so hold it. There is now a lawful, public, standing order in Israel that the men who have joined themselves to Baal are to be executed by the appointed judges. What Phinehas does in verse 8 is not a private outburst. It is the only recorded instance of anyone actually doing what Moses had just told the whole judiciary to do.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As the plague rages and the people weep, an Israelite brazenly brings a Midianite woman into the camp before everyone’s eyes. Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, rises up, takes a spear, and drives it through them both. The plague is stopped. God commends Phinehas’s zeal and gives him “my covenant of peace,” a perpetual priesthood, “because he was jealous for his God and made atonement for the people.”
verseByVerse.theology: Phinehas’s zeal “made atonement for the people” and stayed the plague (vv.11-13); Psalm 106:30-31 says it “was counted to him as righteousness.” His jealousy mirrored God’s own jealousy for his holiness (v.11). This is not a warrant for private vengeance but a picture, in a unique redemptive-historical moment, of holy zeal that loves God enough to confront flagrant, plague-bringing sin. It points to the greater Priest whose zeal (John 2:17) and self-offering truly “made atonement,” turning away wrath forever.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: one man’s holy zeal, in a moment of national apostasy, halted the plague and was counted to him as righteousness.

Now: we are called not to the spear but to the same jealousy for God’s honor — to hate sin, first in ourselves, and to love God’s holiness. And we rest in the Priest whose zeal and blood made the atonement Phinehas only foreshadowed.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, one of the people of Israel came and brought a Midianite woman to his family, in the sight of Moses and in the sight of the whole congregation of the people of Israel, while they were weeping in the entrance of the tent of meeting. When Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose and left the congregation and took a spear in his hand and went after the man of Israel into the chamber and pierced both of them, the man of Israel and the woman through her belly. Thus the plague on the people of Israel was stopped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scene is staged with terrible care. The congregation is at the door of the tabernacle, weeping — a national assembly of grief, the plague already running through the camp, the order to execute the guilty already given. And into that, in broad daylight, one of the people of Israel came and brought a Midianite woman to his family, in the sight of Moses and in the sight of the whole congregation.

This is not a man caught in a weak moment. He walks her past a weeping nation and a grieving prophet, up to the tents, deliberately, while the funeral of his own people is going on around him. It is defiance staged as theatre. And nobody moves. Moses does not move. The judges who were given the order do not move. Israel stands at the tent door and cries and does nothing, and every second of that paralysis is more people dead in the camp behind them.

When Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose and left the congregation and took a spear in his hand. He is the high priest’s son and the high priest’s grandson. He goes into the chamber and kills them both, and the text says with brutal directness: Thus the plague on the people of Israel was stopped.

Modern readers find this passage almost unbearable, and they should not be talked out of that. But be clear what it is and what it is not. It is not vigilantism: Moses had just commanded exactly this execution, and Phinehas was a member of the priestly house charged with guarding the holiness of the camp. It is not racial: Israel had welcomed foreigners from the start, and the red heifer’s cleansing was explicitly for the stranger who sojourns among them (19:10). It is a lawful capital sentence carried out, by the one official in a paralysed nation who was prepared to act, on a man who was committing the crime in public while the sentence was being announced.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, those who died by the plague were twenty-four thousand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, those who died by the plague were twenty-four thousand.

Twenty-four thousand. Set that number against the whole book. The forty years of wandering, the fiery serpents, the earth swallowing Korah — nothing in Numbers killed on this scale in a single episode. And it happened not in the wilderness but in the last camp, in sight of the river, to the generation that had survived everything else. Israel came through the desert and was almost destroyed at the border by a dinner invitation. The enemy that had failed with armies and failed with sorcery succeeded with hospitality.

Paul cites this very plague as a live warning to a church: We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day (1 Cor. 10:8). A careful reader notices the difference in the figures at once, and the question deserves a straight answer rather than a shrug. Paul says in a single day, which Numbers does not; the most natural reading is that the twenty-three thousand were those who fell on the worst day, and the twenty-four thousand is the total of the whole plague, which plainly ran longer than one day since the executions of verses 4–5 preceded it. Both writers are using the round thousands ordinary in ancient reckoning. This is not a contradiction, and it is not a difficulty anyone needs to be nervous about.

What Paul does with the number is the thing to carry away. He writes it to Christians — baptised, communing, confident Christians in a port city — and adds, these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction… Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Cor. 10:11–12). The men who died at Peor had seen the sea open. Past experience of God is no immunity whatever against present sin.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has turned back my wrath from the people of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I did not consume the people of Israel in my jealousy. Therefore say, 'Behold, I give to him my covenant of peace, and it shall be to him and to his descendants after him the covenant of a perpetual priesthood, because he was jealous for his God and made atonement for the people of Israel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s verdict on Phinehas is the part of this chapter that troubles readers most, and it should be read exactly as it stands. He was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I did not consume the people of Israel in my jealousy.

Start with the word, because it is easily misheard. God’s jealousy is not envy; envy wants what belongs to another, and God has no rival to covet. Jealousy in Scripture is the proper refusal of a husband to share his wife — the very opposite of indifference. A man who watches his wife leave with somebody else and feels nothing does not love her. God had married this nation at Sinai, and Israel had gone to Baal’s table; his jealousy is not a blemish on his love but the temperature of it. And Phinehas, alone in the camp, felt about it what God felt about it. That is what the commendation says. Not that he was violent, but that his heart matched God’s heart at a moment when every other heart in Israel had gone numb.

Then the reward, and it is startling: Behold, I give to him my covenant of peace… the covenant of a perpetual priesthood, because he was jealous for his God and made atonement for the people of Israel. A covenant of peace, granted for an act of bloodshed — because the bloodshed had stopped a slaughter. And made atonement is the priest’s own word: what Phinehas did in the doorway of a tent did what a sacrifice does. He stood between a holy God and a doomed people, and the wrath stopped at him. The psalm remembers it in the language of the gospel: Then Phinehas stood up and intervened, and the plague was stayed. And that was counted to him as righteousness (Ps. 106:30–31) — the same phrase used of Abraham’s faith (Gen. 15:6). It was reckoned to him, as faith is reckoned, because the act was faith in motion when everyone else had stopped believing God meant it.

Now say the thing that must be said, plainly, so no reader closes this page confused. This is not a licence for anybody today. Phinehas held a priestly office in a theocratic nation under a specific standing order from God through Moses; no Christian holds that office or that order. The New Testament is emphatic that the church’s zeal is armed differently — the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:4) — and when Paul faces the identical sin in Corinth, flagrant and public, the remedy he commands is exclusion from the fellowship, not a spear (1 Cor. 5:1–5). Zeal for God is still required of us. Its instruments have changed entirely.

And there is one more thing here, which is the reason the chapter is in the Bible at all. Phinehas turned away wrath by the death of the guilty. There is a greater Priest who stood in the same breach and turned away the same wrath by his own death, having done nothing to deserve it; whose covenant of peace was bought at the price of his own body; and whose priesthood is perpetual not for a family line but for ever, in his own person. He himself is our peace (Eph. 2:14). The spear that stopped the plague at Peor was in a priest’s hand. The spear at Calvary went into the priest’s side.

verseByVerse.quote: The name of the slain man of Israel, who was killed with the Midianite woman, was Zimri the son of Salu, chief of a father's house belonging to the Simeonites. And the name of the Midianite woman who was killed was Cozbi the daughter of Zur, who was the tribal head of a father's house in Midian.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only now does the text give us the names, and it gives them with the full genealogy of both: Zimri the son of Salu, chief of a father’s house belonging to the Simeonites, and Cozbi the daughter of Zur, who was the tribal head of a father’s house in Midian.

These were not two ordinary young people who lost their heads. He was a clan chief of Simeon; she was a Midianite princess. This was aristocracy on both sides, and it looks far more like a deliberate alliance than a romance — a leading Israelite family and a leading Midianite family sealing a connection in the most public way available, in the middle of a national crisis, in open contempt of the God whose plague was running through the camp. Verse 18 will confirm it: Cozbi is named there as part of Midian’s wiles.

And the names are written down. That is the sober note. Zimri could have died anonymously, one casualty among twenty-four thousand, and instead his name and his father’s name and his tribe are in the permanent record of the people of God, attached to the worst thing he ever did. What we do in the sight of the whole congregation does not evaporate. There is a book, and things get written in it — which is precisely why the mercy of Christ is described as it is, in the language of a record being dealt with: God canceled the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands… nailing it to the cross (Col. 2:14).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commands Israel to treat the Midianites as enemies, because of their part in the seduction at Peor — the scheme that used their own women, at Balaam’s counsel, to lead Israel into deadly sin. The reckoning with Midian, carried out later in chapter 31, begins here.
verseByVerse.theology: The command against Midian (vv.17-18) is God’s judgment on those who deliberately engineered Israel’s downfall through seduction into idolatry. It underscores how seriously God takes those who lead his people into sin (cf. Matt 18:6-7, the millstone warning). The Peor episode leaves a permanent mark: it becomes a byword for apostasy (Ps 106:28-29; Hos 9:10), and a lasting warning built into Israel’s memory.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: those who plotted to corrupt God’s people came under God’s judgment — the seducers were not treated lightly.

Now: God still regards with the utmost gravity those who deliberately lead others into sin. “It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck” (Luke 17:2). To tempt God’s people is to invite God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Harass the Midianites and strike them down, for they have harassed you with their wiles, with which they beguiled you in the matter of Peor, and in the matter of Cozbi, the daughter of the chief of Midian, their sister, who was killed on the day of the plague on account of Peor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes by turning to the people who set the trap. Harass the Midianites and strike them down, for they have harassed you with their wiles, with which they beguiled you in the matter of Peor.

Two things stand in that sentence. The first is that God does not accept the excuse of the seducer. Israel sinned freely and Israel was judged for it — twenty-four thousand graves say so — and the men who engineered the temptation are also held to account. Both are true at once. Nobody at Peor got to plead that they were only tempted, and nobody in Midian got to plead that they only offered. Jesus holds the same two truths together without any strain: he tells a man to cut off his own hand rather than sin, and in the same breath says of the one who causes a little one to stumble that it would be better for him to have a great millstone fastened round his neck and to be drowned in the depth of the sea (Matt. 18:6–8).

The second is the word wiles. Midian did not defeat Israel; Midian beguiled her. Paul uses precisely this vocabulary of the enemy the church actually faces — the schemes of the devil (Eph. 6:11) — and it is the plain lesson of chapters 22 to 25 read as one story. Balak tried a curse and failed. Balak tried an army and never dared. Balaam tried divination from three mountains and could not raise a syllable against them. And then a dinner invitation on a warm evening at Shittim brought down more of Israel than every enemy in the book combined.

The people of God have never been in real danger from the mountain. Twenty-one altars and the most expensive sorcery in the ancient world produced nothing but blessing, because the blessing was God’s and no one could reach it. What ruined them walked into the camp smiling and was invited to stay. And that is why the Lord Jesus, praying for his own on the last night, did not ask for them to be taken off the field or shielded from their enemies. He asked for the one thing Israel lacked at Shittim: I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one (John 17:15).

26.title: The Second Census: A New Generation, an Old Faithfulness
26.text: <sup>1</sup>After the plague, the LORD said to Moses and to Eleazar the son of Aaron, the priest,<sup>2</sup>"Take a census of all the congregation of the people of Israel, from twenty years old and upward, by their fathers' houses, all in Israel who are able to go to war."<sup>3</sup>And Moses and Eleazar the priest spoke with them in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying,<sup>4</sup>"Take a census of the people, from twenty years old and upward," as the LORD commanded Moses. The people of Israel who came out of the land of Egypt were:<sup>5</sup>Reuben, the firstborn of Israel; the sons of Reuben: of Hanoch, the clan of the Hanochites; of Pallu, the clan of the Palluites;<sup>6</sup>of Hezron, the clan of the Hezronites; of Carmi, the clan of the Carmites.<sup>7</sup>These are the clans of the Reubenites, and those listed were 43,730.<sup>8</sup>And the sons of Pallu: Eliab.<sup>9</sup>The sons of Eliab: Nemuel, Dathan, and Abiram. And the names of the daughters of Zelophehad were Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.<sup>34</sup>These are the clans of Manasseh, and those listed were 52,700.<sup>35</sup>These are the sons of Ephraim according to their clans: of Shuthelah, the clan of the Shuthelahites; of Becher, the clan of the Becherites; of Tahan, the clan of the Tahanites.<sup>36</sup>And these are the sons of Shuthelah: of Eran, the clan of the Eranites.<sup>37</sup>These are the clans of the sons of Ephraim as they were listed, 32,500.
