These are the clans of Dan according to their clans.<sup>43</sup>All the clans of the Shuhamites, as they were listed, were 64,400.<sup>44</sup>The sons of Asher according to their clans: of Imnah, the clan of the Imnites; of Ishvi, the clan of the Ishvites; of Beriah, the clan of the Beriites.<sup>45</sup>Of the sons of Beriah: of Heber, the clan of the Heberites; of Malchiel, the clan of the Malchielites.<sup>46</sup>And the name of the daughter of Asher was Serah.<sup>47</sup>These are the clans of the sons of Asher as they were listed, 53,400.<sup>48</sup>The sons of Naphtali according to their clans: of Jahzeel, the clan of the Jahzeelites; of Guni, the clan of the Gunites;<sup>49</sup>of Jezer, the clan of the Jezerites; of Shillem, the clan of the Shillemites.<sup>50</sup>These are the clans of Naphtali according to their clans, and those listed were 45,400.<sup>51</sup>This was the list of the people of Israel, 601,730.<sup>52</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>53</sup>"Among these the land shall be divided for inheritance according to the number of names.<sup>54</sup>To a large tribe you shall give a large inheritance, and to a small tribe you shall give a small inheritance; every tribe shall be given its inheritance in proportion to its list.<sup>55</sup>But the land shall be divided by lot. According to the names of the tribes of their fathers they shall inherit.<sup>56</sup>Their inheritance shall be divided according to lot between the larger and the smaller."<sup>57</sup>This was the list of the Levites according to their clans: of Gershon, the clan of the Gershonites; of Kohath, the clan of the Kohathites; of Merari, the clan of the Merarites.<sup>58</sup>These are the clans of Levi: the clan of the Libnites, the clan of the Hebronites, the clan of the Mahlites, the clan of the Mushites, the clan of the Korahites. And Kohath was the father of Amram.<sup>59</sup>The name of Amram's wife was Jochebed the daughter of Levi, who was born to Levi in Egypt. And she bore to Amram Aaron and Moses and Miriam their sister.<sup>60</sup>And to Aaron were born Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.<sup>61</sup>But Nadab and Abihu died when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD.<sup>62</sup>And those listed were 23,000, every male from a month old and upward. For they were not listed among the people of Israel, because there was no inheritance given to them among the people of Israel.<sup>63</sup>These were those listed by Moses and Eleazar the priest, who listed the people of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.<sup>64</sup>But among these there was not one of those listed by Moses and Aaron the priest, who had listed the people of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai.<sup>65</sup>For the LORD had said of them, "They shall die in the wilderness." Not one of them was left, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun.
26.overview:
A second census bookends the book. Forty years after the first counting at Sinai, a new generation is numbered on the plains of Moab, poised once more at the edge of the Promised Land. The juxtaposition is breathtaking. The first census numbered the generation that would die in the wilderness for their unbelief; this one numbers the generation that will enter the land. The whole tragic interval of chapters 11–25 lies between the two countings.

The most moving verses are the closing ones (vv. 64–65): “among these there was not one of those listed by Moses and Aaron… not one of them was left, except Caleb… and Joshua.” The sentence of chapter 14 has been fully carried out. An entire generation — over 600,000 men — has died in the desert, just as God said. The wages of unbelief have been paid in full. Yet here is the staggering grace: God did not abandon the project. He did not give up on Israel. He raised up a new generation and brought them, against every odd, back to the border of promise. Sproul observed that here we see both the severity and the kindness of God (Rom 11:22): severity toward the unbelieving generation, kindness toward the new one. The promise outlived the failure.

This is the great comfort of the chapter: God's faithfulness spans the generations. The covenant did not die with the rebels in the sand. What God promised to Abraham, he will perform, even if it means burying one generation and raising up another. Ferguson notes that the church too is carried forward across generations by the faithfulness of God, not the constancy of men. Every funeral in the wilderness was real, but so was every birth; and the same God who kept his word of judgment kept his word of promise. He is faithful to a thousand generations, and the inheritance he pledged will surely be given, for it rests on him and not on us.
26.theology:
God's faithfulness across generations. The covenant did not die with the unbelieving generation. God raised up a new people and kept his promise, faithful to a thousand generations.

Severity and kindness. Both are displayed (Rom 11:22): judgment fully carried out on the rebels, kindness extended to the new generation brought to the border of promise.

Grace in unexpected places. The sons of Korah did not die; the rebel's line was preserved to sing God's praises, a token of mercy reaching even into the family of judgment.
26.examples:
Then: A new generation was numbered at the border, nearly matching the first, while not one of the unbelieving generation remained except Caleb and Joshua.

Now: God's promises outlive every failure and span every generation. He buries one generation and raises another, never abandoning his covenant. The inheritance is sure because it rests on his faithfulness, not yours. Behold the severity and the kindness of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–51 — The Census of the New Generation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A second census is taken, tribe by tribe, of all the men of fighting age — but this is not the same generation counted in chapter 1. That generation has died in the wilderness under God’s judgment. This is their children, the new generation who will actually enter the land. The long lists of names and numbers are, in truth, a monument to God’s faithfulness: the promise did not die with the fathers; it lives on in their sons.
verseByVerse.theology: The second census marks a decisive transition: the generation that refused the land is gone, and a new generation stands ready to receive it. Judgment fell (the fathers died), but the promise endured (the children remain and are numbered for the conquest). God’s purposes are not defeated by one generation’s unbelief; “the word of the Lord remains forever” (1 Pet 1:25). Even the roll-call of tribes preaches that God keeps covenant to a thousand generations (Deut 7:9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the sons of the men who died in the desert now stood counted and ready — proof that the promise outlived the faithless generation.

Now: God’s purposes march on across the generations. Where one generation fails, he raises up another; his promise never dies with those who forfeit it (Ps 145:4).

verseByVerse.quote: After the plague, the LORD said to Moses and to Eleazar the son of Aaron, the priest, "Take a census of all the congregation of the people of Israel, from twenty years old and upward, by their fathers' houses, all in Israel who are able to go to war." And Moses and Eleazar the priest spoke with them in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying, "Take a census of the people, from twenty years old and upward," as the LORD commanded Moses. The people of Israel who came out of the land of Egypt were:
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the plague, the LORD said to Moses and to Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest, “Take a census.” Four words set the scene, and they are the saddest and the most hopeful in the chapter. The counting begins over twenty-four thousand fresh graves.

The purpose is stated twice: from twenty years old and upward… all in Israel who are able to go to war, and then in verse 53, among these the land shall be divided for inheritance. So this document is two things at once — a muster roll and a deed register. It lists the men who must fight for the land and the families who will own it, and it is the same list, because in God’s arrangement the people who receive the inheritance are the people who go in for it.

And the whole exercise has been done before. Chapter 1 counted a nation at Sinai for a march that took eleven days and then collapsed at Kadesh. This is the same procedure, conducted by the same lawgiver, with an entirely different set of men — every one of the first list now dead except two. God is not repeating himself. He is starting again, with the sons of the people who would not go, and this time they will cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Reuben, the firstborn of Israel; the sons of Reuben: of Hanoch, the clan of the Hanochites; of Pallu, the clan of the Palluites; of Hezron, the clan of the Hezronites; of Carmi, the clan of the Carmites. These are the clans of the Reubenites, and those listed were 43,730. And the sons of Pallu: Eliab. The sons of Eliab: Nemuel, Dathan, and Abiram. These are the Dathan and Abiram, chosen from the congregation, who contended against Moses and Aaron in the company of Korah, when they contended against the LORD and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up together with Korah, when that company died, when the fire devoured 250 men, and they became a warning. But the sons of Korah did not die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The register opens with Reuben, and almost at once it stops being a list. Instead of simply naming clans it pauses to retell an old disaster: Dathan and Abiram, who contended against Moses and Aaron in the company of Korah, when they contended against the LORD and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up (26:9–10). A census is not the obvious place for that. But a roll of the covenant people is also a memorial, and God writes into it both the mercy and the warning.

And then eleven words that change everything: But the sons of Korah did not die.

Korah went down alive into the ground with his household and his goods, and his sons were not in the pit. Nobody has ever explained the mechanics and the text does not try. What it does is record the survival — and then Scripture spends the next five hundred years showing what God did with it. Turn to the Psalter and look at the headings: A Maskil of the Sons of Korah stands over eleven psalms, among them the one every homesick believer knows by heart — As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God (Ps. 42:1) — and How lovely is your dwelling place, O LORD of hosts (Ps. 84:1). The descendants of the man who said the tabernacle was not holy enough to be Moses’ business became the singers who stood in it and taught Israel to long for God.

That is not a footnote; that is the gospel written into a genealogy. The blood of the rebel did not settle the destiny of the rebel’s children — the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezek. 18:20) — and God did not merely spare that family, he gave it the music. If you carry a family name you would rather not have, and a history behind you that you did not choose, this verse is in the Bible for you. The sons of Korah did not die. They sang.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Simeon according to their clans: of Nemuel, the clan of the Nemuelites; of Jamin, the clan of the Jaminites; of Jachin, the clan of the Jachinites; of Zerah, the clan of the Zerahites; of Shaul, the clan of the Shaulites. These are the clans of the Simeonites, 22,200. The sons of Gad according to their clans: of Zephon, the clan of the Zephonites; of Haggi, the clan of the Haggites; of Shuni, the clan of the Shunites; of Ozni, the clan of the Oznites; of Eri, the clan of the Erites; of Arod, the clan of the Arodites; of Areli, the clan of the Arelites. These are the clans of the sons of Gad as they were listed, 40,500. The sons of Judah were Er and Onan; and Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. And the sons of Judah according to their clans were: of Shelah, the clan of the Shelanites; of Perez, the clan of the Perezites; of Zerah, the clan of the Zerahites. And the sons of Perez were: of Hezron, the clan of the Hezronites; of Hamul, the clan of the Hamulites. These are the clans of Judah as they were listed, 76,500.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the tribes, clan by clan, with a total after each. Read past the figures for a moment and notice two of them, because the numbers here are telling a story.

Simeon has collapsed. At Sinai the tribe mustered 59,300 fighting men; here it is 22,200 — a loss of nearly two thirds, by far the worst of any tribe, when several others actually grew. And the last chapter told us that the man who paraded a Midianite woman past a weeping nation was Zimri the son of Salu, chief of a father’s house belonging to the Simeonites (25:14). Scripture does not draw the line between those two facts for us, and we should not draw it harder than it does. But the plague at Peor fell heaviest, it seems, on the tribe whose chief had led the way into it, and the ruin of a people can begin with one man of standing who decides that the rules are for other people.

Judah, meanwhile, is the largest tribe in Israel at 76,500, as it was in chapter 1 and as it will be at every later reckoning. Jacob had said on his deathbed that the scepter shall not depart from Judah… and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples (Gen. 49:10). Fourteen hundred years before Bethlehem, the tribe that will carry the King is quietly the strongest name on the list, and nobody counting that morning knew why.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Issachar according to their clans: of Tola, the clan of the Tolaites; of Puvah, the clan of the Punites; of Jashub, the clan of the Jashubites; of Shimron, the clan of the Shimronites. These are the clans of Issachar as they were listed, 64,300. The sons of Zebulun, according to their clans: of Sered, the clan of the Seredites; of Elon, the clan of the Elonites; of Jahleel, the clan of the Jahleelites. These are the clans of the Zebulunites as they were listed, 60,500. The sons of Joseph according to their clans: Manasseh and Ephraim. The sons of Manasseh: of Machir, the clan of the Machirites; and Machir was the father of Gilead; of Gilead, the clan of the Gileadites. These are the sons of Gilead: of Iezer, the clan of the Iezerites; of Helek, the clan of the Helekites; and of Asriel, the clan of the Asrielites; and of Shechem, the clan of the Shechemites; and of Shemida, the clan of the Shemidaites; and of Hepher, the clan of the Hepherites. Now Zelophehad the son of Hepher had no sons, but daughters. And the names of the daughters of Zelophehad were Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. These are the clans of Manasseh, and those listed were 52,700.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The roll continues through Issachar, Zebulun, and the two Joseph tribes — and then, in the middle of a military register, the text does something no ancient muster roll does. At verse 33 it stops and names five women.

Now Zelophehad the son of Hepher had no sons, but daughters, and the names of the daughters of Zelophehad were Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.

This is a list of men who can fight, kept for the purpose of dividing land among men. These five cannot fight and, under every custom of the ancient world, cannot inherit. Their father is dead and their family line has run out. By the logic of the document they are precisely the people who should not appear in it — and God has their names written down, in full, in order, in the census of the covenant people, one chapter before they walk up to Moses and ask for what nobody thought they could have. The next chapter is not a surprising turn of events. It has been prepared for here, in a register, by a God who counted them before they asked.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of Ephraim according to their clans: of Shuthelah, the clan of the Shuthelahites; of Becher, the clan of the Becherites; of Tahan, the clan of the Tahanites. And these are the sons of Shuthelah: of Eran, the clan of the Eranites. These are the clans of the sons of Ephraim as they were listed, 32,500. These are the sons of Joseph according to their clans. The sons of Benjamin according to their clans: of Bela, the clan of the Belaites; of Ashbel, the clan of the Ashbelites; of Ahiram, the clan of the Ahiramites; of Shephupham, the clan of the Shuphamites; of Hupham, the clan of the Huphamites. And the sons of Bela were Ard and Naaman: of Ard, the clan of the Ardites; of Naaman, the clan of the Naamites. These are the sons of Benjamin according to their clans, and those listed were 45,600. These are the sons of Dan according to their clans: of Shuham, the clan of the Shuhamites. These are the clans of Dan according to their clans. All the clans of the Shuhamites, as they were listed, were 64,400. The sons of Asher according to their clans: of Imnah, the clan of the Imnites; of Ishvi, the clan of the Ishvites; of Beriah, the clan of the Beriites. Of the sons of Beriah: of Heber, the clan of the Heberites; of Malchiel, the clan of the Malchielites. And the name of the daughter of Asher was Serah. These are the clans of the sons of Asher as they were listed, 53,400.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin, Dan, Asher — clan after clan, in the same unvarying formula. Modern readers skim these paragraphs. Ask why God did not.

A census is an act of ownership. Nobody counts what does not belong to them, and nobody counts carefully what they do not intend to keep. The repetition that makes the chapter tedious is the whole point of it: God goes through this nation family by family, clan by clan, name by name, and misses nobody. He had done it once at Sinai and every man on that list was now dead in the sand; he does it again on the plains of Moab, unhurried, as though the losses had changed nothing about his method.

And that is exactly how the Lord Jesus describes his own care of his people. Not a headcount but a roll: He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out… I know my own and my own know me (John 10:3, 14). Whatever else these long paragraphs are, they are a picture of a God who does not deal with his people in the mass. There is no such thing, in Scripture, as being lost in the crowd of the redeemed.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Naphtali according to their clans: of Jahzeel, the clan of the Jahzeelites; of Guni, the clan of the Gunites; of Jezer, the clan of the Jezerites; of Shillem, the clan of the Shillemites. These are the clans of Naphtali according to their clans, and those listed were 45,400. This was the list of the people of Israel, 601,730.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was the list of the people of Israel, 601,730.

Set that beside the figure at Sinai forty years earlier: 603,550. The difference is 1,820 men — a fall of less than a third of one per cent. In between, an entire adult generation of six hundred thousand has died in the wilderness under a sentence of judgment, and the nation that arrives at the Jordan is very nearly the same size as the nation that left the mountain.

Take the measure of that. God executed the most severe judgment in the book on this people, carried it through to the last man over the space of thirty-eight years, and at the end of it his promise to Abraham stood exactly where it had stood before. He buried a generation and replaced it, almost one for one, without the covenant losing a step. Judgment fell in full; the promise did not shrink by a thousandth. The numbers on this page are the arithmetic of the sentence that follows in Romans: Note then the kindness and the severity of God (Rom. 11:22). Both. Neither one cancelling the other, and both of them printed in the same column of a census.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 52–56 — The Land Divided by Lot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God directs that the land be divided among the tribes according to their size, but assigned by lot. Larger tribes get larger inheritances; smaller tribes, smaller — yet the specific allotment is left to the lot, which is to say, to God. Fairness and divine sovereignty together: each tribe’s portion is both proportioned and providentially assigned.
verseByVerse.theology: The inheritance is proportioned by size but distributed by lot (vv.54-56) — and “the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Prov 16:33). So the land is apportioned fairly and yet assigned by God’s own hand, not human favoritism. The inheritance is a gift, received by God’s appointment, a foretaste of the eternal inheritance “kept in heaven for you” (1 Pet 1:4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: each tribe’s portion was both fair (sized to the people) and God-given (assigned by lot) — no tribe could boast, none was cheated.

Now: our inheritance too is God’s gift, assigned by his hand, not earned by our merit — “an inheritance that is imperishable... kept in heaven for you” (1 Pet 1:4).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Among these the land shall be divided for inheritance according to the number of names. To a large tribe you shall give a large inheritance, and to a small tribe you shall give a small inheritance; every tribe shall be given its inheritance in proportion to its list. But the land shall be divided by lot. According to the names of the tribes of their fathers they shall inherit. Their inheritance shall be divided according to lot between the larger and the smaller."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the reason for the counting: Among these the land shall be divided for inheritance according to the number of names. To a large tribe you shall give a large inheritance, and to a small tribe you shall give a small inheritance… But the land shall be divided by lot.

Two principles are held together here that look at first as though they must fight. The size of the portion is decided by the census — fair, measured, proportionate, so that no family is crowded and none is given more ground than it can work. The location of the portion is decided by the lot — that is, by God, since the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov. 16:33). Human arithmetic settles how much; divine sovereignty settles where. Nobody lobbied for the good valleys. Nobody was cheated of their acreage.

That combination runs straight into the New Testament and it is a great comfort there. Believers are told that in him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will (Eph. 1:11) — the word behind obtained an inheritance carries the idea of an allotment. Your portion is not a leftover, and it was not drawn by chance, and it was not awarded on the strength of your performance. It was measured out by a Father who knows the size of you, and placed by a hand that never slips.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 57–65 — The Levites, and the Old Generation Gone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levites are counted separately, for they receive no land but the LORD himself as their portion. And the chapter ends with a solemn note: among all those numbered, “there was not one” left of the generation counted at Sinai, except Caleb and Joshua. God had said that unbelieving generation would fall in the wilderness, and it was so, to the last man. His word, in judgment as in mercy, comes exactly true.
verseByVerse.theology: “Not one of them was left” except Caleb and Joshua (vv.64-65) — the precise fulfillment of God’s word of judgment (14:29-30). God’s threatenings are as sure as his promises. Yet grace shines even here: the two men who believed God when the ten spies did not are spared, standing as living proof that “the one who does the will of God abides forever” (1 John 2:17). The Levites’ portion — the LORD himself (cf. 18:20) — is the richest inheritance of all.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the whole unbelieving generation fell, exactly as God had warned — but Caleb and Joshua, who trusted him, still stood.

Now: God’s warnings are as certain as his promises (Heb 3:16-19). Faith is not a small thing — it is the difference between those who fall in the wilderness and those who enter the rest (Heb 4:1-2).

verseByVerse.quote: This was the list of the Levites according to their clans: of Gershon, the clan of the Gershonites; of Kohath, the clan of the Kohathites; of Merari, the clan of the Merarites. These are the clans of Levi: the clan of the Libnites, the clan of the Hebronites, the clan of the Mahlites, the clan of the Mushites, the clan of the Korahites. And Kohath was the father of Amram. The name of Amram's wife was Jochebed the daughter of Levi, who was born to Levi in Egypt. And she bore to Amram Aaron and Moses and Miriam their sister. And to Aaron were born Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. But Nadab and Abihu died when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD. And those listed were 23,000, every male from a month old and upward. For they were not listed among the people of Israel, because there was no inheritance given to them among the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites are counted last and counted differently. Not from twenty years old but every male from a month old and upward — babies included, because this tribe is not being mustered for war. And the closing clause tells us why they are kept off the main roll: they were not listed among the people of Israel, because there was no inheritance given to them among the people of Israel.

Picture the day the land was divided. Eleven tribes walk away holding a map — this ridge, that valley, the terraces, the well. Levi is handed nothing at all: no acres, no boundary stone, no deed. On the face of it, they got the worst of the settlement. But the reason had already been given, and it is one of the great sentences of the Old Testament: You shall have no inheritance in their land… I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel (Num. 18:20). The other tribes were given things God had made. Levi was given God.

The list also pauses over Amram’s family — Aaron and Moses and Miriam, all three now dead — and over Nadab and Abihu, who died when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD. Even the priestly genealogy carries its graves. The tribe that stood nearest the holiness of God was the tribe that had learned most painfully what that nearness costs.

verseByVerse.quote: These were those listed by Moses and Eleazar the priest, who listed the people of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho. But among these there was not one of those listed by Moses and Aaron the priest, who had listed the people of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai. For the LORD had said of them, "They shall die in the wilderness." Not one of them was left, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with an audit, and it is devastating. Among these there was not one of those listed by Moses and Aaron the priest, who had listed the people of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai. For the LORD had said of them, “They shall die in the wilderness.” Not one of them was left, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun.

Two lists, taken forty years apart, and no name appears on both but two. Six hundred thousand men were counted at Sinai; six hundred thousand men are counted at the Jordan; and the overlap between the documents is two men. God had said they shall die in the wilderness — a sentence pronounced in anger at Kadesh when it must have sounded like the kind of thing said in the heat of a moment — and the last verse of this census is the receipt. Every word of it came true, one funeral at a time, over thirty-eight years, until the arithmetic was complete.

But read the exception, because the same faithfulness is in it. Caleb and Joshua had stood up in front of a nation that wanted to stone them and said the LORD is with us; do not fear them (14:9), and God had promised those two men specifically that they would go in. Four decades later, with everyone they had ever known buried behind them, they are standing on the plains of Moab being counted. The God who is exact about his warnings is exact about his promises, and it is the same exactness. He is not more reliable in one direction than the other. The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand for ever (Isa. 40:8) — and a chapter of nothing but names and numbers turns out to be the proof of it.

27.title: The Daughters of Zelophehad; Joshua Commissioned
27.text: <sup>1</sup>Then drew near the daughters of Zelophehad the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, from the clans of Manasseh the son of Joseph. The names of his daughters were: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.<sup>2</sup>And they stood before Moses and before Eleazar the priest and before the chiefs and all the congregation, at the entrance of the tent of meeting, saying,<sup>3</sup>"Our father died in the wilderness. He was not among the company of those who gathered themselves together against the LORD in the company of Korah, but died for his own sin. And he had no sons.<sup>4</sup>Why should the name of our father be taken away from his clan because he had no son? Give to us a possession among our father's brothers."<sup>5</sup>Moses brought their case before the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD said to Moses,<sup>7</sup>"The daughters of Zelophehad are right. You shall give them possession of an inheritance among their father's brothers and transfer the inheritance of their father to them.<sup>8</sup>And you shall speak to the people of Israel, saying, 'If a man dies and has no son, then you shall transfer his inheritance to his daughter.<sup>9</sup>And if he has no daughter, then you shall give his inheritance to his brothers.<sup>10</sup>And if he has no brothers, then you shall give his inheritance to his father's brothers.<sup>11</sup>And if his father has no brothers, then you shall give his inheritance to the nearest kinsman of his clan, and he shall possess it. And it shall be for the people of Israel a statute and rule, as the LORD commanded Moses.'"<sup>12</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Go up into this mountain of Abarim and see the land that I have given to the people of Israel.<sup>13</sup>When you have seen it, you also shall be gathered to your people, as your brother Aaron was,<sup>14</sup>because you rebelled against my word in the wilderness of Zin when the congregation quarreled, failing to uphold me as holy at the waters before their eyes." (These are the waters of Meribah of Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin.)<sup>15</sup>Moses spoke to the LORD, saying,<sup>16</sup>"Let the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation<sup>17</sup>who shall go out before them and come in before them, who shall lead them out and bring them in, that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd."<sup>18</sup>So the LORD said to Moses, "Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him.<sup>19</sup>Make him stand before Eleazar the priest and all the congregation, and you shall commission him in their sight.<sup>20</sup>You shall invest him with some of your authority, that all the congregation of the people of Israel may obey.<sup>21</sup>And he shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before the LORD. At his word they shall go out, and at his word they shall come in, both he and all the people of Israel with him, the whole congregation."<sup>22</sup>And Moses did as the LORD commanded him. He took Joshua and made him stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation,<sup>23</sup>and he laid his hands on him and commissioned him as the LORD directed through Moses.
27.overview:
Chapter 27 holds two stories that, at first, seem unrelated: a daughters' appeal for inheritance, and the commissioning of Israel's next leader. But both turn on the same theme — the future of the people of God, the securing of the inheritance and the leadership that will bring them into it. As the new generation prepares to enter Canaan, God settles both who will inherit and who will lead.

The daughters of Zelophehad come forward with a bold and righteous appeal. Their father died without sons, and under the prevailing custom his name and inheritance would vanish. So five women stand before Moses, the priest, and the whole congregation and ask for their father's inheritance. It is a stunning act of courage and faith — faith, indeed, in the very promise of the land they have not yet entered. And God's verdict is striking: “The daughters of Zelophehad are right.” Wenham notes the dignity God grants these women; their claim is honored, the law is amended to provide for them, and the value of every person before God is upheld. Far from being marginalized, they are vindicated by the Lord himself. Their faith that God would surely give the land was so certain that they staked their future on it.

Then God turns to the matter of succession. Moses is told to go up the mountain and see the land — but, because of his sin at Meribah, he will not enter it. The pathos is deep: the great leader who endured forty years of grumbling will glimpse the land from afar but die outside it. Yet Moses' final concern is not for himself but for the people — “that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd” (v. 17). So God appoints Joshua, “a man in whom is the Spirit,” and Moses lays his hands on him. Ferguson notes the gospel resonance: the shepherd's heart of Moses, and the name Joshua — Yeshua, the Hebrew form of “Jesus.” The Joshua who would lead the people into the earthly rest points to the greater Joshua, Jesus, who leads his people into the true and eternal rest that Moses, and the law, could never give (Heb 4:8–9).
27.theology:
God hears the faithful appeal. The daughters of Zelophehad, bold in faith, are vindicated by God himself. He honors the overlooked and secures the inheritance for those who trust his promise.

The limit of the law. Moses sees the land but cannot enter it. The law-giver cannot bring the people into rest, pointing beyond himself to a greater Leader.

The greater Joshua. Spirit-filled Joshua leads Israel into the land, foreshadowing Jesus, who leads his people into the true and eternal rest (Heb 4:8–9).
27.examples:
Then: God vindicated the daughters' faithful appeal and secured their inheritance, then commissioned Spirit-filled Joshua to shepherd the people into the land Moses could only see from afar.

Now: God hears the bold faith of the overlooked and secures your inheritance in Christ. And the greater Joshua, Jesus, leads you into the eternal rest the law could never give. You will never be left as sheep without a shepherd.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Five sisters, the daughters of Zelophehad, come before Moses with a bold and reasonable plea. Their father died leaving no sons; should his name and inheritance simply vanish? They ask for a share among their father’s brothers. Moses brings their case before the LORD, and God rules in their favor: “The daughters of Zelophehad are right.” A precedent is set, and the dignity and inheritance rights of women are written into the law of Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s ruling (“The daughters of Zelophehad are right,” v.7) establishes a lasting statute protecting the inheritance rights of daughters where there is no son — a striking dignity granted to women in the ancient world. It shows that God’s justice hears the appeal of the voiceless, and that his law is not indifferent to the vulnerable (cf. Ps 68:5). Moses’ habit of bringing hard cases “before the LORD” (v.5) models a leadership that seeks God’s will rather than ruling by mere precedent or preference.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: five sisters with no brother and no power brought their case to God, and God himself declared them right — their inheritance secured.

Now: God still hears the appeal of those the world overlooks, and his justice is never indifferent to the vulnerable. Bring your hard cases “before the LORD” (v.5), as Moses did.

verseByVerse.quote: Then drew near the daughters of Zelophehad the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, from the clans of Manasseh the son of Joseph. The names of his daughters were: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. And they stood before Moses and before Eleazar the priest and before the chiefs and all the congregation, at the entrance of the tent of meeting, saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then drew near the daughters of Zelophehad… and they stood before Moses and before Eleazar the priest and before the chiefs and all the congregation, at the entrance of the tent of meeting.

Stage that scene properly, because everything in the passage depends on it. The plains of Moab, the whole nation assembled, the leadership drawn up at the door of the tabernacle: Moses, the high priest, and the tribal chiefs of Israel. Every person with standing in that gathering is a man. And out of the crowd walk five unmarried women with no father, no brothers, no legal representative and no precedent, and they keep walking until they are at the front.

Note that the text names them, twice — here and in the census a chapter earlier. Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, Tirzah. Not the daughters of Zelophehad as a group but five women with five names, listed as carefully as any chief in the muster roll. And they drew near, which is the word Numbers uses for approaching God at the tent. They did not send a message or lobby an uncle. They came to the front and stood there in the silence until somebody asked them what they wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: "Our father died in the wilderness. He was not among the company of those who gathered themselves together against the LORD in the company of Korah, but died for his own sin. And he had no sons. Why should the name of our father be taken away from his clan because he had no son? Give to us a possession among our father's brothers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What they say is a piece of careful legal reasoning, and they have plainly thought about it for a long time. Our father died in the wilderness. He was not among the company of those who gathered themselves together against the LORD in the company of Korah, but died for his own sin. And he had no sons.

Three moves, in order. First, he died under the general sentence — one of the generation condemned at Kadesh, no better and no worse than six hundred thousand others. Second, and this is the crucial one, he was not with Korah: Korah’s rebellion carried a forfeiture, and they are ruling out the one ground on which the claim could have been refused. Third, he left no sons, which under the custom of every nation around them meant the family was finished. They have anticipated the objection before it is raised.

And then the plea, which is not what a modern reader expects. Not we have nowhere to live. Not this is unfair to us. Why should the name of our father be taken away from his clan? In Israel land and name were one thing. To hold no portion was to have no place in the covenant people, no entry in the map of the twelve tribes, and after a generation no memory. They are not litigating for property. They are fighting for a dead man’s place among the people of God.

Consider also what they are fighting over. Nobody in that assembly has crossed the Jordan. Not one acre of Canaan is in Israelite hands; there is a river, and walls, and armies on the far side. These five women are pressing a claim to a specific field in a country nobody has set foot in, because they believe God will give it. That is faith of a very practical kind — the sort that makes arrangements. Set your own praying beside it. Do you ask God for things you have already begun to plan for, or only for things you would be quietly unsurprised not to receive?

verseByVerse.quote: Moses brought their case before the LORD. And the LORD said to Moses, "The daughters of Zelophehad are right. You shall give them possession of an inheritance among their father's brothers and transfer the inheritance of their father to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses brought their case before the LORD.

Six words, and a great deal of a man in them. Moses is the lawgiver of Israel. He has spoken with God face to face. He is, at this moment, the single most competent human being alive on the question of what the law of Israel requires — and he does not know the answer, and he says so by his actions. He does not improvise a ruling to protect his authority. He does not tell them the matter is settled. He takes their case up the hill.

Anyone who leads anything should read that verse twice. The temptation of office is never to be wrong; it is to appear to know. And the greatest leader in the Old Testament handled a question he could not answer by admitting it and going to God with it.

Then the verdict, and it is startling in its bluntness: The daughters of Zelophehad are right. God does not merely permit their request or make a compassionate exception. He says they are right — that their reading of what the covenant required was correct, and that the assembled leadership of Israel had simply not thought it through. Five women with no standing had understood the mind of God on a point of law better than the chiefs of the twelve tribes. It will not be the last time in Scripture that the people with no standing turn out to have seen furthest: God chose what is low and despised in the world… so that no human being might boast in the presence of God (1 Cor. 1:28–29).

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall speak to the people of Israel, saying, 'If a man dies and has no son, then you shall transfer his inheritance to his daughter. And if he has no daughter, then you shall give his inheritance to his brothers. And if he has no brothers, then you shall give his inheritance to his father's brothers. And if his father has no brothers, then you shall give his inheritance to the nearest kinsman of his clan, and he shall possess it. And it shall be for the people of Israel a statute and rule, as the LORD commanded Moses.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now watch what God does with the answer. He could have granted the petition and moved on. Instead: And you shall speak to the people of Israel, saying, “If a man dies and has no son, then you shall transfer his inheritance to his daughter…” — and there follows a complete order of succession, daughter, brothers, uncles, nearest kinsman, a statute and rule for the whole nation for ever.

One family’s grievance becomes permanent law. Because five women were brave enough to walk to the front of an assembly, every daughter in Israel for the next thousand years had a right she would not otherwise have had. God did not make them a special case; he made them the occasion of a statute. That is characteristic of him. He does not merely relieve the person in front of him; he alters the arrangements so that the next person never has to ask.

And notice where the chain of succession ends: the nearest kinsman of his clan, and he shall possess it. Israel’s whole law of inheritance runs down to a relative close enough and willing enough to take a lost family’s portion and keep it in the family. That is the institution that will save a widow in Bethlehem when Boaz stands up in the gate for Ruth, and it is the picture the New Testament reaches for when it explains what the Son of God did about the inheritance we had forfeited: he had to be made like his brothers in every respect (Heb. 2:17). A kinsman was needed. He became one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–23 — Joshua Appointed to Succeed Moses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Moses to climb a mountain and look at the land he will not enter, for his time is near. Moses’ response is beautiful: not self-pity, but concern for the people — that they not be “as sheep that have no shepherd.” God appoints Joshua, a man “in whom is the Spirit,” and Moses lays his hands on him before all the people. The leader who cannot enter the land makes sure the people are not left leaderless.
verseByVerse.theology: Moses’ prayer that Israel not be “as sheep that have no shepherd” (v.17) is the very compassion Jesus felt for the crowds (Matt 9:36) and answered by being the Good Shepherd (John 10:11). Joshua, “a man in whom is the Spirit” (v.18), is God’s provision of continuity — the work is bigger than any one servant. The laying on of hands (v.23) commissions and empowers. Above all, the passage points to the true Joshua (the same name as “Jesus”) who leads his people into the promised rest (Heb 4:8-9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: knowing he would die outside the land, Moses’ first thought was for the flock — that they have a shepherd — and God provided Joshua.

Now: we have the Shepherd who never dies, Jesus — whose very name is Joshua — who leads his people all the way into the promised rest (Heb 4:8-9; John 10:11).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Go up into this mountain of Abarim and see the land that I have given to the people of Israel. When you have seen it, you also shall be gathered to your people, as your brother Aaron was, because you rebelled against my word in the wilderness of Zin when the congregation quarreled, failing to uphold me as holy at the waters before their eyes." (These are the waters of Meribah of Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go up into this mountain of Abarim and see the land that I have given to the people of Israel. When you have seen it, you also shall be gathered to your people, as your brother Aaron was.

Consider the timing, because the writer has put these two paragraphs side by side deliberately. Moses has just spent a morning securing five women’s title to fields in a country he has been forbidden to enter. He settled the inheritance law of a land he will never own a foot of. And the moment the case is closed, God tells him to climb a hill and look at it and die.

There is severity in this and there is real tenderness, and both must be kept. The severity is stated without softening: because you rebelled against my word… failing to uphold me as holy at the waters before their eyes. One episode, decades of faithfulness either side of it, and the sentence stands. God is not sentimental about his own glory, least of all when it is his friends who obscure it.

But look at what he does give. He does not simply say you shall die. He says see the land… when you have seen it. Moses is taken up and shown the whole thing — Gilead, Dan, Naphtali, Judah, the Negeb, the plain of Jericho, right to the sea (Deut. 34:1–3). He is refused the possession and granted the view, and then he is gathered to his people, which is Scripture’s quiet word for a homecoming and not merely a burial. So the man is denied Canaan and given something else in the same breath. And fourteen centuries later Peter, James and John look up on a mountain and there he is, inside the land at last, in glory, talking with Jesus about his departure (Luke 9:30–31). God’s no to Moses was real, and it was not the last word he ever spoke to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke to the LORD, saying, "Let the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation who shall go out before them and come in before them, who shall lead them out and bring them in, that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man has just been told the date of his own death. Read what he says next.

Let the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation who shall go out before them and come in before them, who shall lead them out and bring them in, that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd.

Not one word about himself. No appeal against the sentence, no request that his own sons be considered — and they are never considered, by him or by God. His entire concern is that this exasperating, ungrateful, murmuring nation, which has broken his heart for forty years and cost him the land, should not be left without someone to walk in front of them. That is the measure of the man, and it explains why God trusted him with them.

Notice the title he uses: the God of the spirits of all flesh. He is asking the only one who knows what is inside every human being to choose, because a man cannot see far enough into another man to make this appointment safely. And notice what he asks for: not an administrator, not a general, but someone who goes out before them — a leader whose place is in front, taking first whatever is coming.

That phrase, sheep that have no shepherd, does not stay in Numbers. It becomes the standing indictment of Israel’s failed leaders in the prophets (Ezek. 34:5), and then one day a man stands on a hillside in Galilee looking at a crowd, and he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd (Matt. 9:36). Moses prayed this prayer for one generation and God answered it for one generation with Joshua. He answered it finally, for every generation, in the one who said I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). Moses asked for a man who would go out before the flock. God sent a Shepherd who went out before them all the way to a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD said to Moses, "Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Make him stand before Eleazar the priest and all the congregation, and you shall commission him in their sight. You shall invest him with some of your authority, that all the congregation of the people of Israel may obey. And he shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before the LORD. At his word they shall go out, and at his word they shall come in, both he and all the people of Israel with him, the whole congregation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. The qualification named is not experience, though Joshua had forty years of it, nor courage, though he had stood alone with Caleb against a nation. It is that the Spirit is in him. And the ceremony is a public one: he is made to stand before Eleazar and the whole congregation, commissioned in their sight, with Moses’ hands laid on him — the first ordination in Israel, and the pattern the church still follows when it sets men apart with the laying on of hands (Acts 6:6; 1 Tim. 4:14).

Then a phrase that repays attention: You shall invest him with some of your authority. Some. Not all. Joshua receives a real commission and a diminished one. Moses spoke with God face to face, as a man speaks to his friend (Exod. 33:11); Joshua must go and stand in front of the priest, who will inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before the LORD — the Urim being the means, kept in the high priest’s breastpiece, by which Israel sought a yes or no from God on a decision. Joshua will not have direct access. He will have to ask through somebody else.

So the authority Moses held alone is deliberately split in two, prophet and priest, and never again given whole to one man in Israel. That is not an accident of administration; it is a gap left open on purpose. The office of the one who both speaks God’s word and stands in God’s presence for the people was left vacant for fourteen centuries — until a man walked out of the Jordan who was Prophet, Priest and King at once, and needed nobody to inquire for him, because the word he spoke was his own.

And the name should not be passed over. Joshua is Yehoshua, the LORD saves — the same name, in its later form, that an angel would give to a child in Nazareth. Hebrews makes the comparison explicit and then leaves it deliberately unfinished: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on (Heb. 4:8). One Joshua took them into Canaan. The other takes his people into rest.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses did as the LORD commanded him. He took Joshua and made him stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation, and he laid his hands on him and commissioned him as the LORD directed through Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Moses did as the LORD commanded him. He took Joshua and made him stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation, and he laid his hands on him and commissioned him as the LORD directed through Moses.

Sit with what that cost. Moses is a dying man being told to hand over, in public, with his own hands, to the person who will do the one thing he has wanted for forty years and been refused. Every step of the ceremony is a rehearsal of his own exclusion. He walks Joshua to the front. He puts his hands on his head. He says the words. The whole nation watches. And Scripture records not a syllable of reluctance — no qualification, no wistful speech about what might have been, no attempt to keep a little of the authority back for the time he has left. Moses did as the LORD commanded him.

Two men are handed something in this chapter that they were not entitled to under the ordinary arrangements: five women who should have inherited nothing, and a servant who should not have followed Moses. And the same chapter takes from the greatest man in Israel the one thing he most wanted. God gives to those with no claim and withholds from the man with every claim, and in both directions he is entirely good, and in both directions the outcome was better than the recipients could see at the time. Moses did not enter Canaan; he entered glory. And he never lost the flock — he handed them to a Joshua, and God would one day hand them to another.

28.title: The Continual Offerings: The Rhythm of Worship
28.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Command the people of Israel and say to them, 'My offering, my food for my food offerings, my pleasing aroma, you shall be careful to offer to me at its appointed time.'<sup>3</sup>And you shall say to them, This is the food offering that you shall offer to the LORD: two male lambs a year old without blemish, day by day, as a regular offering.<sup>4</sup>The one lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the other lamb you shall offer at twilight;<sup>5</sup>also a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with a quarter of a hin of beaten oil.<sup>6</sup>It is a regular burnt offering, which was ordained at Mount Sinai for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>Its drink offering shall be a quarter of a hin for each lamb. In the Holy Place you shall pour out a drink offering of strong drink to the LORD.<sup>8</sup>The other lamb you shall offer at twilight. Like the grain offering of the morning, and like its drink offering, you shall offer it as a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>9</sup>"On the Sabbath day, two male lambs a year old without blemish, and two tenths of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, and its drink offering:<sup>10</sup>this is the burnt offering of every Sabbath, besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.<sup>11</sup>"At the beginnings of your months, you shall offer a burnt offering to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish;<sup>12</sup>also three tenths of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, for each bull, and two tenths of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, for the one ram;<sup>13</sup>and a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering for every lamb; for a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>14</sup>Their drink offerings shall be half a hin of wine for a bull, a third of a hin for a ram, and a quarter of a hin for a lamb. This is the burnt offering of each month throughout the months of the year.<sup>15</sup>Also one male goat for a sin offering to the LORD; it shall be offered besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.<sup>16</sup>"On the fourteenth day of the first month is the LORD's Passover,<sup>17</sup>and on the fifteenth day of this month is a feast. Seven days shall unleavened bread be eaten.<sup>18</sup>On the first day there shall be a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work,<sup>19</sup>but offer a food offering, a burnt offering to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old; see that they are without blemish;<sup>20</sup>also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil; three tenths of an ephah shall you offer for a bull, and two tenths for a ram;<sup>21</sup>a tenth shall you offer for each of the seven lambs;<sup>22</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, to make atonement for you.<sup>23</sup>You shall offer these besides the burnt offering of the morning, which is for a regular burnt offering.<sup>24</sup>In the same way you shall offer daily, for seven days, the food of a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. It shall be offered besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.<sup>25</sup>And on the seventh day you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work.<sup>26</sup>"On the day of the firstfruits, when you offer a grain offering of new grain to the LORD at your Feast of Weeks, you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work,<sup>27</sup>but offer a burnt offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old;<sup>28</sup>also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for each bull, two tenths for one ram,<sup>29</sup>a tenth for each of the seven lambs;<sup>30</sup>with one male goat, to make atonement for you.<sup>31</sup>Besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, you shall offer them and their drink offering. See that they are without blemish.
28.overview:
As the new generation prepares to enter the land, God renews the calendar of worship — the daily, weekly, monthly, and seasonal offerings that are to mark the rhythm of their life with him. Chapter 28 may read like a liturgical timetable, but beneath it lies a glorious truth: God means to be worshipped continually, woven into the very fabric of time. Morning and evening, week by week, season by season, the smoke of sacrifice was to rise without ceasing before the LORD.

The foundation is the “regular” or “continual” burnt offering: two lambs every single day, one in the morning and one at twilight, never interrupted. Calvin noted that this daily, unbroken sacrifice taught Israel that fellowship with God is not occasional but constant; the people were to begin and end each day at the altar. Worship was not a weekly event but the heartbeat of daily existence. Upon this daily foundation are layered the Sabbath offerings, the monthly new-moon offerings, and the great festival offerings — an ascending rhythm of devotion that filled the whole calendar with the worship of God.

The book of Hebrews gathers up all these endless offerings and shows their meaning: “Every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Heb 10:11–12). The very endlessness of the daily offerings preached their insufficiency; they had to be repeated because they could never finish the work. But there is a deeper gospel note still: the continual offering points to the continual intercession of Christ, our Great High Priest, who “always lives to make intercession” for us (Heb 7:25). MacArthur observed that the unceasing smoke of the morning and evening lamb is a shadow of the unceasing advocacy of Christ before the Father. Day and night, without interruption, our Mediator presents his finished sacrifice and pleads for his people. The altar never went cold, because the love of God never sleeps.
28.theology:
Continual worship. The daily morning and evening offering taught that fellowship with God is constant, not occasional. Worship is to be the heartbeat of daily life, the altar never going cold.

The continual intercession of Christ. The unceasing offering foreshadows our Great High Priest who always lives to make intercession (Heb 7:25), pleading his finished sacrifice without interruption.

Time made holy. Day, week, month, and season are all consecrated to God. The whole calendar is filled with worship, anticipating eternal worship before the throne.
28.examples:
Then: Israel offered the continual morning and evening sacrifice, with added offerings for Sabbaths, new moons, and feasts, so that worship filled the whole calendar.

Now: The endless offerings that could never finish are fulfilled in Christ's one finished sacrifice and his unceasing intercession. Day and night your Mediator pleads for you. Let your life be a continual offering of worship to the God who never sleeps.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As the new generation prepares for the land, God restates the rhythm of worship that must mark their life there. It begins with the daily offering: a lamb every morning and a lamb every evening, without fail. Before anything else in the calendar of worship, there is this steady heartbeat — day in, day out, a continual offering rising to God. Worship is not only for festivals; it is the daily air God’s people breathe.
verseByVerse.theology: The tamid, the continual daily offering (vv.3-6), frames all of Israel’s worship: before the feasts and festivals, there is the unbroken daily approach to God, morning and evening. It teaches that communion with God is meant to be constant, not occasional (cf. Ps 55:17; Dan 6:10). The daily lamb points to “the Lamb of God” (John 1:29), whose one offering is continually sufficient, so that we now “draw near” at every hour (Heb 10:19-22).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: every single morning and evening, without fail, a lamb was offered — the steady heartbeat of a life lived before God.

Now: worship is daily, not just Sunday. “Evening and morning... I utter my complaint” (Ps 55:17). Through the once-for-all Lamb, we draw near continually (Heb 10:22).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Command the people of Israel and say to them, 'My offering, my food for my food offerings, my pleasing aroma, you shall be careful to offer to me at its appointed time.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a single animal is named, God says whose these offerings are, and he says it four times in one sentence: My offering, my food for my food offerings, my pleasing aroma, you shall be careful to offer to me at its appointed time.

That is the frame for the next two chapters, and without it the whole calendar reads as religious bookkeeping. This is not Israel arranging her devotional life. It is a covenant Lord telling his people what belongs to him and when he expects it. Worship in Scripture is never first an expression of how the worshipper feels; it is a response to a claim.

The language of my food and a pleasing aroma is startling and needs a word, because Israel’s neighbours meant it literally — their gods were fed by sacrifice and grew hungry if the temples closed. Scripture flatly denies that: If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine (Ps. 50:12). God takes the vocabulary of the ancient altar and empties it of the pagan idea while keeping the warmth: the smoke rising is not nourishment, it is pleasure. He likes it. And Paul lifts the very phrase onto the cross — Christ gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Eph. 5:2) — and then, astonishingly, onto a gift sent to a missionary in prison, a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God (Phil. 4:18).

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall say to them, This is the food offering that you shall offer to the LORD: two male lambs a year old without blemish, day by day, as a regular offering. The one lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the other lamb you shall offer at twilight; also a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with a quarter of a hin of beaten oil. It is a regular burnt offering, which was ordained at Mount Sinai for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. Its drink offering shall be a quarter of a hin for each lamb. In the Holy Place you shall pour out a drink offering of strong drink to the LORD. The other lamb you shall offer at twilight. Like the grain offering of the morning, and like its drink offering, you shall offer it as a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The foundation of the whole calendar is the smallest item in it: two male lambs a year old without blemish, day by day, as a regular offering — one in the morning, one at twilight, with flour and oil and wine, every day without exception.

The Hebrew word behind regular is tamid, continual. This is the offering that never stopped. Whatever else was happening in Israel — harvest, war, plague, a good king or a bad one — a lamb died at dawn and a lamb died at dusk, and the smoke went up from that altar for the best part of a thousand years. Every feast in the rest of the chapter is described as being offered besides the regular burnt offering. The special days are added on top; they never replace the daily one.

Two things follow, one for the eye and one for the heart. For the eye: this is what it cost, in an economy of subsistence farmers, to keep an altar burning — seven hundred and thirty lambs a year, for centuries, and none of them ever finished the matter, which is precisely the argument of Hebrews. Every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down (Heb. 10:11–12). The old altar never sat down because the work was never done.

And for the heart: the day of the believer is still bracketed the same way. Israel began at the altar and ended at the altar, and the ordinary hours in between were lived under a sacrifice at each end. Nobody in that camp had to wonder, at three in the afternoon, whether God had been approached that day. He had, at dawn, and he would be again at dusk. That is exactly the assurance Christians have, permanently — not because we keep the rhythm, but because he always lives to make intercession (Heb. 7:25). The tamid never stopped in Israel. It has not stopped now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Sabbath and New Moon Offerings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the Sabbath the offering is doubled; at the start of each month, a fuller set of sacrifices marks the new moon. Worship is layered through time — daily, weekly, monthly — so that the passing of days and seasons is continually consecrated to God. The calendar itself becomes an act of worship.
verseByVerse.theology: The Sabbath and new-moon offerings (vv.9-15) build worship into the very structure of time — day, week, and month all marked by approach to God. Israel’s calendar was designed so that time itself belonged to the LORD, its rhythms punctuated by worship. It trains God’s people to sanctify their days, receiving each season from his hand (cf. Ps 31:15, “my times are in your hand”).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the week and the month, not just the day, were consecrated to God — time itself woven through with worship.

Now: we still sanctify our time to God — the Lord’s Day set apart, our weeks and seasons received from his hand. “My times are in your hand” (Ps 31:15).

verseByVerse.quote: "On the Sabbath day, two male lambs a year old without blemish, and two tenths of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, and its drink offering: this is the burnt offering of every Sabbath, besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering. "At the beginnings of your months, you shall offer a burnt offering to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish; also three tenths of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, for each bull, and two tenths of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, for the one ram; and a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering for every lamb; for a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. Their drink offerings shall be half a hin of wine for a bull, a third of a hin for a ram, and a quarter of a hin for a lamb. This is the burnt offering of each month throughout the months of the year. Also one male goat for a sin offering to the LORD; it shall be offered besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the rhythm widens. On the Sabbath the offering is doubled; at the start of each month the new moon brings bulls, a ram, seven lambs and a goat for a sin offering.

Take the Sabbath first, because it corrects an instinct. The day of rest is the day when worship increases, not the day it slackens. Ceasing from work was never an end in itself; it was cleared ground, made so that a nation could turn its attention to God without the plough in the way. A Sabbath spent resting from labour and also resting from God is not what the commandment was for.

Then the months. God claims the day at dawn and dusk, the week at its seventh day, the month at its first, and — in the next chapter — the year at its climax. By the end of the calendar there is no unit of time left unconsecrated. That is the deliberate design: Israel could not look at a sunrise, a week, a moon or a season without being reminded whose it was. Isaiah takes the same two markers and throws them forward to the end of all things: From new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath, all flesh shall come to worship before me, declares the LORD (Isa. 66:23).

And note the small, sober detail in the monthly list: one male goat for a sin offering to the LORD. Every month, at the very moment Israel marked the turning of the season, sin was named again. The calendar of a redeemed people still had a sin offering built into every month of it, because God knew exactly what a month does to his people, and made provision in advance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–31 — Passover, Unleavened Bread, and Firstfruits
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The annual feasts follow: Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, remembering the exodus; and the Feast of Weeks (Firstfruits) at the wheat harvest. Each has its appointed offerings. Israel’s year is a gospel story told again and again — redemption remembered, the harvest of the Spirit anticipated — all fulfilled in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: The feasts are prophecy on a calendar (cf. Lev 23). Passover proclaims redemption by the lamb’s blood — “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Cor 5:7); Unleavened Bread calls for purity, sweeping out the leaven of sin (1 Cor 5:8); Firstfruits/Weeks becomes Pentecost, the firstfruits of the Spirit’s harvest (Acts 2). The prescribed offerings surround each feast with worship, but their deepest meaning is the redemption they rehearse, now accomplished in Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: year by year Israel kept Passover and Firstfruits, retelling the story of their rescue and thanking God for the harvest.

Now: our Passover Lamb has been sacrificed (1 Cor 5:7); the firstfruits of the Spirit have come (Acts 2). The feasts pointed forward; in Christ they are kept.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the fourteenth day of the first month is the LORD's Passover, and on the fifteenth day of this month is a feast. Seven days shall unleavened bread be eaten. On the first day there shall be a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work, but offer a food offering, a burnt offering to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old; see that they are without blemish; also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil; three tenths of an ephah shall you offer for a bull, and two tenths for a ram; a tenth shall you offer for each of the seven lambs; also one male goat for a sin offering, to make atonement for you. You shall offer these besides the burnt offering of the morning, which is for a regular burnt offering. In the same way you shall offer daily, for seven days, the food of a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. It shall be offered besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering. And on the seventh day you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the fourteenth day of the first month is the LORD’s Passover, and the seven days of Unleavened Bread follow it. The year opens where the nation opened — with the night in Egypt when the blood was on the doorposts and the destroyer passed over.

Israel’s calendar is a memory system. The feasts are not seasonal festivals with a religious varnish; every one of them re-tells a saving act, so that a child born forty years after the exodus could not grow up without living through it annually. And the New Testament takes both halves of this spring feast and applies them to the church in a single verse: Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump… For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor. 5:7).

The two belong together in that order and must not be reversed. First the lamb, then the leaven: the sacrifice is not the reward for the housecleaning, it is the reason for it. Israel did not earn Passover by removing the yeast; she removed the yeast because the lamb had died and she was leaving Egypt in the morning. A Christian who tries to put the purging first has misread the feast, and will spend his life sweeping.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the day of the firstfruits, when you offer a grain offering of new grain to the LORD at your Feast of Weeks, you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work, but offer a burnt offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old; also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for each bull, two tenths for one ram, a tenth for each of the seven lambs; with one male goat, to make atonement for you. Besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, you shall offer them and their drink offering. See that they are without blemish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with the day of the firstfruits… your Feast of Weeks — fifty days after Passover, when the first of the new grain was brought in and offered before any of it was eaten.

The logic of firstfruits is one of the loveliest in the Old Testament. A farmer brings the first sheaf, not the last, and he brings it before the harvest is safely in. It is an act of confidence: this handful is a pledge that the rest is coming. Which is precisely the word Paul reaches for at the empty tomb — Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor. 15:20). The resurrection of Jesus is not an isolated marvel. It is the first sheaf of a harvest, carried into the presence of God as the guarantee of every believer’s body coming up out of the ground behind him.

And the date should not be missed. Fifty days after the Passover at which Jesus died, on the very day Israel had brought her first grain for fourteen centuries, the Spirit fell in Jerusalem and three thousand were gathered in one afternoon (Acts 2:41). Israel kept harvesting a field. God was keeping an appointment.

The last words of the chapter are the same words that opened it: Besides the regular burnt offering… See that they are without blemish. After every feast, back to the daily lamb; and every animal, on every day of the year, without a flaw. For a thousand years Israel searched her flocks for something perfect enough to offer, and never once found anything better than a lamb. Then John the Baptist stood by a river, looked at his cousin walking toward him, and said the sentence the whole calendar had been waiting for: Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29).

29.title: The Feasts of the Seventh Month: The Climax of the Worship Year

It is a day for you to blow the trumpets,<sup>2</sup>and you shall offer a burnt offering, for a pleasing aroma to the LORD: one bull from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish;<sup>3</sup>also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for the bull, two tenths for the ram,<sup>4</sup>and one tenth for each of the seven lambs;<sup>5</sup>with one male goat for a sin offering, to make atonement for you;<sup>6</sup>besides the burnt offering of the new moon, and its grain offering, and the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offering, according to the rule for them, for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>"On the tenth day of this seventh month you shall have a holy convocation and afflict yourselves.
