You shall not do any ordinary work, and you shall keep a feast to the LORD seven days.<sup>13</sup>And you shall offer a burnt offering, a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD, thirteen bulls from the herd, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old; they shall be without blemish;<sup>14</sup>and their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for each of the thirteen bulls, two tenths for each of the two rams,<sup>15</sup>and a tenth for each of the fourteen lambs;<sup>16</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>17</sup>"On the second day twelve bulls from the herd, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>18</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>19</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offerings.<sup>20</sup>"On the third day eleven bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>21</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>22</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>23</sup>"On the fourth day ten bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>24</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>25</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>26</sup>"On the fifth day nine bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>27</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>28</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>29</sup>"On the sixth day eight bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>30</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>31</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offerings.<sup>32</sup>"On the seventh day seven bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>33</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>34</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offering.<sup>35</sup>"On the eighth day you shall have a solemn assembly. You shall not do any ordinary work,<sup>36</sup>but you shall offer a burnt offering, a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD: one bull, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>37</sup>and the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bull, for the ram, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>38</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>39</sup>"These you shall offer to the LORD at your appointed feasts, in addition to your vow offerings and your freewill offerings, for your burnt offerings, and for your grain offerings, and for your drink offerings, and for your peace offerings."<sup>40</sup>So Moses told the people of Israel everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
29.overview:
Chapter 29 continues the festal calendar into the seventh month, the holiest and fullest month of Israel's worship year, crowded with sacred days: the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the great Feast of Booths. If chapter 28 established the daily rhythm, chapter 29 brings the calendar to its glorious climax. The sheer abundance of sacrifice in this month — hundreds of animals offered over its festivals — proclaims the lavishness of worship that God's redemption deserves.

At the center stands the Day of Atonement (vv. 7–11), the most solemn day of the year, when the people afflicted their souls and the high priest made atonement for the sins of the whole nation. Even here, in Numbers' summary of the offerings, there is the “sin offering of atonement” — the costly reminder that a sinful people can dwell with a holy God only through blood. The book of Hebrews lavishes attention on this day, showing that the high priest entered the Most Holy Place once a year with blood that could never finally cleanse, until Christ “entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Heb 9:12).

The month ends with the Feast of Booths, the great harvest festival of joy, when Israel dwelt in temporary shelters to remember their wilderness pilgrimage. Over its seven days, an astonishing number of bulls were offered — seventy in all, which the rabbis took to represent the nations of the world. Ferguson and others note the missionary hint: even Israel's joy looked outward, anticipating the day when the nations would be gathered to worship the God of Israel. The whole sweep of the chapter — trumpets sounding, atonement made, harvest joy overflowing — points to the consummation, when the trumpet shall sound (1 Cor 15:52), atonement is complete in Christ, and the redeemed from every nation dwell forever in the booth of God's presence. “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Rev 21:3). The worship year of Numbers is a rehearsal for eternity.
29.theology:
The lavishness of worship. The abundance of offerings in the seventh month proclaims that God's redemption deserves extravagant, joyful worship, the climax of the whole sacred calendar.

Atonement at the center. The Day of Atonement points to Christ, who entered once for all with his own blood to secure eternal redemption (Heb 9:12), fulfilling what the annual day could only foreshadow.

A rehearsal for eternity. Trumpets, atonement, and the ingathering of booths anticipate the last trumpet, the finished work of Christ, and the nations gathered to dwell forever with God.
29.examples:
Then: Israel's holiest month overflowed with worship — trumpets sounding, atonement made for the nation, and the joyful Feast of Booths recalling their pilgrimage and looking to the harvest.

Now: The trumpet will sound, atonement is finished in Christ who entered once for all, and the redeemed of every nation will dwell forever in the booth of God's presence. Worship the God whose every feast was a rehearsal for the eternal joy now yours in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Trumpets and the Day of Atonement
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The seventh month is the holiest of the year, and it opens with the Feast of Trumpets — a day of blast and holy convocation — and reaches its solemn peak on the Day of Atonement, when Israel afflicts itself and the high priest makes atonement for all the people. The trumpet calls the nation to attention; the Day of Atonement cleanses it. Worship rises from joyful summons to solemn cleansing.
verseByVerse.theology: The trumpet blast (v.1) summons God’s people to holy attention — a call to wake and gather before God (cf. the last trumpet, 1 Cor 15:52; 1 Thess 4:16). The Day of Atonement (vv.7-11), with its affliction of soul and its sin offering, is the yearly cleansing of the nation (Lev 16), fulfilled once for all when Christ “entered... by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Heb 9:12). The extra offerings here surround with worship what the blood accomplishes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the trumpet woke the nation to worship, and the Day of Atonement humbled and cleansed them before God.

Now: the trumpet still summons (1 Cor 15:52), and the atonement is finished — Christ has entered the true sanctuary with his own blood, once for all (Heb 9:12). We are cleansed, and we wait for the trumpet.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the first day of the seventh month you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work. It is a day for you to blow the trumpets, and you shall offer a burnt offering, for a pleasing aroma to the LORD: one bull from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish; also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for the bull, two tenths for the ram, and one tenth for each of the seven lambs; with one male goat for a sin offering, to make atonement for you; besides the burnt offering of the new moon, and its grain offering, and the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offering, according to the rule for them, for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh month is to Israel’s year what the seventh day is to her week, and it opens with noise. It is a day for you to blow the trumpets.

Numbers has already explained what the trumpets are for. They summon the congregation, they sound the alarm in war, and they are blown over the sacrifices so that they may be a reminder of you before your God (10:9–10). A trumpet is not music; it is an interruption. It cuts across whatever a man is doing and tells him that something has begun and he is required.

So the holiest month of the year does not open with a sacrifice or a fast but with a sound, ordering a whole nation to stop and pay attention. And the trumpet keeps that meaning right to the end of the Bible. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable (1 Cor. 15:52); the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God (1 Thess. 4:16). Every autumn for a thousand years Israel heard a blast over the camp and stopped what she was doing. One day a blast will go out over the whole earth, and every man who ever lived will stop what he is doing.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the tenth day of this seventh month you shall have a holy convocation and afflict yourselves. You shall do no work, but you shall offer a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma: one bull from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old: see that they are without blemish. And their grain offering shall be of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for the bull, two tenths for the one ram, a tenth for each of the seven lambs: also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the sin offering of atonement, and the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nine days later comes the most solemn day in the calendar: On the tenth day of this seventh month you shall have a holy convocation and afflict yourselves. You shall do no work.

Afflict yourselves is the standing phrase for fasting and self-humbling, and this is the only fast the law of Moses ever commanded. Once a year the whole nation stopped eating and stopped working and did nothing but attend to its own sin while the high priest went in behind the curtain with blood. Leviticus 16 gives the ceremony; Numbers here simply adds the offerings — because by this point in the Bible the reader is expected to know what the tenth of the seventh month means.

Hebrews builds its central argument out of this one day. Into the second room only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood (Heb. 9:7). Once a year, one man, one room, and a curtain to be got past — the Holy Spirit indicating, the writer says, that the way in was not yet open. And then the contrast: we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19–20).

Notice the two commands of the day, and what has become of them. Israel was told to afflict herself and to do no work. The affliction has been answered — the sin that had to be mourned every autumn has been dealt with once — and the resting has been deepened, for the Christian rests from his own work not for a day but permanently: whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his (Heb. 4:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The seventh month closes with the joyful Feast of Booths (Tabernacles), a seven-day celebration of the harvest and of God’s care during the wilderness years, when Israel lived in tents. It required more offerings than any other feast — an abundance of worship to match an abundance of joy. Having remembered redemption and been cleansed, the people now rejoice before God, dwelling in booths, giving thanks for the harvest and for his faithfulness through the wilderness.
verseByVerse.theology: Booths (Tabernacles) celebrated both the ingathering harvest and God’s faithful care in the wilderness (Lev 23:42-43), Israel dwelling in temporary shelters as a reminder of their pilgrim past. Its lavish offerings express overflowing gratitude. It looked forward to the final ingathering, and Jesus used its great water ceremony to cry, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). Ultimately it anticipates the day God will “tabernacle” with his people forever (Rev 21:3), when the harvest is home and the pilgrimage is done.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: for seven joyful days Israel dwelt in booths, giving thanks for the harvest and remembering God’s care through the desert.

Now: we are still pilgrims in temporary tents (2 Cor 5:1), giving thanks, longing for the day God will dwell with us forever and “wipe away every tear” (Rev 21:3-4). The great feast is still ahead.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work, and you shall keep a feast to the LORD seven days. And you shall offer a burnt offering, a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD, thirteen bulls from the herd, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old; they shall be without blemish; and their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for each of the thirteen bulls, two tenths for each of the two rams, and a tenth for each of the fourteen lambs; also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five days after the fast, the greatest celebration of the year begins. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month… you shall keep a feast to the LORD seven days — the Feast of Booths, with an offering on the first day of thirteen bulls, two rams and fourteen lambs, the largest single day of sacrifice in the calendar.

The command that gives the feast its name is in Leviticus: You shall dwell in booths for seven days… that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt (Lev. 23:42–43). For one week every year the entire nation moved out of its houses and slept in shelters of branches.

Consider who was being told to do this and when. A generation on the edge of a land full of houses they did not build and vineyards they did not plant (Deut. 6:10–11) is instructed to camp out, annually, for ever. God knew exactly what settled prosperity does to memory. He built into the calendar one week a year in which a wealthy farmer had to sleep under leaves and look at the sky and remember that his family once had nothing and was carried. It is the same instinct behind the Lord’s Supper — a small, physical, repeated act designed to keep a people from forgetting the thing that saved them.

And this is the feast that the writer to the Hebrews says Abraham never came out of. He lived in tents… for he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God (Heb. 11:9–10). One week a year, Israel was made to live like a pilgrim again — which is, in fact, what she still was, and what the church has never stopped being.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the second day twelve bulls from the herd, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offerings. "On the third day eleven bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering. "On the fourth day ten bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering and its drink offering. "On the fifth day nine bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering. "On the sixth day eight bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offerings. "On the seventh day seven bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then eighteen verses in which almost nothing changes. Second day, twelve bulls. Third day, eleven. Then ten, nine, eight, and seven — with the same two rams, the same fourteen lambs, the same goat for a sin offering, and the same grain and drink offerings in the prescribed quantities, day after day.

Only one thing moves, and it moves deliberately: the bulls count down, thirteen to seven, and the total across the week is exactly seventy. Jewish interpreters noticed that long ago and connected it with the seventy nations of Genesis 10, reading the week as Israel offering on behalf of the whole world. Numbers does not say so, and no honest reader should claim more than the text gives. But the instinct behind the reading is thoroughly biblical, because this is the feast that Zechariah says the nations will one day come and keep: Then everyone who survives of all the nations that have come against Jerusalem shall go up year after year to worship the King, the LORD of hosts, and to keep the Feast of Booths (Zech. 14:16).

The repetition itself teaches something. This is the most expensive week in Israel’s year by a wide margin — a herd of cattle burned in seven days by a nation of subsistence farmers, at the busiest point of the harvest — and it is the week of greatest joy. Costly worship and glad worship are not opposites here. They are the same week. Israel gave away more in the feast of rejoicing than at any other time in the year, and nobody in the text suggests that this made the rejoicing harder.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the eighth day you shall have a solemn assembly. You shall not do any ordinary work, but you shall offer a burnt offering, a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD: one bull, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish, and the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bull, for the ram, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the eighth day you shall have a solemn assembly. The seven days of booths are over, and an extra day is added — quieter, smaller, one bull instead of thirteen, a final gathering before everyone goes home.

By the time of Jesus this last day had acquired a ceremony that is not in the law but had become the emotional summit of the whole year. Each morning of the feast a priest went down to the pool of Siloam, filled a golden pitcher, and carried it back up through the city to pour out at the base of the altar, while the people sang from Isaiah: With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation (Isa. 12:3). It was a prayer for rain and a remembrance of the water from the rock in the wilderness — the very rock of Numbers 20.

And John records what happened one year at that moment. On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ‘Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water’” (John 7:37–38). At the very second the water hit the stones, in front of the whole nation, he stood up and said that he was what the ceremony had been asking for. And a few hours later, with the great lamps of the feast burning in the temple court, he said, I am the light of the world (John 8:12).

That is what the eighth day was for. A thousand years of pouring out water at the foot of an altar, and then a carpenter from Nazareth stood up in the middle of it and offered himself to anyone in the crowd who was thirsty. The feast had been asking a question every autumn since Moses. He answered it out loud.

verseByVerse.quote: "These you shall offer to the LORD at your appointed feasts, in addition to your vow offerings and your freewill offerings, for your burnt offerings, and for your grain offerings, and for your drink offerings, and for your peace offerings." So Moses told the people of Israel everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The calendar closes with a sentence that keeps it from becoming a cage: These you shall offer to the LORD at your appointed feasts, in addition to your vow offerings and your freewill offerings.

Everything in chapters 28 and 29 is the floor, not the ceiling. God has specified the minimum — what is due, when it is due, and how much — and then in one clause makes room for everything a grateful Israelite might want to bring beyond it. A freewill offering is precisely what its name says: nobody commanded it and nobody counted it. The appointed times do not exhaust worship; they establish it, and then leave the heart free to go further.

That balance is easy to lose in either direction. A believer can reduce his whole relationship with God to the appointed times and never once come to him uninvited; or he can despise the appointed times as mere routine and end up worshipping only when he feels like it. Israel was given both, in the same paragraph, and told to keep both.

And the last verse is the quietest in the chapter: So Moses told the people of Israel everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses. Everything, just as. Not a summary, not the interesting parts. An old man with weeks to live stood in front of a nation and read out every bull, every ram, every tenth of an ephah, exactly as it had been given to him. The whole calendar of Israel’s worship reached the people because one man refused to abbreviate what God had said.

30.title: Vows: The Integrity of the Word
30.text: <sup>1</sup>Moses spoke to the heads of the tribes of the people of Israel, saying, "This is what the LORD has commanded.<sup>2</sup>If a man vows a vow to the LORD, or swears an oath to bind himself by a pledge, he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.<sup>3</sup>"If a woman vows a vow to the LORD and binds herself by a pledge, while within her father's house in her youth,<sup>4</sup>and her father hears of her vow and of her pledge by which she has bound herself and says nothing to her, then all her vows shall stand, and every pledge by which she has bound herself shall stand.<sup>5</sup>But if her father opposes her on the day that he hears of it, no vow of hers, no pledge by which she has bound herself shall stand. And the LORD will forgive her, because her father opposed her.<sup>6</sup>"If she marries a husband, while under her vows or any thoughtless utterance of her lips by which she has bound herself,<sup>7</sup>and her husband hears of it and says nothing to her on the day that he hears, then her vows shall stand, and her pledges by which she has bound herself shall stand.<sup>8</sup>But if, on the day that her husband comes to hear of it, he opposes her, then he makes void her vow that was on her, and the thoughtless utterance of her lips by which she bound herself. And the LORD will forgive her.<sup>9</sup>(But any vow of a widow or of a divorced woman, anything by which she has bound herself, shall stand against her.)<sup>10</sup>And if she vowed in her husband's house or bound herself by a pledge with an oath,<sup>11</sup>and her husband heard of it and said nothing to her and did not oppose her, then all her vows shall stand, and every pledge by which she bound herself shall stand.<sup>12</sup>But if her husband makes them null and void on the day that he hears them, then whatever proceeds out of her lips concerning her vows or concerning her pledge of herself shall not stand. Her husband has made them void, and the LORD will forgive her.<sup>13</sup>Any vow and any binding oath to afflict herself, her husband may establish, or her husband may make void.<sup>14</sup>But if her husband says nothing to her from day to day, then he establishes all her vows or all her pledges that are upon her. He has established them, because he said nothing to her on the day that he heard of them.<sup>15</sup>But if he makes them null and void after he has heard of them, then he shall bear her iniquity."<sup>16</sup>These are the statutes that the LORD commanded Moses about a man and his wife and about a father and his daughter while she is in her youth within her father's house.
30.overview:
From the grand sweep of the festal calendar, the book turns to something quieter but no less serious: the binding nature of vows. “If a man vows a vow to the LORD… he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.” In a world where words are cheap and promises are broken without a second thought, this chapter recovers the weight and holiness of human speech. A vow made before God is not to be trifled with; the word, once given, binds.

The chapter is built on the conviction that words matter to God because God himself is a God of his word. He is the God who keeps his promises, whose “yes” is yes and whose covenant cannot be broken. And his people, made in his image and redeemed by his faithfulness, are to be people of their word. Calvin noted that to break a vow made to God is to lie before the One who is Truth itself; the integrity of our speech reflects the integrity of the God we serve. Ecclesiastes warns, “When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it… It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay” (Eccl 5:4–5).

The remaining laws address vows made by women within the household — a daughter under her father, a wife under her husband — and the provision that the head of the household may, on the day he hears it, affirm or annul the vow. To modern ears this sounds strange, but Wenham notes the protective intent: it guards against rash or harmful vows and locates accountability within the covenant household, while still upholding the seriousness of every word given to God. The deeper point endures for all: our words are sacred, and faithfulness in speech is a mark of those who belong to the faithful God. Jesus would later intensify this: “Let what you say be simply 'Yes' or 'No'” (Matt 5:37), calling his people to such transparent integrity that elaborate oaths become unnecessary. The Christian's word should be as good as a vow, because the Christian serves the God who cannot lie.
30.theology:
The sanctity of speech. A vow to God binds; the word once given must be kept. Faithfulness in speech reflects the integrity of the God of truth, who keeps every promise.

Words matter to God. Because God is a God of his word, his people are to be people of their word. To break a vow to God is to lie before the One who is Truth itself.

Yes be yes. Jesus calls his people to such transparent integrity (Matt 5:37) that their plain word is as trustworthy as any oath, for they serve the God who cannot lie.
30.examples:
Then: Israel was bound to keep every vow made to the LORD, with the household head able to confirm or annul vows made by dependents, guarding against rash pledges.

Now: Your word is sacred because you serve the God whose word never fails. Let your yes be yes and your no be no. Be a person of integrity in speech, reflecting the faithfulness of the God who cannot lie and keeps every promise in Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A chapter on the seriousness of vows. When a person makes a vow to the LORD, “he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.” The chapter also addresses vows made by women within a household, and the role of a father or husband in confirming or annulling them. Behind all the detail is one great principle: words spoken to God are binding, and integrity of speech matters to him.
verseByVerse.theology: “He shall not break his word” (v.2) — a vow to God is a serious, binding thing (cf. Deut 23:21-23; Eccl 5:4-5, “When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it”). God cares deeply about the integrity of our speech; a promise made in his hearing is not to be treated lightly. The provisions for annulling a woman’s vow within the household reflect the ordered authority structures of that society, yet the governing principle — keep your word to God — is timeless. Jesus deepens it: let your “yes be yes” (Matt 5:37), so that vows become almost unnecessary among truthful people.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a vow to God was no light matter; the one who made it was bound to keep it.

Now: God still weighs our words. “Let what you say be simply Yes or No” (Matt 5:37). Be slow to promise, and faithful to perform — for “it is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay” (Eccl 5:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke to the heads of the tribes of the people of Israel, saying, "This is what the LORD has commanded. If a man vows a vow to the LORD, or swears an oath to bind himself by a pledge, he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a man vows a vow to the LORD, or swears an oath to bind himself by a pledge, he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.

Start here, because everything else in the chapter is measured against it. For a man there is no release clause. None. No father can annul his vow, no elder can review it, no circumstance is listed under which it lapses. He said it; he does it. The chapter that is so often read as a restriction on women opens by binding men absolutely and giving them no way out at all.

And the reason is not that words are magic but that God keeps his. A vow was made to the LORD, and to break it was to imply that the God who hears is the kind of God who lets things slide, which is a lie about his character told with your life. Ecclesiastes puts it bluntly: It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay (Eccl. 5:5).

Scripture has some grim examples of what the absence of a release clause meant. Jephthah made a rash vow and destroyed his own daughter with it (Judg. 11:30–39). Herod made a drunken promise at a birthday party and beheaded John the Baptist rather than look weak in front of his guests (Mark 6:23–26). Both men would have been better off breaking their word. Both had built their identity on being men whose word was iron, and it cost somebody else everything. There is a kind of pride that dresses up as integrity, and it is at its most dangerous when it is refusing to admit it should never have spoken.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a woman vows a vow to the LORD and binds herself by a pledge, while within her father's house in her youth, and her father hears of her vow and of her pledge by which she has bound herself and says nothing to her, then all her vows shall stand, and every pledge by which she has bound herself shall stand. But if her father opposes her on the day that he hears of it, no vow of hers, no pledge by which she has bound herself shall stand. And the LORD will forgive her, because her father opposed her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the qualified cases, and they need reading slowly because they are misread constantly. If a woman vows a vow to the LORD… while within her father’s house in her youth, and her father hears and says nothing, the vow stands. If he opposes her on the day that he hears of it, it does not stand — and the LORD will forgive her, because her father opposed her.

Four things govern how this works, and every one of them limits the father rather than the daughter. First, the window is a single day. He must speak the day he hears; after that the vow is fixed and he has no power over it for the rest of his life. Second, it applies only to an unmarried girl still living in her father’s household — verse 16 says so explicitly — which in that economy meant a young woman with no property of her own, who might well have pledged goods, land or labour that were not hers to pledge. Third, he can only annul; he can never impose a vow on her. And fourth, the release is not grudging: the LORD will forgive her. God will not hold a woman liable for a promise she has been prevented from keeping.

Read plainly, the provision is a protection. But be honest about what it is: household law for a society organised around the family as a single economic unit, not a pronouncement on the worth of women. And it should be read three chapters after the one where five women with no legal standing walked to the front of the assembly, and God said the daughters of Zelophehad are right, and changed the inheritance law of Israel because of them. The same book, the same Lawgiver, within a few weeks. Whatever chapter 30 is doing, contempt is not available as a reading.

verseByVerse.quote: "If she marries a husband, while under her vows or any thoughtless utterance of her lips by which she has bound herself, and her husband hears of it and says nothing to her on the day that he hears, then her vows shall stand, and her pledges by which she has bound herself shall stand. But if, on the day that her husband comes to hear of it, he opposes her, then he makes void her vow that was on her, and the thoughtless utterance of her lips by which she bound herself. And the LORD will forgive her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second case is a woman who marries while a vow is already on her. The husband gets the same single day and the same limited power, and the same gracious clause follows: the LORD will forgive her.

But notice the phrase the law uses for what she may have said: any thoughtless utterance of her lips by which she has bound herself. The Hebrew describes a word blurted out — spoken quickly, before the cost was counted. That is the human situation the whole chapter is built around, and everyone knows it from the inside. Things get promised at gravesides and in hospital corridors and on the worst night of a person’s life. If you will only do this, I will never again… A vow made in that state can be sincere, godly in its motive, and completely unpayable.

The law does not mock such promises, and neither does it treat them as unbreakable chains. It provides that somebody who loves the person, and who is standing outside the emotion of the moment, may look at the vow within a day and say: this must not be allowed to bind you for forty years. And God underwrites the release himself. That is not a loophole; it is mercy written into the statute book, and it tells us something about the God who wrote it. He is not looking for ways to hold his people to their worst moments.

verseByVerse.quote: (But any vow of a widow or of a divorced woman, anything by which she has bound herself, shall stand against her.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
But any vow of a widow or of a divorced woman, anything by which she has bound herself, shall stand against her.

The verse sits in brackets and is easily skimmed, and it carries more than it looks. A widow and a divorced woman have no father over them and no husband beside them. Nobody can annul what they say. Their word goes straight to God and binds them exactly as a man’s does.

There are two sides to that and both are true. On one side it is a statement of full standing. Whatever the surrounding culture thought of a woman alone, the law of Israel treats her promises as the promises of an adult who answers to God directly, with no intermediary required. On the other side, it is a real exposure: she has nobody to catch a rash word before it hardens, and the law says so without softening it.

Which is precisely why Scripture is so insistent that these are the people God watches over personally. Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation (Ps. 68:5). The woman with no one standing over her in this chapter is the woman God repeatedly names as his own particular concern. She is not less protected. Her protection has simply been taken up by somebody higher than a household.

verseByVerse.quote: And if she vowed in her husband's house or bound herself by a pledge with an oath, and her husband heard of it and said nothing to her and did not oppose her, then all her vows shall stand, and every pledge by which she bound herself shall stand. But if her husband makes them null and void on the day that he hears them, then whatever proceeds out of her lips concerning her vows or concerning her pledge of herself shall not stand. Her husband has made them void, and the LORD will forgive her. Any vow and any binding oath to afflict herself, her husband may establish, or her husband may make void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third case is a wife who makes a vow while in her husband’s house. The pattern holds — one day to object, silence means consent, annulment brings forgiveness — and then verse 13 tells us the kind of vow chiefly in view: Any vow and any binding oath to afflict herself.

That changes the picture considerably. The vows the law is most concerned about are vows of self-denial: fasting, abstaining, going without. So the authority described here is overwhelmingly a power to stop somebody from hurting herself, not a power to stop her serving God. A wife who in a season of grief or guilt pledges to fast for a year, or to give away what the household needs to live on, can be relieved of it. This is not the muzzling of devotion. It is a brake on self-punishment.

And that guard is still needed. Religious people do this — they try to settle an account with God by taking something away from themselves, and the more ashamed they are the heavier the pledge. The gospel has no place for it. Such regulations indeed have an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh (Col. 2:23). God did not ask for Israel’s self-affliction as the price of anything, and the law itself provided a way out of the vows in which she offered it.

verseByVerse.quote: But if her husband says nothing to her from day to day, then he establishes all her vows or all her pledges that are upon her. He has established them, because he said nothing to her on the day that he heard of them. But if he makes them null and void after he has heard of them, then he shall bear her iniquity." These are the statutes that the LORD commanded Moses about a man and his wife and about a father and his daughter while she is in her youth within her father's house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two clauses close the chapter, and they are the two that decide how it should be read.

The first: if her husband says nothing to her from day to day, then he establishes all her vows. Silence is not neutrality. By saying nothing he has ratified it, as surely as if he had said so aloud, and the text is emphatic — he has established them, because he said nothing. A man who simply declines to engage with what is happening in his own household has not thereby avoided responsibility for it. He has taken it on by default.

The second is the sentence the whole chapter turns on: But if he makes them null and void after he has heard of them, then he shall bear her iniquity. If he lets the vow stand and then later prevents her from keeping it, the guilt does not fall on her. It transfers to him. He carries it.

Everything in the chapter that sounds like unchecked male authority dies on that clause. The power is bounded by a single day, it can only release and never impose, and its misuse is charged to the man’s account before God. That is the biblical shape of headship wherever it appears — never a licence, always a liability, and always measured by Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Eph. 5:25).

And read that last phrase once more, on its own: he shall bear her iniquity. A husband carrying his wife’s guilt because of a promise. Here it happens through his failure; there was another Husband who did it by deliberate choice, who heard what his bride had bound herself to and could not pay, and did not annul it but assumed it — the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isa. 53:6). Israel could be released from a rash vow by a word from a man who loved her. The church was released from an unpayable debt by a Man who took it and bore it out of the world.

31.title: War Against Midian: Holy War and the Seriousness of Sin
31.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Avenge the people of Israel on the Midianites. Afterward you shall be gathered to your people."<sup>3</sup>So Moses spoke to the people, saying, "Arm men from among you for the war, that they may go against Midian to execute the LORD's vengeance on Midian.<sup>4</sup>You shall send a thousand from each of the tribes of Israel to the war."<sup>5</sup>So there were provided, out of the thousands of Israel, a thousand from each tribe, twelve thousand armed for war.<sup>6</sup>And Moses sent them to the war, a thousand from each tribe, together with Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, with the vessels of the sanctuary and the trumpets for the alarm in his hand.<sup>7</sup>They warred against Midian, as the LORD commanded Moses, and killed every male.<sup>8</sup>They killed the kings of Midian with the rest of their slain, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, the five kings of Midian. 31.overview:
Chapter 31 records God's judgment on Midian, the nation that, on Balaam's counsel, had seduced Israel into the deadly sin of Peor (ch. 25). This is one of the hardest chapters in Numbers for modern readers, a chapter of holy war, and it must be read with care, reverence, and trembling. The Midianites were not innocent bystanders; they had deliberately set out to corrupt and destroy the people of God through enticement to idolatry and immorality, and twenty-four thousand Israelites had died as a result. The judgment here is God's response to a calculated assault on his covenant people and his holiness.

We must resist two errors. The first is to recoil and judge God by the squeamish sentiments of our age. Sproul reminded us that the real wonder is not that God judges sin but that he is so patient with it; the holiness of God means that sin is far more serious than we imagine. The second error is to make this a charter for human violence; it is not. These were unique, God-commanded acts of judgment in redemptive history, never a model for the church, whose warfare is “not against flesh and blood” (Eph 6:12) and whose weapons are the gospel and prayer.

Tellingly, the narrative also notes the death of Balaam himself (v. 8) — the seer who could not curse Israel but taught Balak how to seduce them now perishes in the judgment. And the chapter devotes great attention to the purification of the warriors and the plunder: those who fought must remain outside the camp seven days and be cleansed, for even righteous warfare brings the defilement of death. Ferguson notes the sobering lesson: contact with death defiles, and the people of God must be purified. The chapter's deepest note is the holiness of God and the deadly seriousness of sin — the very sin that no curse could impose but seduction nearly destroyed. It drives us to the cross, where the judgment our sin deserves fell on Christ, that we might be cleansed and spared.
31.theology:
The seriousness of sin. The judgment on Midian responds to a calculated seduction that nearly destroyed Israel. God's holiness means sin is graver than we dare imagine; the wonder is his patience.

Death defiles. Even righteous warriors must be purified, for contact with death contaminates. Holiness is required to dwell with God, pointing to the deeper cleansing of Christ's blood.

The corrupter judged. Balaam, who could not curse but taught seduction, perishes in the judgment. The one who loves the wages of unrighteousness reaps its end (2 Pet 2:15).
31.examples:
Then: God judged Midian for seducing Israel into the sin of Peor; Balaam perished, the warriors were purified from death's defilement, and a portion of the spoil was given to the LORD.

Now: Read this trembling text in its redemptive setting, never as a charter for human violence. Let it teach the deadly seriousness of sin and the holiness of God, and drive you to the cross, where the judgment your sin deserved fell on Christ that you might be spared and cleansed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s command from chapter 25 is now carried out: Israel goes to war against Midian for their part in the seduction at Peor. It is a solemn act of divine judgment on those who deliberately schemed to destroy God’s people through idolatry and immorality. Among the slain is Balaam himself — the prophet who could not curse Israel, and so taught Balak how to corrupt them, now falls under the judgment his own counsel unleashed.
verseByVerse.theology: The Midian war is judgment on those who engineered Israel’s fall at Peor (25:16-18; 31:16). Balaam’s death (v.8) closes his tragic story: gifted with true oracles, he loved “gain from wrongdoing” (2 Pet 2:15) and perished with God’s enemies. These conquest-era judgments belong to a unique moment in redemptive history and must not be made a template for the church, whose “weapons... are not of the flesh” (2 Cor 10:4); yet they reveal the real severity of God against those who deliberately lead his people into sin (Luke 17:1-2).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the seducers of Peor faced God’s judgment, and Balaam, who sold his gift for profit, died among them.

Now: we war not with swords but against sin and the schemes that corrupt (Eph 6:12; 2 Cor 10:4). Yet the warning stands: God takes with deadly seriousness those who lead his people astray, and the love of gain can ruin even a gifted soul (2 Pet 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Avenge the people of Israel on the Midianites. Afterward you shall be gathered to your people." So Moses spoke to the people, saying, "Arm men from among you for the war, that they may go against Midian to execute the LORD's vengeance on Midian. You shall send a thousand from each of the tribes of Israel to the war." So there were provided, out of the thousands of Israel, a thousand from each tribe, twelve thousand armed for war. And Moses sent them to the war, a thousand from each tribe, together with Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, with the vessels of the sanctuary and the trumpets for the alarm in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Avenge the people of Israel on the Midianites. Afterward you shall be gathered to your people. This is the last thing God gives Moses to do. And notice how Moses passes the order on: not avenge yourselves but to execute the LORD’s vengeance on Midian. It is not tribal payback. It is a judicial sentence, and the judge is God.

The size of the force says the same thing. A thousand from each of the tribes of Israel, twelve thousand armed for war — out of a nation that had just counted 601,730 fighting men. Two per cent. Nobody sends two per cent of an army to conquer a country. This is not annexation and it is not plunder-hunting; it is a punitive expedition of fixed size against a fixed target, and the men are sent out with Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, with the vessels of the sanctuary and the trumpets for the alarm in his hand. A priest goes at the head of it carrying holy things. Whatever else this is, Israel is not being turned loose.

And the target is precise. Moab began the seduction at Shittim (25:1) and Moab is not touched, because God had forbidden it: Do not harass Moab or contend with them in battle (Deut. 2:9). Midian is judged, because Midian is the party that worked with Balaam to engineer the whole thing. God’s judgments in Scripture are not indiscriminate sweeps. They land where the guilt is and stop.

verseByVerse.quote: They warred against Midian, as the LORD commanded Moses, and killed every male. They killed the kings of Midian with the rest of their slain, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, the five kings of Midian. And they also killed Balaam the son of Beor with the sword. And the people of Israel took captive the women of Midian and their little ones, and they took as plunder all their cattle, their flocks, and all their goods. All their cities in the places where they lived, and all their encampments, they burned with fire, and took all the spoil and all the plunder, both of man and of beast. Then they brought the captives and the plunder and the spoil to Moses, and to Eleazar the priest, and to the congregation of the people of Israel, at the camp on the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The battle is reported in a sentence, and then the text pauses over the names of the dead: Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, the five kings of Midian. One of them ought to be familiar. Zur was the tribal head of a father’s house in Midian and the father of Cozbi, the woman Phinehas killed in the tent (25:15). The men at the top of Midian had put their own daughters into the plan.

And then, almost in passing: And they also killed Balaam the son of Beor with the sword.

Stop there, because that is the end of a story we have been following for ten chapters. This is the man who stood on a mountain, with the Spirit of God upon him, and said Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his (23:10). He announced that he was going home to his own people (24:25). He did not go. He was still in Midian, months later, on the payroll, and when the sword came through he was standing in the enemy line against the nation he had blessed four times. He could not sell a curse, so he sold a strategy instead, and the fee killed him.

The New Testament will not let him be forgotten, and never mentions him without the money: he loved gain from wrongdoing (2 Pet. 2:15), men abandon themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error (Jude 11), and the risen Christ names the teaching of Balaam as a live danger in a Christian congregation (Rev. 2:14). A man may hold flawless doctrine, speak genuine prophecy, and receive real revelation, and still be lost — because none of that is the same as loving God more than what God’s enemies are offering to pay.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The returning soldiers, and all they have touched in war, must be purified before re-entering the camp. Contact with death has made them unclean, and even the spoil must pass through fire and water. Even a war fought at God’s command leaves the mark of death that must be cleansed. Nothing touched by death comes casually back into the presence of a holy God.
verseByVerse.theology: Even a divinely commanded war leaves death-defilement that must be cleansed (vv.19-24; cf. Num 19). This preserves the truth that death is the enemy and the wage of sin (Rom 6:23), never something God’s people handle lightly. The purification of the soldiers and the spoil by water and fire underscores that holiness is not suspended even in righteous conflict, and that all who have touched death need cleansing before they draw near.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: even victorious soldiers, and their plunder, had to be cleansed of death’s defilement before returning to the camp.

Now: we never handle sin and death casually, even when we must confront them. The one who has touched what defiles comes back to be cleansed (1 John 1:7-9), for holiness is never suspended.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses and Eleazar the priest and all the chiefs of the congregation went to meet them outside the camp. And Moses was angry with the officers of the army, the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, who had come from service in the war. Moses said to them, "Have you let all the women live? Behold, these, on Balaam's advice, caused the people of Israel to act treacherously against the LORD in the incident of Peor, and so the plague came among the congregation of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The army comes home victorious and Moses is furious. Have you let all the women live?

Verse 16 is the hinge of the whole chapter and it must be read before the next two verses are read: Behold, these, on Balaam’s advice, caused the people of Israel to act treacherously against the LORD in the incident of Peor, and so the plague came among the congregation of the LORD.

This is the sentence that finally tells us what happened at Shittim. It was not an accident of proximity, a case of soldiers and local women. It was a designed operation. Balaam worked out that a people God has blessed cannot be cursed from outside but can be corrupted from within, sold the plan to Midian, and Midian executed it — using their own women, including a chief’s daughter, as the instrument. Twenty-four thousand Israelites died. The women in front of Moses at this moment are not a random civilian population. They are, in the text’s own account, the operatives of that plan.

That does not make what follows easy. It does mean that a reader who treats this as an unprovoked massacre of bystanders has not read verse 16.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore, kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman who has known man by lying with him. But all the young girls who have not known man by lying with him keep alive for yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the two hardest verses in the book of Numbers, and there is no honest way to make them comfortable. Now therefore, kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman who has known man by lying with him. But all the young girls who have not known man by lying with him keep alive for yourselves.

If that appals you, you are reading it correctly. Scripture does not ask anyone to feel nothing here, and a commentary that hurries past it, or explains it away, or pretends the words say something gentler than they do, is not serving the reader. So let us take it slowly and say what can honestly be said, and then say plainly what cannot.

First, what the passage is. This is herem — the devoted judgment of God on a particular people, at a particular moment, through a specific command, in the unrepeatable period when God was governing one nation directly as its king. It is dated, bounded and explicitly commanded, and Scripture never generalises it. The women judged are the ones verse 16 has just identified. The command is given to a levied force under a priest, not to a mob, and it is over within days.

Second, what the passage is not, and this cannot be said too strongly: it is not a model for anyone, anywhere, ever again. No church, nation, movement or individual has the authority Israel had here, and the New Testament removes the possibility explicitly. My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36). For though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:3–4). Every time in history that Christians have reached for this chapter to justify violence, they have been reading it against the plain teaching of their own Lord.

Third, the girls who were spared. Keep alive for yourselves reads horribly in English and needs its legal context, because Israel had one. The law that governs a woman taken captive in war is Deuteronomy 21:10–14, and it is unlike anything else in the ancient world: she is brought into the house, given a full month to mourn her father and mother, and may then be married — not used — and if the man does not want her she must be let go free, and he may never sell her or treat her as property, since you have humiliated her. That is the framework these girls entered. It is not our world and it is not painless, but it is a long way from what a modern reader instinctively assumes.

Fourth, the question underneath the question. What genuinely troubles us is not really Israel; it is God. Does God have the right to end human lives? He does, and he exercises it in every generation without asking us — every person who has ever lived has died at a time he appointed, and Scripture is entirely open about the fact that this is his prerogative and no one else’s: See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god beside me; I kill and I make alive (Deut. 32:39). What is unusual in Numbers 31 is not that God judges, but that he does it visibly, through a named instrument, on a dated afternoon, where we can watch. The judgments we do not see trouble us less only because we do not see them.

And here is where an honest reader is left. Abraham’s question stands and Scripture never withdraws it: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Gen. 18:25) — asked, notice, by a man arguing with God about the destruction of cities, and asked as a confidence rather than an accusation. We are not given a full account of this chapter. We are given something better: proof, from somewhere else, of what kind of God is doing the judging. He did not settle the question of his own justice by explaining Numbers 31. He settled it by coming himself, and standing under the judgment his own justice required, and dying of it — God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:8). A reader who cannot see the bottom of this chapter is being asked to trust the character of the One who bled at Calvary. That is not evasion. It is the only ground on which anybody has ever been able to stand and look at the severity of God without despair.

verseByVerse.quote: Encamp outside the camp seven days. Whoever of you has killed any person and whoever has touched any slain, purify yourselves and your captives on the third day and on the seventh day. You shall purify every garment, every article of skin, all work of goats' hair, and every article of wood." Then Eleazar the priest said to the men in the army who had gone to battle: "This is the statute of the law that the LORD has commanded Moses: only the gold, the silver, the bronze, the iron, the tin, and the lead, everything that can stand the fire, you shall pass through the fire, and it shall be clean. Nevertheless, it shall also be purified with the water for impurity. And whatever cannot stand the fire, you shall pass through the water. You must wash your clothes on the seventh day, and you shall be clean. And afterward you may come into the camp."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What comes next is easy to miss and morally enormous. The army has just carried out a God-commanded judgment, and God does not send them home as heroes. He sends them outside the camp. Encamp outside the camp seven days. Whoever of you has killed any person and whoever has touched any slain, purify yourselves and your captives on the third day and on the seventh day.

Seven days of exclusion, and the cleansing agent is the water made from the ashes of the red heifer in chapter 19 — the provision for defilement by death. Israel’s soldiers came back from obeying God and were unclean. Not guilty; unclean. There is no garland here, no parade, no suggestion that killing at God’s command left a man untouched by it. He had handled death, and death defiles whoever handles it, and he had to be washed before he could worship.

That single provision is one of the most humane things in the Old Testament, and it should be set against every triumphalist use this chapter has ever been put to. A religion that sends its soldiers home to a week outside the camp and a sprinkling of water is not a religion that glories in blood.

Eleazar adds the rule for the plunder: everything that can stand the fire, you shall pass through the fire… and whatever cannot stand the fire, you shall pass through the water. Gold, silver, bronze, iron, tin, lead — through the flame; everything else through the water. Nothing comes into the camp of God unpurified, and the test applied is the material’s own capacity to survive. Paul reaches for exactly this image for the day when every Christian’s work is examined: each one’s work will become manifest… because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done (1 Cor. 3:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The plunder of the war is carefully divided — half to the soldiers, half to the congregation — and from each a tribute is set apart for the LORD and the Levites. Then the officers, having found not one man missing from their ranks, bring a freewill offering of gold to the LORD in gratitude. Even the spoils of war are consecrated; even victory is met with worship and thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.theology: A portion of everything is set apart “as a contribution to the LORD” (vv.28-29) — even the spoils of war belong first to God, who gave the victory (cf. 1 Chr 29:14). The officers’ freewill offering after finding no soldier lost (vv.48-50) is thanksgiving for God’s protecting hand. Victory is received as grace and returned in worship; the God who wins the battle is given the glory and the firstfruits of its reward.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: not a single Israelite soldier had fallen, and the grateful officers brought their gold to the LORD in thanks for his protection.

Now: every victory, every safe deliverance, calls for worship and thanksgiving. What we receive from God’s hand we return to him in gratitude, for “from you comes all things, and of your own have we given you” (1 Chr 29:14).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Take the count of the plunder that was taken, both of man and of beast, you and Eleazar the priest and the heads of the fathers' houses of the congregation, and divide the plunder into two parts between the warriors who went out to battle and all the congregation. And levy for the LORD a tribute from the men of war who went out to battle, one out of five hundred, of the people and of the oxen and of the donkeys and of the flocks. Take it from their half and give it to Eleazar the priest as a contribution to the LORD. And from the people of Israel's half you shall take one drawn out of every fifty, of the people, of the oxen, of the donkeys, and of the flocks, of all the cattle, and give them to the Levites who keep guard over the tabernacle of the LORD." And Moses and Eleazar the priest did as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The division of the spoil is governed by two principles, and both of them are fairer than anybody would have arranged on their own.

First, the plunder is split into two parts between the warriors who went out to battle and all the congregation. Twelve thousand men did the fighting; half the proceeds go to the other five hundred and ninety thousand who stayed at home. That is a startling concession, and it is exactly the ruling David will make centuries later when his soldiers want to cut out the men who guarded the baggage: as his share is who goes down into the battle, so shall his share be who stays by the baggage; they shall share alike (1 Sam. 30:24). The people of God share the outcome of a work that only some of them were able to do.

Second, the tribute to God is levied unequally, and in the direction nobody would expect. The men who fought give one out of five hundred; the congregation who stayed home gives one drawn out of every fifty — ten times as much. The ones who bore the risk are taxed at a tenth of the rate of the ones who did not. God’s arithmetic takes account of what a thing cost the giver, which is precisely the principle Jesus applies while watching a widow put in two small coins: they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had (Mark 12:44).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the plunder remaining of the spoil that the army took was 675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, 61,000 donkeys, and 32,000 persons in all, women who had not known man by lying with him. And the half, the portion of those who had gone out in the army, numbered 337,500 sheep, and the LORD's tribute of sheep was 675. The cattle were 36,000, of which the LORD's tribute was 72. The donkeys were 30,500, of which the LORD's tribute was 61. The persons were 16,000, of which the LORD's tribute was 32 persons. And Moses gave the tribute, which was the contribution for the LORD, to Eleazar the priest, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the accounts, in full: 675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, 61,000 donkeys, and 32,000 captives, halved down the middle and the LORD’s tribute worked out to the animal — 675 sheep, 72 cattle, 61 donkeys, 32 persons.

Modern readers skim it. Consider instead who is doing the counting: you and Eleazar the priest and the heads of the fathers’ houses of the congregation. The lawgiver, the high priest and the tribal heads together, in public, with the figures written down to the last head of livestock. No single man handles it and nothing is taken on trust.

That is not incidental to the story of a religious community. It is exactly the standard Paul held himself to when carrying the church’s money: We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man (2 Cor. 8:20–21). Wherever God’s people handle wealth, the books are to be open. A ledger is a spiritual document.

verseByVerse.quote: From the people of Israel's half, which Moses separated from that of the men who had served in the army— now the congregation's half was 337,500 sheep, 36,000 cattle, and 30,500 donkeys, and 16,000 persons— from the people of Israel's half Moses took one of every 50, both of persons and of beasts, and gave them to the Levites who kept guard over the tabernacle of the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The congregation’s half is listed again with the same precision — 337,500 sheep, 36,000 cattle, 30,500 donkeys, 16,000 persons — and out of it Moses takes one in fifty and gave them to the Levites who kept guard over the tabernacle of the LORD.

The Levites did not fight, did not travel, and own no land anywhere in Israel; and out of a war they took no part in, they are given a portion. That is the pattern the whole book has been laying down. The tribe with no inheritance is provided for by the inheritance of everyone else, so that men can stand at the tabernacle full time and Israel can be a worshipping nation.

Paul draws a straight line from this arrangement to the support of gospel ministry, and does it without apology: Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple… In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Cor. 9:13–14). The provision made for the Levites out of the spoils of Midian is, in the New Testament’s own reading, the same provision a congregation makes when it supports its pastor.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the officers who were over the thousands of the army, the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, came near to Moses and said to Moses, "Your servants have counted the men of war who are under our command, and there is not a man missing from us. And we have brought the LORD's offering, what each man found, articles of gold, armlets and bracelets, signet rings, earrings, and beads, to make atonement for ourselves before the LORD." And Moses and Eleazar the priest received from them the gold, all crafted articles. And all the gold of the contribution that they presented to the LORD, from the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, was 16,750 shekels. (The men in the army had each taken plunder for himself.) And Moses and Eleazar the priest received the gold from the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and brought it into the tent of meeting, as a memorial for the people of Israel before the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officers come to Moses with a report and an offering, and both are remarkable.

The report first: Your servants have counted the men of war who are under our command, and there is not a man missing from us. Twelve thousand men went out against five kings and twelve thousand came back. They had counted, which is what commanders do after a battle, and the number matched. In an ancient war that is not luck and they did not think it was.

Then the offering, and it is the surprising part. Men who have won a total victory without a single casualty do not usually respond like this: we have brought the LORD’s offering, what each man found, articles of gold, armlets and bracelets, signet rings, earrings, and beads, to make atonement for ourselves before the LORD. Atonement. Not thanksgiving — atonement. They had lost nobody, and their instinct was that they needed covering.

These are the men who had spent a week outside the camp being sprinkled with the water for impurity, and they had understood what it meant. Coming home alive is not a verdict on your worthiness. Twenty-four thousand of their countrymen had died at Peor and these twelve thousand had not, and the difference was mercy and nothing else. So they emptied their pockets of the gold they had picked up on the battlefield and gave it away.

Sixteen thousand seven hundred and fifty shekels of it, brought into the tent of meeting, as a memorial for the people of Israel before the LORD. Not melted down, not spent, not made into anything — laid up in God’s house as a reminder. So the last act of the last war Moses ever ordered was a pile of enemy jewellery in the tabernacle, put there by soldiers who came home whole and could think of nothing to say about it except that they had been spared and had not earned it. There are worse epitaphs for a campaign, and there is no better posture for anybody who has come through something they did not deserve to come through.

32.title: The Tribes East of Jordan: The Danger of Settling for Less
32.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the people of Reuben and the people of Gad had a very great number of livestock. And they saw the land of Jazer and the land of Gilead, and behold, the place was a place for livestock.<sup>2</sup>So the people of Gad and the people of Reuben came and said to Moses and to Eleazar the priest and to the chiefs of the congregation,<sup>3</sup>"Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sebam, Nebo, and Beon,<sup>4</sup>the land that the LORD struck down before the congregation of Israel, is a land for livestock, and your servants have livestock."<sup>5</sup>And they said, "If we have found favor in your sight, let this land be given to your servants for a possession. Do not take us across the Jordan."<sup>6</sup>But Moses said to the people of Gad and to the people of Reuben, "Shall your brothers go to the war while you sit here?<sup>7</sup>Why will you discourage the heart of the people of Israel from going over into the land that the LORD has given them?<sup>8</sup>Your fathers did this, when I sent them from Kadesh-barnea to see the land.<sup>9</sup>For when they went up to the Valley of Eshcol and saw the land, they discouraged the heart of the people of Israel from going into the land that the LORD had given them.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD's anger was kindled on that day, and he swore, saying,<sup>11</sup>'Surely none of the men who came up out of Egypt, from twenty years old and upward, shall see the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, because they have not wholly followed me,<sup>12</sup>none except Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite and Joshua the son of Nun, for they have wholly followed the LORD.'<sup>13</sup>And the LORD's anger was kindled against Israel, and he made them wander in the wilderness forty years, until all the generation that had done evil in the sight of the LORD was gone.<sup>14</sup>And behold, you have risen in your fathers' place, a brood of sinful men, to increase still more the fierce anger of the LORD against Israel!<sup>15</sup>For if you turn away from following him, he will again abandon them in the wilderness, and you will destroy all this people."<sup>16</sup>Then they came near to him and said, "We will build sheepfolds here for our livestock, and cities for our little ones,<sup>17</sup>but we will take up arms, ready to go before the people of Israel, until we have brought them to their place. And our little ones shall live in the fortified cities because of the inhabitants of the land.<sup>18</sup>We will not return to our homes until each of the people of Israel has gained his inheritance.<sup>19</sup>For we will not inherit with them on the other side of the Jordan and beyond, because our inheritance has come to us on this side of the Jordan to the east."<sup>20</sup>So Moses said to them, "If you will do this, if you will take up arms to go before the LORD for the war,<sup>21</sup>and every armed man of you will pass over the Jordan before the LORD, until he has driven out his enemies from before him<sup>22</sup>and the land is subdued before the LORD; then after that you shall return and be free of obligation to the LORD and to Israel, and this land shall be your possession before the LORD.<sup>23</sup>But if you will not do so, behold, you have sinned against the LORD, and be sure your sin will find you out.<sup>24</sup>Build cities for your little ones and folds for your sheep, and do what you have promised."<sup>25</sup>And the people of Gad and the people of Reuben said to Moses, "Your servants will do as my lord commands.<sup>26</sup>Our little
